interaction.content: Thank you in advance!
Thank you.
Hello, I’m the counselor. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about today?
I’m a 46-year-old woman. I’d like to talk about my mother, who lives alone.
Thank you for your reply. So it’s about your mother. What’s been going on?

For about ten years my father had a stroke and was paralyzed, and my mother was caring for him at home, but he passed away a year ago. I think the caregiving fatigue is part of it, but she has various physical problems (with no clear cause). And it seems like when she’s at home she feels unwell, and when she goes out she feels a bit better. When she’s not feeling well, she says she can’t even go out, and she calls me in the middle of the night.
I see… That sounds really hard for both you and your mother. Does your mother live far away from you?
It’s about an hour by car from my place. I go to check on her about twice a month, and when I do she’s relatively okay.
I see. Maybe your mother feels more at ease when her daughter comes to see her. For you, in this situation right now, what would you say is your biggest concern?

When I’m busy and there’s a bit of a gap before I can get to my parents’ house, she calls and says she’s worn out and not feeling well. I wish I could go more often, but realistically I just can’t right now.
So you’re worried about your mother, but when you look at things realistically, it’s hard to increase how often you go to your parents’ place, and that’s weighing on you.
That’s right.
How do you think your mother is taking your father’s death?

She says that because my father was physically in so much pain, she feels relieved that he’s freed from his suffering and that she’s freed from the hardship of caregiving. She says she doesn’t feel lonely.
She really went through a lot, didn’t she. From your point of view, how does your mother seem? How do you think she’s feeling now?
My father and mother never really got along to begin with, so I think she really does feel like a burden has been lifted and she’s relieved.
So she’s feeling relieved. By the way, does your mother call you about things other than not feeling well?

She calls about little everyday problems, like how to use her smartphone or that an appliance isn’t working. I’ve told her it’s fine to call even if there’s nothing in particular, but it seems like she’s trying to hold back as much as she can.
I see. Does your mother have any neighbors she’s close with?
She does. But in the last few years there are fewer of them.
I see. So it’s also hard to rely on the neighbors. Have you talked with any home-care services or the local community support center?
No, I haven’t.
If you’re open to it, one option might be to contact the local government office where your parents’ home is and have a consultation there.
Thank you very much.
Thank you as well!

extra.topic_sub: 母の介護による身体的不調や精神的ストレス

interaction.content: Hello. I’m the counselor.
Hello. Thank you for seeing me!
To start, could you tell me your gender and age?
I’m a 21-year-old woman.
Thank you for answering my questions. What would you like to talk about today?
I want to take some distance from a friend. But she doesn’t seem to feel that way and keeps inviting me to hang out, so I’m not sure what to do.
I see. So you’d like to take some distance from your friend. I’d like to call you by a nickname, if that’s okay with you.
Please call me Mochi!
Thank you, Mochi. When you want to take some distance, but your friend keeps inviting you, how does that make you feel?
It’s this kind of unsettled feeling. If it were a friend I really like, I’d reply right away like, “If I’m free, I want to hang out,” but…
Mm-hmm, so it leaves you with that unsettled feeling. Your friend wants to hang out with you, Mochi. And when it’s a friend you like, spending time together is fun, isn’t it.
Yeah, that’s right, so I’ve been gently turning her down… but if that keeps going, I feel like she’ll start overthinking it.
I see. Yeah, that makes sense. It doesn’t feel good if someone starts reading into things. Have you ever talked about this with a friend you do like?
No, I haven’t.

Mochi, I really get the sense you’re a kind person who cares about your friends. When you want to say no but can’t, it’s exhausting, isn’t it. I’d like to think together about ways to ease that exhaustion, even a little.

Thank you. Hearing you say that makes me happy. I think what I don’t like is that this friend lives in another prefecture, so she only contacts me when she comes back to our hometown, and it feels like I’m being used.
I see… Feeling like you’re being used must be really hard for you, Mochi. It sounds like that friend probably hasn’t noticed how you feel.

Yeah. And I’ve been hiding it this whole time, so I’m also like, “Just be clear already,” at myself… I’m torn between whether I should tell her how I feel, or just keep gently turning her down without saying it.
I see. It sounds like your mind is really busy with all of this. Do you have other friends you’re close with in your hometown?
I do.
So you do have them. Hometown friends often have strong bonds, don’t they. Is that friend close with the friend you’re not comfortable with?
They’re not close. The friend I’m close with is from high school, and the one who lives outside the prefecture is from junior high.
I see, so they’re not close.
Right, they don’t really have any connection.
Mochi, I imagine you’re getting worn out because you still treat even the friend you want distance from properly. How would it be to try talking a bit with your high school friend about this?
Maybe that’s true? I’m not really aware of it myself… But yeah, you’re right, I think I’ll try talking to them once.
I’m guessing that the friend you want to distance yourself from probably relies on you when she comes back to your hometown.
I don’t even know what it is about me she could rely on…
Thank you very much!
Thank you very much!

extra.topic_sub: 友達との距離を置く問題

interaction.content: Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for being here today.
Hello. Thank you.
Could you tell me what you’d like to talk about today?

I’ve never really been able to find the kind of work I truly want to do, and when I see everyone around me living with their feet firmly on the ground, I can’t help wondering why I’m the only one like this, and it makes me so anxious I can’t stand it.
You’ve been continuing to look for work you really want to do, then. If you don’t mind, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m a man in my 50s. I know I’m not really at the age to be saying things like this anymore, but I’d like to do what I want to do at the end of my life… I just can’t seem to find it…
Thank you for telling me. Those feelings really come from it being your own life. More concretely, have you tried anything, like taking on some kind of challenge?
Yeah… I don’t want things to just end like this, and I do feel like I want to work in a way that feels meaningful. I just can’t find anything where I feel, “This is what I want to do.”
It sounds like you care very deeply about your own life and about your work. And I get the sense that you really value that feeling of “wanting” to do something.
I do have that feeling.
Earlier you said, “I can’t find anything where I feel this is what I want to do.” Up until now, has there been anything you were interested in?

When I was young, I liked Hollywood movies, so I wanted to work in that kind of field. I went to study in the U.S. and planned to transfer to a film school, but the tuition was expensive and the exams were tough, so I ended up giving up.
How do you feel about that dream now?

After that, I tried pursuing things I became a bit interested in, but none of them were quite it, and I’d feel they were different and end up giving up. I don’t have that strong a feeling about it anymore.

You’ve tried starting things you were interested in, and you’ve been actively engaging with how you live and your work. Have you ever talked with people around you about what you’re bringing to counseling today?

Yeah… when I was younger, I still believed in my possibilities, but as I’ve gotten older, there are more and more limits on what I can start doing now… I’ve mentioned it in everyday conversation, but I don’t think I’ve really talked about it as a “consultation.”
I see. Could you tell me a bit more about what you mean by “limits”?
I don’t really talk to people about things much, and there’s also the embarrassment of thinking they might be like, “Now? At your age?”
It feels like our messages keep crossing and missing each other somehow… I’m sorry about that.
I mean whether there are actually places that would accept someone starting something new at my age. I’m the one who should apologize. 💦
Thank you for talking about those “limits.” It sounds like your age weighs on your mind and makes you hesitate to take the next step.
That’s a big reason, yes.
What kind of advantages do you think you might have precisely because of your age and experience?
Yeah… maybe the advantage is that I can patiently keep things running and support the people around me. I’m sorry, the time ran out so my answer ended up being kind of half-finished.
(I really had no idea where to land this, I’m sorry about that…) Thank you very much.
No, I’m the one who’s sorry. Thank you very much.
We’ll wrap up here.

extra.topic_sub: やりたい仕事の見つけ方の不安

interaction.content: Good evening, this is the counselor. Thank you for coming to talk today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m 23, female. I’ve lost sight of what the point of job hunting is, and I don’t know what I’m supposed to do anymore.
So you’re struggling with job hunting. Looking for a job is really tough, isn’t it.
The capable ones just get offers smoothly though.
Things like that can involve luck too, you know. How would you like me to address you?
Is it really luck? Everyone says it’s about ability and being efficient… You can just be “you.”
Thanks for your reply. I was thinking a little that there might be some luck involved, like the order of the interviews and so on. By the way, what are you doing at the moment?
What do you mean by the order?

I was just feeling that sometimes it’s like, everyone’s great but the number of positions is fixed… something like that. I’m sorry if that sounds off. What kind of job hunting have you been doing up to now? I’d like to know more about you.
I submit entry sheets and then just repeat waiting for interview offers.
I see. That waiting time can be really hard, feeling restless and unable to calm down. Do you have any places where you feel, “I want to work here”?
I don’t really have high hopes, so “excited” isn’t quite right. When I think about why I’m even applying, that’s what feels hard.
So it doesn’t feel like excitement. How do you feel while you’re waiting?
Just exhausted.
It just feels like it’s nothing but exhausting, huh. When it’s only hard all the time, it really wears you down, doesn’t it.
It’s like the meaning and the purpose are all jumbled up now.
Yeah. Do you feel like you absolutely want to get a job, or is it more like, if you didn’t have to, you’d rather not rush into a job right now?
If I don’t get a job I won’t have any income, and my parents will nag me, so I think it’s better to get a job if I can. But it’s hard.
Yeah… I hear you. But if you keep going while it’s this hard, your heart is just going to get more and more worn out.
Yeah.
For example, how would it be to work a part-time job while doing job hunting in parallel?
Yeah, I was thinking it’s probably better if I can get a job as a new graduate, but… do you think I should give up on that?

Inside you, even though it’s hard, there’s the part that wants to get a job as a new graduate, and there’s also the part that wants to take better care of yourself. Which one feels stronger right now?
Probably getting a job.

Mm-hmm, so the wish to get a job is stronger. I think it’s really impressive how firm your conviction is. Since job hunting is hard for you right now, if you’re going to keep going, how about setting a time limit for yourself?
Yeah, I’ll think about it. Thank you.
Thank you as well. If you’d like, please do think it over. Have you been able to say what you wanted to talk about today?
Yes, thank you.

It can be complaints or grumbling or anything at all, please feel free to come talk again if you’d like. I’m glad I got to talk with you. When it gets too hard, try doing something you like to give yourself a break. I’ll be here cheering you on from afar. I’ll send the closing message now.

extra.topic_sub: 就職活動の意義喪失

interaction.content: Hello. Thank you for coming to talk today.
Hello. Thank you for seeing me today.
Thank you. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m a 40-year-old woman.
Thank you. What would you like to talk about today?
Today I’d like to talk about relationships at work.
So there’s something difficult going on with relationships at your workplace.
Yes. I don’t know if it’s that this person is just really negative, but whenever we talk, they only ever say negative things, and they don’t take in any of the advice I offer.

I see. Thank you for telling me about that. Hearing negative things all the time can be really hard. Is this person a coworker? Or are they your supervisor? And sorry, how would you like me to address you?

Please call me Lala. We’re coworkers and the same age, but right now they’re my boss. I actually have more years of experience, so it’s a relationship where they come to me for advice and I give suggestions and so on.

Being coworkers but also having them be your boss sounds like a bit of a complicated relationship. And in the middle of that, having them talk to you in such a negative way all the time sounds like a really tough work environment. When you say they’re negative, what kind of things do they say, for example?

They say they’re in the gray zone, and they’ve told me that they’ve always had trouble with relationships. They say things like, “Someone like me is hopeless anyway,” or “Everyone thinks you’re better than me, Lala.” I don’t feel that way at all, and when they say that, it makes me sad. 

And when they come to consult with me, it feels like they’ve already decided on a direction before they talk to me. They have this really strong “This is what I want to do!!” kind of will. So even if I give advice, they rarely actually take it in.
That sounds really hard. You said that at first you were coworkers—have they always acted like this from the beginning? Or was there some kind of turning point?

No. At first, I think they didn’t have much confidence… they gave off this vibe of wanting to be taught. I guess things changed after they became the owner… Now they say things like, “I’m the owner so I decide,” “It’s my job so it’s my call.” 

I believe that thinking things through as a team rather than alone leads to better outcomes, but with them, I really feel they strongly want to avoid getting involved with people because they’re not good at interacting or communicating with others.

I see. So around the time your relationship shifted a bit, their attitude also started to change. It sounds like not only their negative way of talking, but also how they think about work feels a bit different from you, Lala. You value teamwork, and they prefer to work alone, right.

Lately I’ve been feeling like we just value different things. I’m like, “Is this what people mean by different values?” It’s hard to really understand someone whose values are different from yours, and my friends tell me, “Why don’t you just leave?” or “Why don’t you go independent, Lala?”

I also get the sense that there’s a difference in values and ways of thinking between the two of you. If you were to keep working at the same place from here on, what kind of relationship would you want to have with this person? Or do you feel like you might be okay with going independent, like your friends suggest?
Thank you very much.
I’m sorry we had to stop in the middle. Thank you again.

extra.topic_sub: 上司とのコミュニケーションの難しさ

interaction.content: Hello, this is the counselor. To start, could you tell me your gender and age?
I’m in my thirties. Male.
Thank you for answering. What would you like to talk about today?
I’m struggling with relationships at work.
So you’re having a hard time with relationships in your workplace. What’s been going on?
I don’t get along with my boss or my seniors.
I see, so you don’t get along with your boss or your seniors. In what ways do you feel you don’t match with them?
They lack kindness, consideration, and the way they talk, and they seem really proud, so they’re hard to deal with.
So they’re maybe a bit too cool or on edge. That can definitely make it hard to get along with them.
They’re all more than ten years older than me too, so it’s difficult.
Yeah, when there’s an age gap like that, it’s hard to share the same values, and that can be tough.
Yeah.

In terms of work, I imagine there are many situations where you need to communicate, but I don’t think you have to force yourself to communicate more than necessary or constantly worry about their mood. And in those situations where you still have to talk with your boss or seniors, it might help to stand at about a 45-degree angle, at a distance where your shoulders don’t touch.
What do you mean by a 45-degree angle?
Like this: person–person, in this kind of position.
What does that mean, exactly?

Facing each other straight on can sometimes give a sense of confrontation, but standing at a 45-degree angle puts you closer to their personal space in a softer way. I’ve heard that when someone is in that kind of position, it’s harder for them to take a very strong or aggressive stance.
I see.
I also often do this when I talk with people who have a harsh personality, and I find it makes it easier to have a calm exchange.
I see, I didn’t know that.

We can’t control other people, but if you change your own behavior just a little, the way others come across to you might shift a bit, and that can make things feel a little easier. If you’d like, please give it a try.
Got it. I’ll give it a try.
We’re just about out of time now. I wish I could have listened a bit more, so I’m sorry about that.
No, I’m the one who should apologize.
If anything else is bothering you, please feel free to come talk again. Thank you for today.
Thank you as well.
Alright then, I’ll say goodbye for now.

extra.topic_sub: 上司や先輩とのコミュニケーションのギャップ

interaction.content: I’d like to start the role-play now. Thank you in advance.
Thank you.
Thank you for coming to talk with me today.
May I talk to you about my situation?
Yes, of course. So first, could you tell me your gender, age, and what you’d like to talk about today?
Female, 39, it’s about my work.
Thank you. So it’s about your work. It sounds like there’s something you’re struggling with. What kind of things are you worried about?
Yeah. My current job isn’t really what I want to be doing, but the job I do want to do is hard to do given my situation.
So your current job isn’t what you really want to be doing. And there’s something else you’d really like to do.
Right. The job I have now is something I did want to try at least once in my life, but it’s not the number one thing I want to do.
I see. How long have you been in your current job?
This is my fifth year in this job.
So you’ve been working hard at it for five years. From about when did you start feeling that you wanted to do the thing you most want to do?
This is my third job. My first job was the one I wanted to do the most. I changed jobs because of family circumstances. I started my second job eight years ago.

I see, that makes sense. You’ve built up a lot of different experiences. You were able to do the work you most wanted to do, but you had to change jobs because of circumstances. If it’s not too hard to talk about, could you tell me how you felt at that time?

When my child was born, I felt that working night shifts would be difficult. My husband goes on long business trips, and he also works on weekends, so I thought it wouldn’t be good for the mother to be away… so I changed jobs for my family. I felt my family was more important than my work. But when I meet friends who have continued doing the work they want to do, there’s a part of me that feels, that’s nice, I wish I could do that too.
You really value your family and come across as a very loving person. You sound like a really wonderful mother.
Thank you. It’s a daily struggle inside. But I’m glad to hear you say that.

And at the same time, when you see friends who are doing the work they want to do, those kinds of feelings come up for you… I can really feel how strong those feelings are. If we imagine taking away all the barriers, what would your truly ideal way of being look like?

Being able to work on what I love, at the times I want, not for the money. That kind of life is my ideal. But then I end up thinking maybe it’s better to stay a full-time employee for the sake of my pension.

Your kindness really comes through. A life where you can do the work you want to do is wonderful, isn’t it. And you’re also carefully thinking about the financial side of things… that’s really great. When you think about the work you want to do, is there any small step you feel you might be able to take now?

Yeah, right. But in reality… it’s tough. I see, so it also means I’m thinking about the financial side of things. Sometimes I catch myself thinking, if only I’d married someone rich so I wouldn’t have to worry about money… The grass really does look greener on the other side.
By the way, have you ever talked with your partner about this? From where I’m sitting, your own character looks very “green and lush” to me.
I have talked to him about it, and sometimes he says, “Well then, just do what you like,” and other times he says, “I’m really grateful you’re working while thinking things through.”
It’s really good that you’re talking with your partner about it!
Yeah. Half the time his answers make me mad though… Thank you very much!!
We had to stop in the middle of your story, but thank you for coming to talk with me.

extra.topic_sub: やりたい仕事と家庭の両立に関する葛藤

interaction.content: Thank you for reaching out. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and where you live?
I’m a 54-year-old woman, living in Yamaguchi Prefecture.
About earlier, sorry for the typo. I meant to say where you live “at.” What would you like to talk about today?
Right now I’ve quit my job and moved back to the countryside to take care of my parents, but sometimes I feel like I’m about to be crushed by anxiety.
You’re caring for your parents and feeling full of anxiety. What kind of worries make you feel like you’re being crushed?

My parents’ health… my father has cancer and various other illnesses, and he keeps going in and out of the hospital, so I’m afraid he might not have much time left. And then I’m also anxious about my own income in the future.
That would definitely make you feel anxious. I really respect that you quit your job to focus on caring for your parents. Are you currently not working at all there in the countryside?
No. It’s so rural that there really aren’t many jobs, and my parents have to go to the hospital so often that it’s hard to work.
When the hospital visits are that frequent, it’s hard to commit to a job, isn’t it. Besides you, is there anyone else who helps take care of your parents?
Yes, I have an older brother. But he’s working full-time now, and, well, he’s a man so there are parts where he’s not really that reliable. Especially for my mother, she says she wants her daughter…

So your parents really rely on you. It sounds like you’re basically doing the caregiving on your own, which must be tough. Have you ever talked to your brother or anyone else about these worries you have now? By the way, how would you like me to address you?

I talk about the surface-level worries, but I can’t really talk about the deeper parts with anyone. You can call me Ritsuko. And it’s not just my parents—there’s also our elderly dog, and when I think that someday I’ll lose them too, I get anxious.
Thank you for telling me, Ritsuko. You’re also taking care of your dog.
Yes. Everything just overflows sometimes and I can’t stop crying.
It’s really painful to think about what you might lose from now on, isn’t it. Ritsuko, how do you wish things could be going forward?
That’s a hard question, but anyway I’m trying to cherish each day and live so that I’ll have as few regrets as possible.

In such a difficult situation, the way you’re trying to spend your days carefully and positively is really wonderful, I think. And even so, you still end up feeling anxious, right. In what moments do you feel like you’re being crushed by anxiety?

Yeah, it’s when I think about the future… I guess. I’m probably putting a lid on my anxious feelings to get through the days, so maybe sometimes those feelings just overflow. Would it be better not to put a lid on them?
It feels like your emotions are overflowing, then. As you’re talking now about what you’re anxious about, how does that make you feel?
Talking like this, I end up crying after all. Normally I try to stay as cheerful as I can in front of my family.

You’re hiding your anxiety from your family and doing your best, aren’t you. Having to hold back your own feelings is painful too. If crying helps you feel a bit clearer, it’s okay to let the tears come. How do you feel after you cry?
If I could really cry my heart out, I might feel refreshed, but it’s hard to do that in the house, so sometimes I go outside to cry (like up on a mountain), but it’s cold now so it’s not easy…
Yeah, the cold is no fun… I can really feel how you want to keep a smile on at home. Besides crying, is there anything else that helps you feel clearer or take your mind off things, Ritsuko?
I try to move my body as much as I can to change my mood. And sometimes I’m allowed to go back to Kobe.
Moving your body is great! Is Kobe where you used to work? What kind of place is Kobe for you, Ritsuko?
There are mountains I love and lots of friends there, so it’s a city I really love! I spent 30 years in Kobe working and raising my kids!
I see. So when you go to that city you love, Kobe, it puts you in a more positive mood! Hearing that you have such a special place makes me feel relieved.
Thank you for listening to me today.
Thank you as well!! It really is difficult, isn’t it. Let’s both keep doing our best from here on.

extra.topic_sub: 両親の介護に伴う不安とストレス

interaction.content: (Thank you for being here today. We’ll get started once it’s time.)
Thank you.
Thank you for coming to talk today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’re struggling with? Thank you.
I’m 35, female. Dealing with people has started to feel like such a burden and it’s kind of painful.
I see. Could you tell me if there was any particular trigger for why interacting with people started to feel so burdensome?
I’ve gotten worn out from dealing with the other moms. It’s exhausting having to hang out with them for my child’s sake even though we don’t get along.
Yeah, it is tiring to feel like you have to spend time with people you don’t really click with. Since about when have you been feeling this exhaustion?

I realized within a few months that we didn’t really get along. It’s been about a year now, and she’s started even interfering in how I raise my child, and I’m getting to the point where I can’t stand it anymore.
I see. Having someone butt in like that is really hard, isn’t it. How do you see these other moms, the mom friends?
I see her as someone who’s oblivious to others and selfish and arrogant. She’s kind of like the queen bee of the mom group.
So that’s how you see her. You mentioned selfish—what makes you feel that way about her?

She invites me out for lunch or coffee and I turn her down, but then she’ll say things like, “You can come for at least 30 minutes, right?” or “I’m really having a hard time, I just need you to listen a little,” and it’s always about trying to get me to come. She doesn’t even notice that she’s making me feel guilty, and she often says things that make it sound like I’m the worst for not going. Just saying no is a whole ordeal most of the time. In those moments I really feel she’s selfish.
So she often says things that make you feel like you’re the worst. Having to struggle just to say no is really hard. For you, what kind of presence are these mom friends in your life?
Yeah… Mom friends are people I feel I have to deal with because our kids get along, I guess.
So that’s how you think about it. For you, what would an ideal relationship with mom friends look like?

Ideally it would just be a light relationship where we say hi when we see each other and that’s it. I don’t really want to get involved with them, and I don’t want them getting involved with me either. But this mom, from how she is with others too, just seems like the type of person who wants to be involved with people.
I see. What makes a “light relationship where just saying hi is enough” your ideal?

Back in my twenties I had a friend who was similar to this mom, and I got caught up in some interpersonal drama. Ever since then, when I meet that kind of person, I find myself wanting a more distant, light relationship. I just realized this about myself now, but I seem to have that tendency.
I see, so that’s what happened. The trouble you had in past relationships is connected to what’s happening now. Going forward, how would you like things to be with this mom friend?

Honestly, I don’t want to be involved with her. I’m keeping my distance in my own way, but she keeps trying to get closer, and it just feels unbearably burdensome. I’ve thought about telling her directly, but I’m scared it’ll affect the kids’ relationship, and I don’t know how she’d react, so I end up just worrying about it.
Right, thinking about your child makes it feel scary, doesn’t it. Have you talked to anyone about this before?
I’ve talked to my husband and a friend about it. There is one other mom friend I feel like I might be able to talk to, but I haven’t, because I don’t know how the story might get twisted or spread.

Yeah, it really does take courage to talk to another mom about this. From what you’ve shared, I feel you’re someone very kind who puts your child first and really cares about them. What do you see as the possible pros and cons of talking to that mom friend?

Thank you for sharing that. In that kind of environment, you haven’t been able to talk to anyone and you’ve been holding on to that anxiety all this time. That must have been really hard. Is there anyone at work you talk with?
I only talk about work, and I don’t talk to anyone during breaks.
Is there anyone you talk to outside of work? For example, family or friends.
When I talked to my mother about work, she just nodded and listened. It felt like she wasn’t really listening to my worries.
You felt like she wasn’t really listening to your worries.

interaction.content: Hello. I’m the counselor. To start, could you tell me your gender and age, and what you’d like to talk about today?
I’m a 28-year-old woman. Today it’s about how I always end up doing too much.
Thank you. So you’d like to talk about how you always end up doing too many things.
Yeah. I do too much and end up collapsing, so lately I’ve been trying to be careful.
Thank you. What does that look like more specifically? Ah, sorry, I cut across you there. You do too much and end up collapsing… That is worrying.

The problem is, when I overdo it and collapse, people around me get really worried, so I know I have to not overdo it, but I end up cramming in too many plans. I don’t realize it myself until I collapse, so I know I have to stop somewhere, but I just keep going, and I’m not sure what to do about that part.
I see. So even though you yourself feel, “This isn’t good,” you still end up “packing in too many plans.”
Yeah.
Is it like you “pack in too many plans” around things you’re interested in?
Partly interests, but to do the things I’m interested in, work and social obligations end up filling all my time except when I’m sleeping. I just can’t say no.
I see. And then you run out of time and, in the end, you collapse.
Yeah. It’s not all the time, but.
I understand. From what you’re saying, I get the sense that part of you feels, “This situation isn’t ideal.”
I kind of feel that way because if I’m not healthy it feels like I might die. But there are also a lot of things I have to do.
There’s a lot you have to do. But if you try to do it all, your body can’t take it. It sounds like a pretty tough situation.
My mind and body just aren’t keeping up.
Do people around you, when they see how you’re doing, say anything or make any adjustments for you?
Some people force me to take breaks, and others are like, “We really need you to come,” so I guess some people are considerate and some aren’t.
It sounds like you’re in a pretty difficult situation. There’s the gratitude that people have expectations of you. But realistically, there are parts where your body and mind just can’t keep up…
Yeah. I thought about it a lot. I’ve realized that right now I can’t stop myself, so I’m trying to lean on other people, and little by little I’m practicing saying no and building in rest time.
I feel relieved hearing that. I was worried your body and mind might be crying out. When you say that to people around you, do they seem to accept it?
Thank you for worrying about me. The “forcing me to rest” group is really pulling me along. But I’m still influenced by the “work until you drop” group too.
I see. So there really is a sense of being caught in the middle. I’m sorry to interrupt, but instead of saying “you” all the time, how would you like me to address you?
Ryosan is fine.

Ryosan, okay. Thank you. In that kind of situation, is there anything like “how you’d like things to be going forward”? For example, wanting to move more in the direction of resting your mind and body.

I still have dreams and I want to keep running until I make them happen, but doing it 24 hours a day is obviously too much, so I’d like to ask someone to help me carve out at least a few hours of rest. It’s not going well yet, so I’m thinking I’ll just keep trying different things. Thank you for the role-play!
I see. So you have “dreams you want to make come true.” In a way, it’s because you have those dreams that there’s also a “part of you that can keep pushing yourself,” is that right?

interaction.content: Hello, this is the counselor. Thank you for reaching out today. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m 43, female. Thank you for seeing me.
Thank you for letting me know. It’s nice to meet you. What would you like to talk about today?
When I talk with people or do something, I get worried about making mistakes and can’t calm down. How can I live more casually, without feeling so tense?

I see, you end up feeling worried. In what specific situations does the worry get stronger and make you feel unsettled? If nothing specific comes to mind, you can just tell me about how you usually feel day to day—that would be really helpful.

On mornings when I’m going out to meet people, when I think about the day’s plans, I get this unsettled feeling like, “Will I be able to get through today properly?” After a while I forget about it, but it’s like I automatically think I have to handle everything perfectly… Even before I start, I get anxious, like, “What if I mess up?” If possible, I’d like to not feel that way and be able to start things with a lighter, more comfortable feeling.
It’s really hard when even everyday things feel like you have to do them perfectly.
Exactly. I get all worked up and can’t relax. What should I do?
Since about when have you been feeling that way?
I think it started after my kids began going to school. I’ve always been the type to worry about things, but…
So you have children. When your children started going to school, did anything change in how you felt?
Yes, I have two. I started feeling like I have to raise them properly, and that if I mess something up, it’ll have a negative impact on them.
I see. That must feel like a lot of pressure. When it’s not just about you but about your children, does that make you even more worried?

Yes. In kindergarten and elementary school, I’d worry that if people disliked me, my kids would get left out… I was so worried and so sensitive to fitting in with everyone around me that I feel like I eventually couldn’t let go of that tension.
Since you can’t directly see how your kids are doing at school and such, it’s natural to worry. Before they started school, how strong were those worries for you?

Right. From how my kids act, I can tell they’re not being bullied or anything, but my anxiety runs ahead of me and I get tense, and instead of enjoying conversations, it feels more like I’m just getting through them. When I was a student, I was also scared of being excluded, so I tended to go along with everyone. After becoming an adult and before my kids started school, I don’t think I worried that much and I felt more at ease. Maybe the fact that I went to an all-girls school where relationships were pretty harsh has something to do with it…?

People do say that all-female environments can be pretty harsh… I think that environment may play a part, but it also sounds like you’ve always been someone who can read the room and act accordingly. Now that you have children, that part of you might be even more pronounced, and that could be making your tension and fear of making mistakes stronger. Does that sound like what’s happening?

Yeah… it’s like, while I kept those “sensors” up, I ended up not being able to get out of that mode. I was originally kind of insensitive, and people around me said various things to me, so I gradually widened my “sensors,” and now I feel like I’ve finally gotten worn out.
I see. Like you said earlier, when those sensors are always up, even for everyday things like meeting or talking with people, your mind is bound to get exhausted.
Yeah… Is there any good way to relax?
I can really sense how hard you’ve been trying all this time.
Thank you. I’m kind of at the point where I don’t want to keep pushing myself anymore.

Yeah, constantly pushing yourself is exhausting… For example, even just small everyday things is fine—are there situations where you think, “It would be so much easier if I could do this without being on guard”?

Relationships, I guess. Once I start talking, sometimes it becomes fun and I stop worrying, but I tend to avoid communication with people I feel I have to be careful around. I try not to put myself in situations I’m not good with as much as possible.
So, relationships. When there’s another person involved, you naturally end up being more careful. I actually think not putting yourself in situations you’re not good with is a really good idea.

Yeah. Like, if I see someone I’m not that close to, I’ll take a detour so they don’t notice me. I think to myself, “I’m doing something kind of lame,” but I end up avoiding contact because I don’t want to be stuck worrying about things afterward. Really? To me it feels less “nice idea” and more sneaky or sly.
I see. What makes you feel it’s sneaky? If you’re comfortable answering, I’d like to hear more.
Hmm… I want to be able to casually say hello and chat. Thank you for listening today. Somehow I feel clearer, like a weight’s been lifted a bit.
I’m sorry I couldn’t express things very well… but thank you so much as well. I learned a lot.
I look forward to talking again sometime!

interaction.content: Hello. Thank you for being here today. Could you tell me what you’d like to talk about, and your age and gender?
Thank you. I’m 51, female. What I want to talk about is that I keep having unpleasant interactions with my boss at work, and I’m struggling because that relationship just doesn’t change.
I see, so you’d like to talk about your relationship with your boss at work. When you say unpleasant interactions, in what kinds of situations does that happen, specifically?
Yes. My boss is in sales, and I do sales admin work, but it happens when I pass on requests from the clients he’s in charge of and ask him to handle them…
I see. Sales work can be really tough in a lot of ways.

I have to pass on the clients’ requests and get him to do them, but he forgets, doesn’t do them, and throws all the annoying parts back at me. In the end, the complaints from clients all come back to me.

I see. Even though these are requests from clients your boss is in charge of, you’re the one who ends up stepping in and going through all this trouble. How is your usual working relationship with your boss, day to day?
It’s bad. He really doesn’t like me. And as a male boss, he also has this discriminatory attitude toward women.
So your boss is a man.
That’s right. Sorry I didn’t explain that properly. He’s about seven years older than me.

Not at all, thank you for letting me know. Just feeling discriminated against simply because you’re a woman must be really hard while you’re trying to work. And even so, you’re still dealing with things when something happens with his clients, so I think you’re really doing your best.

Everyone in my sales support team is a woman. The other members are all going through the same unpleasant things, so part of the problem is that I end up thinking I have to be the one to take it on somehow.
I see. So there are those circumstances too. When there’s some kind of trouble with your boss’s clients, does it end up feeling like it’s your responsibility?
In the end, the responsibility falls on that boss, but I’m the one who gets the initial anger. Even when I explain that, he doesn’t say anything appreciative, and I’m always left feeling empty.

I see. That’s really very hard. Just taking in someone’s anger is exhausting in itself, isn’t it. From what you’ve said about the other support members feeling the same way, I get the sense that your team probably understands your efforts and what you’re going through. How does that feel to you?

Yes, that alone really saves me. We’re all united, we thank and appreciate each other, and the team atmosphere is really good. I tried changing my behavior, like trying to switch my mindset toward my boss and treat him kindly, but then he started to depend on me in this weird way, and I felt like our relationship was actually getting worse.
I see, you’re really putting in effort every day. You’re thinking about so many things beyond just your own tasks, and I really respect that. You’re very kind.
Thank you. Nobody really praises me, so that makes me happy. I’m trying different things every day, but I started wondering if maybe I’m the one who’s weird for thinking so much about it.

There are times when it gets hard to trust yourself, aren’t there. I think that shows just how much you’re going through. You have your own clients to take care of, and you also feel like your boss is depending on you, so for example, how would it be to ask someone higher up in management than your boss for support? Or, if you and your team members could approach your boss together, there might be a chance the situation changes a little.
I see. I have reported it to his superior, but I think that person also holds back with him and doesn’t say anything, and seems to think that even if they did, he wouldn’t change.

I see. So you’ve already been taking various actions. You’ve been adjusting how you deal with your boss and following up on his work, and you really are putting in a lot of effort every day. I think that’s wonderful. If the final responsibility for the work lies with your boss himself, then maybe it would be okay for you to try not to feel quite so responsible for his work.

Thank you! Yes. The reality is that I can’t completely avoid being involved with him. I might be feeling too responsible because I think, "If I don’t do it, some other staff member will have to go through the same thing."

Right, but I think that just shows how kind you are and how seriously you take your work. How would it be to decide for yourself some kind of rule about the limits of how far you’ll go to follow up for him?

Yeah, that’s true. You’re right. I hadn’t set that, so I think I can make some rules. But even if I do, since it’s just a rule I decided on my own like, "This is as far as I go," I feel like it won’t really change my relationship with my boss.

I see. It’s true that since you see him every day, it might be hard to change the situation quickly. But if setting some rules and clarifying where your responsibility begins and ends at work could ease your burden and the pain you’re feeling even a little, it might be one possible approach to try.
Yes. Honestly, I’ll try saying, "It’s affecting my work, so I need you to handle things up to this point yourself. Let’s follow this rule." Thank you so much for listening to all of this!!
Yes, I hope things change for the better. I’m cheering you on! Thank you for today.
Thank you very much.
Alright then, we’ll end our session here.

Yeah… we really didn’t have any space. The way things are now, I end up feeling like I don’t want to be with my husband.

I’m sorry to interrupt in the middle of your consultation, but we’re coming up on the end of our time. Today you talked about your relationship with your husband—how was it for you to talk about that?
Okay. Being able to vent about my husband made me feel a bit lighter. Thank you.
You’re always welcome to come back, whether it’s to continue what we talked about today or to bring something completely different. Thank you for talking with me today.
Thank you as well.

I don’t know if what I’ve been working on will go well, but I prepared more earnestly than usual, so even if the result isn’t good, I want to really enjoy it so that I can feel like doing it again.
I see, so there was something you’d been working on. It’s really nice when we can approach things with a sense of enjoyment. Let’s keep talking.
I started to feel that enjoying something is the most important thing for being able to keep going with what you’ve started.

I think that’s a really lovely way of thinking. Let me ask: in what kind of situations do you feel like, “Okay, I’m going to give this my best”? For example, when you have a goal, or when you have a reward waiting for you—there are lots of possibilities.

For example, in this case, maybe it’s when I feel like I’ve noticed something new, or that I might be able to take on a new challenge. I guess I feel like trying hard so I can keep doing the things I want to continue.

Mm-hmm, so it’s like you can see ahead to the next goal, maybe? Having a goal all the time can become a kind of anchor that helps you keep wanting to try, so I thought that might be something good for you right now, and I wanted to share that.
Yeah. Constantly setting goals and thinking about what I can do to clear them and then actually trying it out might be an important element in enjoying things.

Yes, I think that’s important. And when you clear a goal, that feeling of “this is fun” can really grow, I imagine. How does that sound? Once you’ve tasted that feeling, it seems like you’d be able to try again next time too.
Yeah. And those goals should be ones where I’m not placing big expectations on other people, but ones that seem manageable if I just do my best as I am now.

Yes, exactly. If you suddenly set a huge goal, it can become really exhausting, so I think it’s fine to start with small goals. For example, on a day-by-day basis, starting from affirming yourself like, “I did this today, so that’s OK,” or “I tried to do my best today, so that’s OK.” Or any kind of goal that feels easy for you to set—I think that’s perfectly good. How does that sound to you?
I’ll set one goal that seems doable tomorrow and try to carry it out.

I’m really glad to hear you say that. My impression is that you’re someone who thinks carefully about yourself, so I believe you can move in a good direction. Just be careful not to slip into a perfectionistic mindset like, “I have to do this” in order to clear your goals, okay?
You’re right, I do have a tendency to try to be overly precise to the point of being neurotic, so I’ll try to be careful not to focus on the wrong things.

If that happens, it just gets even more painful, doesn’t it. This is a bit of self-disclosure, but I’m a perfectionist and have struggled in that way myself, so like I mentioned, I worked on adjusting it through small moments of self-affirmation in my daily life. Just for your reference.
Thank you for sharing something so valuable.

I’m glad to hear you say that. We’re just about out of time for today. This time we mainly talked about “finding joy through small goals,” but I think there are many other elements of enjoyment too. I’m glad I could talk about this. Thank you very much.
Thank you as well. We’ll end our session here.

I'm tired of living.

Yes, I wonder what I'm even living for.

Yes.

It's the three of us, my husband and me and our child.

I don't even know myself.

Yes.

Yes.

Yes, but he just said something like, 'Don't overdo it.'

Yes.

I thought, 'That's it?'

Yes, I don't want to be alive anymore.

Even if I do, when I go back to daily life, I feel the same way again.

Yes.

At night after my child falls asleep, I soak in the bath by myself.

Yes, that sounds like a good time. When your body warms up, your heart can soften a bit too. I'm glad you're able to have even a little time like that. Other than your husband, have you ever talked to anyone about how hard this feels?

Next to me.

Yes. I think that’s important!
I’m glad you feel that way. Thank you for coming here today and sharing so much with me. How was it for you?
Putting my thoughts into words made me feel like they became more organized. Thank you.
I’m glad to hear that. Please feel free to come talk with me again anytime.
Yes, thank you very much.

interaction.content: (Good morning. Thank you for being here today.)
Good morning. Thank you as well.
(It’s before the scheduled time, but would you like to start at the appointed time?)
Yes, please, let’s start at 10.
(Understood.) Good morning. I’m the counselor. To begin, if you’re comfortable, please tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about.
Good morning. I’m a woman in my 40s.
Okay.
Lately, I’ve been having trouble because I get down easily.
I see. That must be troubling for you.
Yes.
Was there anything that might have triggered it?

There wasn’t any specific trigger, but my family told me, “It’s strange to get that sad over something like that,” and I’ve been wondering if that’s true. When it’s really bad, I sometimes run out of the house, and sometimes I think I want to die.
I see. That sounds really painful.
I know I mustn’t do that, so struggling with those feelings and thoughts is painful too.
I see. You’re in such a painful situation that you feel that way.
It’s not all the time; it’s more like when I get down.
I see. So you only feel that way at those times. Could you tell me what kinds of things your family referred to as “something like that”?

It’s when I point something out to my husband or children and they don’t take it in, and I feel sad, or when I tell them, “This behavior of yours hurt me.” Simply put, they say it when I’m hurt by their words or actions and get down.
I see. You were speaking out of concern for your family, so it’s sad when they don’t take it in.

Yes. But my family says I get too sad, that I’m too easily hurt. That makes it even more painful, and I feel denied. So I end up thinking it’s my fault for getting hurt, but I can’t stop it, and I want to run away.
I see. That must feel unbearable. What kinds of words from your family actually hurt you?
Various things, like saying I’m selfish, or that I talk too long and they don’t want to listen anymore, or not to try to make things go my way...
I see. From your perspective, you’re talking because you care about your family, so it’s sad when they won’t listen.

Yes. But everyone has their own thoughts and feelings, so I do think it can’t be helped to some extent that they argue back. Still, I wish I could listen to those words without getting down over every little thing, and keep a calm face... But I can’t, and I want to stop getting to the point where I think, “I want to die.”
I see. It would be good if you could listen in that way. You mentioned that you’ve started having these feelings recently. What was it like before?
When someone said something to me, I would get down, but I don’t think it was as bad as it is now.
I see. What differences do you think there are between then and now? Is there anything that comes to mind, such as your physical condition or changes in your family?

For me, it’s clear that I’m more tired than before from facing my family and clashing with them. As for changes in my family, simply put, everyone has become busier. Also, because I get down easily, I feel like I’ve become more negative than before.
I see. When you feel that you’ve become busier than before, what kinds of things are different?
The ones who have become busy are my family members other than me. My children have moved up a grade, for example.
Mm-hmm.
My husband’s workload has increased and he’s been working more overtime.
Yes.
Each of them has more to do and has become busier.
I see. Your family members have each become busier, and along with that, you’ve also had more things to do. You would want your family to understand that too, wouldn’t you?
I haven’t become that much busier. I understand that my family has become busy.
I see. From what you’ve shared, recently you’ve been struggling because your family’s words and actions make you feel down and make you think negatively.
Yes.
And going forward, you’d like to not feel that way.
I can’t change my family’s words or actions (though I’d be happy if that happened), so I want to stop getting this down.
That’s true. It’s hard to change other people. It would be good if you could avoid getting so down. What kinds of methods do you think might help with that?
That’s what I don’t know.
I see. Then I’d like us to think through it together. How does that sound?

I want to know how. When I feel like I’m about to get down, I’ve tried going into a room where I can be alone and putting distance between myself and the other person, but it made me feel even more distressed. I’ve also tried holding back tears so I wouldn’t get emotional.
I see. You’ve been trying various ways to cope on your own. And even so, you’re still in a painful situation.
Yes. But I’m just feeling my way through and I don’t know, so I started wanting to hear someone’s advice.
I see. That’s why you found the courage to come here to talk with me. Thank you.
I’m sorry it’s such a heavy topic...
No, it’s all right. Please talk about anything. After sharing all of this, how are you feeling now?
I feel like I’m wondering whether there’s some good way to deal with it, and also like my heart feels a little lighter because someone listened to me.
I see. I’m glad to hear that. Please come talk anytime. Talking to someone can make you feel relieved, can’t it?
Yes.

As you yourself mentioned, I heard that you can’t change your family’s words and actions. From what you’ve told me, I do think that with your family, there may be parts they can understand. What do you think? I wonder if you might face your family once more and tell them how you’re feeling now.
Yes... but I’m a little afraid that they’ll deny me again somehow, and I’ll get down.
Yes, it’s understandable that you would feel that way. And when that happens, please do come and talk with me.
When I think that next time I’ll have to fight against the thought that I want to die again...
Yes.
It’s really hard to say it.
That makes sense. For yourself, how about trying things that help you relax, like soaking in the bath, using aroma oils, or listening to music you like?
Do you mean taking care of myself?
Rather than taking care of yourself, how about thinking of it as taking yourself somewhere more comfortable than where you are now?
I see. I’ll try that when it gets painful.
Please do try it. I’m rooting for you. Thank you for coming here today. Please come and let me hear from you anytime.
Thank you very much. I’ll come again.
(Thank you very much. I learned a lot.)
Thank you as well.

interaction.content: (Hello. Thank you for joining me for today’s role-play starting at 3:00 p.m. It’s time now, so I’ll begin. Thank you.)
(Thank you.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in for a consultation today. To start, may I ask what name I should call you here, and your age and gender, if you’re comfortable sharing?
I’m 39, female. Please call me Mitch.
Mitch, then. Thank you for coming today. To get started, may I ask what you’d like to talk about?
Yes. I lost my job in April, and then the part-time job I started after that was cut too. Somehow I just don’t feel motivated to do anything anymore.

I see. That must have been very disappointing, and it would make you feel anxious too. I think it’s completely understandable that you’re having trouble feeling motivated. How are you spending your day-to-day life right now?
Yes. Right now even things around the house feel like a hassle, and I’m somehow managing to make meals for my children, but physically it’s hard too.

You have children, then. When you’re feeling this way, housework and childcare must be really exhausting. I can really understand how hard that is. What happened with your work? Would you be willing to tell me, as much as you feel comfortable sharing, why you lost the jobs?
I don’t know. Both times it was sudden. They told me it was because the economy is bad.
I see... Being told something like that so suddenly must have been such a shock. How did that feel for you, Mitch?
I thought I was working pretty normally at the company, so I never imagined it would happen. And there are still other people working there.
I see. That was unexpected. I imagine it may have felt like you were betrayed. How does that sound?
Yes. My former colleagues who are still there said things like, “There’s no way Mitch should be the one let go,” but somehow, it’s frustrating, and I also wonder if I’m just not needed.
Yes, that makes sense. It would feel frustrating, and it would make you anxious, wondering whether you’re not needed.
Yes. Somehow I just don’t feel like job hunting anymore.
Yes. When you’ve had an experience like that, it can really shake your confidence. How are things financially right now? Is there anyone supporting you?
My husband has an income, but it has gone down after all. Also, my children are preparing for university and high school entrance exams, so honestly, it’s hard unless I work.
I see. Your children are at an age when expenses are high, so in a situation like this, it makes sense that you would feel pressured.
My youngest is in elementary school, so I still can’t really take a job with much overtime.
I see. As for job hunting itself, are you moving forward with it even though you don’t feel motivated?
I was told the part-time job is only until the end of September, and right now I haven’t done anything yet.
I see. So even while things are painful right now, you’re still working, and also taking care of the housework and childcare.
Before, things at home didn’t feel like a burden, but now I’m only doing the bare minimum.

Thank you for telling me. I feel I have a clear sense of the situation you’re in, Mitch. You’ve worked so hard up to now, and after going through something so frustrating, in a situation where it’s very hard to feel positive, doing housework and working must be extremely exhausting. You really have been doing your best. Let’s think together about what might help with these painful feelings you’re having now.
Yes. Thank you.
Mitch, you said that what you’re struggling with now is not being able to feel motivated.
Yes. It’s painful, and sometimes I cry.

It seems to me that you’re in a very hurt state right now, Mitch. When something like this happens twice with work you were trying hard at, it takes away your confidence, and it feels frustrating, and of course it can bring you to tears.
Yes. My body feels worn out too.
Yes, I hear you. Since this may be a time for healing yourself, how would it be to rest a little?
Yes. I’d like to do that, but I can’t get the income issue out of my head.
Yes, of course. You’re suffering with the financial pressure too. But if you keep spending your days feeling this much pain, I worry that your heart may break down. What do you think?
Yes. It’s painful and I want to get out of it, but I don’t know how.

Even if it’s just for one day, how would it be to do something you like that you’ve been holding back on, have your family take care of all the housework, spend the day slowly, and hold a kind of “healing day” for Mitch, who has worked so hard? You’ve worked hard to the point of feeling this much pain, so let’s let you receive a reward.
I had never thought of that. My family is kind, but I’ve been doing everything, so I wonder if I can ask them.
Your family sees how hard you usually work, Mitch, so I’m sure they’ll be happy to do it for you.
If I take a break from housework, maybe I’ll feel a little less worn out. I’ll try talking to my family.
Please come back here and tell me how it went, and what happened afterward too. I’ll be here whenever you need.
Thank you. I feel like I might try taking a little rest.
I’m glad. You’ve worked so hard, so please take your time and be kind to yourself. I think we’ll end here for today. How does that sound?
Yes. Thank you. Having you listen has made me feel a little lighter.
I’m glad. Please do come talk again. I’ll send the closing message now. Thank you very much for today.
Thank you very much.
(Thank you for the role-play. I learned a lot. I look forward to working with you again.)

25, male, living is painful.

I don’t remember. Probably always.
I see. So would you say you also haven’t been working for a while?
It’s not so much “for a while”—I’ve never worked.
In that case, the worries about where you’ll live and also going out to work for the first time are overlapping in a really big way, so I think it’s natural that this would feel painful.
That made it even more painful.
I hear you. I’d like to ask about your health. You mentioned that you have a mental illness—are you currently seeing a doctor or receiving treatment?
More or less.
I see. Would you say things are stable?
More or less.
That’s a relief. Going back a little, when you said you have to leave your parents’ house starting next year, were there any particular circumstances behind that?
It’s my parents’ order.
That really does feel sudden. Even if it’s an order from your parents, did they have some intention behind it? Have you asked them in detail about the reason?
I don’t know.

I don’t know. It’s already decided, so there’s no point thinking about that, right?

If I could do that, I wouldn’t be here.
You’re right. You came here to talk because you’re in such a painful situation. I’m sorry.
That hurt me.
I do understand how you feel. Then, assuming that it’s already decided, I’d like us to think together about what comes next. Would that be all right?
Do you really understand? Have you ever had a mental illness?
I myself have not had a mental illness, but I once lost a subordinate to suicide, so I do have some involvement with situations like that.
But the situation is different, isn’t it?
Yes. It is different from your situation.
I’m sorry, but I can’t trust you. I’m sorry, I’ll leave it here.

I’m very sorry that I wasn’t able to understand your feelings. We’re also limited by time today, but if you feel able to reach out again, please feel free to consult anytime. Next time, I will listen to your story again from the beginning.

interaction.content: (Good evening. Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.)
Good evening. Thank you.
Good evening. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
25-year-old woman. I want to die.
You’re feeling like you want to die. Could you tell me what’s been happening that’s made you feel that way? You can start wherever you feel able to talk.
A lot has happened, for a long time… I’ve felt that way for a long time.
That must be painful, having felt that way for so long. For example, what kinds of things have been going on?
Living feels exhausting.
Yes.
And I feel empty.
You’re feeling exhausted and empty. When do you tend to feel that way?
When I’m tired from work, or when I’m talking with my boyfriend.
I see. Is work busy for you?
Yes. My boss is strict, and there’s a lot of pressure.
I see. So you’ve been working in that kind of situation. That would take a lot out of you emotionally, and it must be exhausting.
Yes. Even when I’m talking with my boyfriend, when I’m really lonely, I feel like he isn’t there for me, and I feel empty.
That’s how it feels for you. Are you able to talk with your boyfriend about how hard work has been and things like that?
No. Even though it’s something I chose to do because I like it, somehow both work and love feel empty. I’ve always had that kind of side to me.
I see. Is it a feeling of wanting someone to be by your side, but they aren’t, and that emptiness is there?
Rather than that, even though I like something, or feel happy, or have fun, something small can suddenly make me feel empty. I’ve been like that since I was a student.
I see. Do you have any thoughts about where that emptiness might be coming from?
I’m not sure… It’s like I can’t concentrate… maybe there’s a feeling that I can’t feel safe. Even at work, when I try really hard and people around me praise me, I end up doubting it.
I see. So there’s also a feeling of doubting whether the reactions from people around you are real.
Even in my relationship, when my boyfriend tells me he loves me, I feel like I can’t fully believe it. Yes. When I think this is going to keep going on forever, I feel despair.
I see. Feeling that way must be painful.
Yes.

Listening to what you’ve shared, it sounds like even at work, when people around you praise you, you doubt it, and you can’t fully believe your boyfriend’s words either, so it seems like you can’t fully feel safe. How does that sound to you?
That’s right. Actually, yesterday, I thought I would die, and I was looking up all kinds of things online.
I see. What kinds of things did you look up?
I thought about things like taking pills, cutting my wrists, or whether I should jump from somewhere. I thought it would be good if I could die easily.
You were looking for a way to die easily.
I thought maybe pills would be good, but it doesn’t seem like I can get them easily.

In the end, it’s empty. Living feels empty, and dying feels empty too.
I see. For you, the feeling of “emptiness” is the strongest of all.

Does emptiness go away? Loneliness and anxiety might be closest. It’s not that I have no motivation, and it’s not that I’ve lost something.

I see. Are the loneliness and anxiety stronger at work or in your private life? Is it okay if we keep talking? If you’re willing, could you tell me more? Earlier, you asked whether emptiness goes away, and I think one thing is that feeling emptiness isn’t a bad thing, so it may also help to acknowledge the part of yourself that feels that way. I hope you’ll share your feelings with us again here. Thank you for coming today.
Thank you.

interaction.content: (Hello. Thank you for meeting with me today.)
Hello. Thank you as well.
Hello, I’m a counselor. Thank you for coming to talk with me. To start, could you tell me your gender, age, and what you’d like to discuss?
Hello. I’m 35, male, and I’m struggling with my body shape. People tell me I’m fat.
Thank you for sharing that with me. I see, that would be something to struggle with. I’d like to ask a bit more—was there something that led you to start feeling this way?
Yes. I don’t really think so myself, but my friends say it to me every time, and I’ve been trying hard to lose weight.
I see. Even though you don’t feel that way yourself, being told that by your friends must feel confusing.
Yes. Is being fat a bad thing?
I don’t think it’s a bad thing, and I think it’s okay as long as you yourself are okay with it.
Right. I’m glad you understand.

Yes, I get the sense that you want to accept yourself as you are, and I think that’s a wonderful thing. Even so, you’ve been making efforts because your friends have said these things to you. What kinds of things have you tried so far?
I tried fasting and training, but none of it lasted very long.
I see… You really made a lot of effort. Is there anything else?
Nothing else. I guess I’ve given up, or I’ve lost the energy to try to lose weight. When I think, “I have to lose weight,” my body starts feeling wrong.
Yes, when you go through something so hard and it doesn’t pay off, it makes sense that you’d start feeling that way.
Yes.
I see, that sounds painful in a different way. What happened physically when your body started feeling wrong?
My body shakes, and I start sweating. My breathing gets irregular too, and I’ve even collapsed before.

That’s serious…! If it ends up harming your health, that defeats the purpose. After going through something so difficult and having it not work out, you don’t feel anymore that you want to lose weight—is that right?
I do think maybe it would be better if I lost weight, but I’m scared of feeling sick. I didn’t know what to do, so I came to talk about it.

That makes sense. It’s better not to do anything so extreme that it makes you feel unwell. In that case, one option might be to have a professional help you manage your health and reduce weight gently, little by little. How does that sound?
Yes… I feel a little hesitant about being managed by someone, but I’ll think about it.
Yes, having someone oversee things may feel a little uncomfortable.
Yes…

Yes, that takes courage. I was wondering if maybe there are mixed feelings there—part of you feeling like it might be okay to give up for now, and another part wondering if you should lose weight after all. How does that feel to you?
Yes, I think there’s a conflict inside me.
Yes, it’s hard to know what to do. I imagine that conflict may be there because you have a wish to take care of yourself. How does that sound?
I think that’s true. But I’m also really bothered by what other people say.
Yes, I see. Is it only your friends who say that to you? Or are there other people too? It’s true, if someone says something like that to your face, it’s hard not to be bothered by it.
My friends, my family, and people at work say it too.
I see, so it’s not just your friends. That would get to you… For example, during health checkups and things like that, have you also been advised to lose weight?
Yes, the numbers show that I’m obese.
I see, so that may be part of why you feel you have to lose weight.
Maybe that’s true.
Yes. Does that not seem very related?
I’m sorry, but more than being fat or losing weight, I’m more concerned about the fact that I start feeling physically unwell.
That makes sense. It’s your important body, so I also think the most important thing is for your health to be in a good state.
Yes. Could it be some kind of illness?
You’re worried it might be an illness because when you try to lose weight, you start feeling physically unwell—is that right?
Yes. When I think, “I have to lose weight,” I get palpitations, I have trouble breathing, and I can’t stop sweating.
I see. I can only imagine how exhausting that must be… It sounds like you feel pushed that far into a corner.
Yes, it’s really exhausting.
While you’re going through something that exhausting, thinking about losing weight seems, at least for now, very painful. How does that feel to you?
Yes, it’s very painful. So I should just not think about trying to lose weight, right?
Thinking about things that lead to losing weight, or taking actions toward it, is itself causing your health to worsen… That sounds really exhausting.
Yes.
If that’s the case, I feel that the top priority right now may be to care for your precious mind and body. How does that sound?
Yes, first I’ll take care of my body and my mind.
You’re very worried about your health getting worse, and as I said earlier, I think that’s because you have a strong desire to take good care of your body.
Is that so? I hadn’t really noticed that myself.
Yes, that’s what I felt as I listened to you. When we worry about someone, isn’t it sometimes because that person is important to us?
That’s true. Yes, that happens.
Yes, it may be unconscious, but I think you are someone who values your own body and mind. And you, just as you are, are truly wonderful. You are okay just as you are.
Thank you. No one has ever said that to me before.

Yes, I truly feel that way. I think it’s wonderful that you care about yourself. I think having your health be stable matters more than anything. So if there’s something you’re worried about, having a specialist take a look can also be one reassuring option. What do you think? And if you feel conflicted again, or feel like you need to let things out, please come here anytime.
Yes, I understand. Thank you. My anxiety has eased quite a lot.
I’m glad to hear that! I sincerely hope your feelings stay calmer and your health remains stable. If you ever feel anxious again, please do let me hear about it.
Yes, I’ll come again. Thank you.

Yes, thank you for coming to talk with me today. I imagine even letting your feelings out may have been exhausting. You did really well. And thank you as well—I look forward to speaking with you again. With that, we’ll end the consultation here.
Thank you very much. Thank you for your time.
Thank you very much. (Thank you for speaking with me. Thank you for your time.)
Thank you very much.

Thank you. But I'm going to a junior high school team starting next year, so I'm anxious.
I see. When you're moving to a new team, you don't know what it will be like, so of course that feels worrying.
Yes. I've been told that if I stay unable to eat like this, my body won't get stronger and I won't be able to keep up, so I'm anxious.
I see. If people say that to you, it makes you feel like you have to make your body bigger quickly, and that can make you panic. I can really feel how anxious you are, Tomoki.
Yes, coaches and people around me say it too, so I want to do something about it.
I see. What does your family say?
My parents say, if I can't eat, then maybe I don't have to force myself to eat.
I see. Thank you for telling me all of that. Would it be alright if I go over the situation here?
Yes, please.

Thank you. Tomoki, you're on a strong soccer team, you've kept going with tough practices for five years, and you're playing in about half the games, right? That takes a lot of effort, and I feel that it's really admirable that you've continued this far.
Thank you.

But as you're moving up to a junior high school team next year, people around you and your coaches have told you that if things stay the way they are, you won't be able to keep up, and you're feeling very anxious and rushed. It must be really painful to think that you might not be able to keep up in soccer, after working so hard at it. You want to somehow eat more and make your body bigger, but you can't really eat, and that makes the pressure build more and more.
Yes. That's right.
I can really feel how anxious you are, Tomoki. Let's think together about what you can do!
Please!
Tomoki, how much do you feel like you have to eat?
Everyone around me eats two bowls of rice, so I think I need to eat about that much.
I see. Two bowls of rice at every meal?
At lunch after practice, or dinner.
I see. Right now, how many meals are you able to eat in a day?
Usually three meals.

Thank you. So right now, Tomoki, you're eating one bowl of rice each at breakfast, lunch, and dinner. And you're thinking it would be good if you could eat one more bowl each at lunch and dinner—is that right?
Yes, that's right.
But when you eat one bowl, you get full and it feels uncomfortable, right... How would it be to make it into rice balls and eat them outside of regular mealtimes?
I might be able to eat that way. I'll ask my parents!
I'm glad to hear that. If you can get the amount you're aiming for over the whole day, I think your body will probably grow bigger too.
Yes, I understand. Thank you!

Thank you for sharing your anxious feelings with me. If you feel unsure again about what to do, let's think it through together here. You're welcome anytime. I'm thinking we'll end here for today—how does that sound?
Yes, that's okay! If it doesn't go well, I'll come talk again!
(Thank you for your time despite being busy. I learned a lot. I look forward to working with you again.) Do your best. I'm rooting for you! I'll send the closing message now.
