interaction.content: (Hello, we’ll begin when it’s time. Thank you.)
(Hello. Thank you, I appreciate your time.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming to talk with me today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to discuss?
(I have another appointment scheduled right after this. Please understand.)
(Thank you for letting me know.)
I’m 48, female, and my concern is that I can’t stop drinking because of stress. (I’m sorry. Thank you.)
Thank you for sharing that. That sounds really hard. When did this start happening?
I think it was about five years ago, after my husband started changing jobs repeatedly.
I see. You’ve been struggling with this for a long time. The stress must be quite significant if it’s to the point where you can’t stop drinking. What kinds of things are you feeling stressed about?

There are various things, but he changed jobs without even discussing it with me, and even though I work while also doing housework and raising the children, I’m treated like it’s just expected that I work. Right now I’m taking care of two children on my own, including taking them to lessons and activities, so I have no time.
I see. Thank you for telling me. With your husband, your children, and the housework, you’ve been doing so much on your own.
Yes. My husband only has to work, and then if things don’t go well, he quits right away. We keep losing more and more money, and it’s really hard.
I see. That would really build up a lot of emotional strain. Is there anyone you can talk to about this?
I have talked to friends about my husband’s work. But I haven’t told anyone about the money issues or about not being able to stop drinking.
I see. I’m glad you have friends you can talk to about your husband’s work. The money and drinking have been things that are hard to talk about. How much do you drink?
Yes. It’s hard to say even to friends. I drink almost every day. I think the amount is probably a lot too.
I see. If the amount is also a lot, I wonder if your sleep might be shallow. How is that for you?
I don’t often wake up in the middle of the night, but when I’m drinking, I can’t stop, and I end up going to bed late.
I see. So it ends up getting late at night. Does your husband know that you’re carrying this much?
He knows, but he’s the kind of person who thinks of himself first, so I don’t think he’s that worried about it.
I see. When someone thinks that way, it can feel lonely.
Yes. If I try to talk to him, it only turns into a fight, so I feel like there’s no point in consulting him.
I see. Fighting takes a lot of energy too, doesn’t it.
Yes. It’s always been that way. I just wish he would at least bring in money properly, but he keeps changing jobs, and I may be past the point of anger now.

I see... Up to now, you’ve told me a lot: about your husband changing jobs without discussing it with you, feeling like you’re expected to handle childcare and housework, struggling financially, and wanting to stop drinking. I truly think you’re getting through each day while working so hard, in such a difficult situation, as a wife and as a mother. What is the thing you most want to change right now?
I want to stop drinking for my children’s sake too. At least I’d like to make it only on weekends or something.
Yes, it would be good if you could go from drinking every day to only on weekends. What do you think might help you make it only weekends?
I’ve tried many times to drink other beverages on weekdays, but it didn’t last. Other than that, maybe not buying alcohol... I’ve also thought before about going to a doctor and getting medication.
I see. The fact that you tried shows you have the ability to take action. I think trying to stop many times is a positive effort. Did you end up seeing a doctor?
I haven’t seen a doctor.
I see. When you buy alcohol, how do you usually buy it?
I buy it while I’m shopping for groceries, or at convenience stores and places like that.
I see. By the way, how much do you buy at one time?
Something like around three cans, or one pack of six cans.
I see... I have one suggestion about the alcohol. Would it be okay if I shared it with you?
Yes, please.

Thank you. When you buy alcohol, please try to buy just one can at a time. If it isn’t on hand, I think the amount you drink won’t increase. It’s a strategy to reduce the amount by making drinking take more effort. How does that sound?
I see. By the way, what do you mean by making drinking take more effort?
Yes, I mean that in order to drink, you would have to go out of your way to buy it.
I go shopping almost every day, so I end up buying it while I’m there, but I’ll try buying it thinking, “Just this one for today.”
That sounds good. If you think, “Just this one for today,” it may also help you drink more slowly. Does that feel like something you can start right away?
Yes. I’ll try doing that on weekdays.
Yes, please do give it a try. On days off, how do you do your shopping?
On days off, I sometimes go shopping with my children.
I see. That sounds like a nice time. How would it be to keep buying just one can then too?
On days off, I do feel like I want to enjoy drinking...

I think that feeling of wanting to enjoy it is lovely. Instead of just the amount, it might also be nice to enjoy the different brands. If you have your children choose one by the label design, you might be able to enjoy it even with a smaller amount.
Yes, that’s another way to enjoy it, isn’t it.
Yes, please do try it. I think your children are lucky to have a mother who wants to stop drinking for their sake too. I’m rooting for you as you work toward change.
Thank you. I’ll try it.
We’re almost out of time. How was it for you, talking up to this point?
I feel relieved because the things I can probably do have become clear.
I’m glad. I think you have the strength to change yourself. For yourself, and for your precious children, please try starting today.
Yes. Thank you! (I learned a great deal today. Thank you very much. I will complete the evaluation today. I’m also sorry about the timing.)
I’ll send the closing message now. If you’d like, please come back and tell me how it went with what you tried starting today. I’m rooting for you. Thank you for today.
(Thank you.)
(Likewise, there was a good sense of tension, and I learned from it. Thank you.)

interaction.content: I’m sorry for being late. Thank you for your time today.
(Hello. Thank you.) (I’m available until 1:00, but thank you for your time.)
Thank you for coming to talk today. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m in my 20s, female. I’m taking time off from work.
(Yes, thank you. Until 1:00, then. Thank you.)
I’d like to talk about what I should do from here.
Thank you for answering my questions. I see. Since when have you been taking time off from work?
Since last month.
I see. What would you like me to call you here?
“You” is fine.
Understood. Please feel free to talk about anything here.
Thank you.
So you’ve been taking time off from work since last month. If there was any particular trigger or anything, please tell me.
I started feeling unwell, and when I tried to go to work, I couldn’t get up.
I see. That sounds really painful. Are you feeling okay physically now?
Yes. It was hard for a while after I took time off from work, but now my health is starting to improve.
I see, I’m glad to hear that. Do you feel that what was happening at work had a big effect on starting to feel that way in the mornings?
I think it was probably mostly because of work.
I see. If there was anything specific, please tell me, only as much as you feel comfortable sharing.
My boss was always scolding me. I think it was because I couldn’t do my job properly.
So that was happening. Being scolded all the time must have felt very sad.
Yes. I was sad, and in the end I became scared to do my work.
Yes. That must have been really sad. Even through that, you kept working hard right up until the limit.
Yes. I feel like I did my best.

I really think you were working hard to keep going to work. That must have been painful. Have you talked to anyone about how you feel now or what you’re struggling with, or consulted anyone at the company?
Not really. I don’t think they would understand.
I see. In that case, I’m very glad that you came here today to talk like this. I hope we can think through this together so things can move even a little in a better direction.
Thank you.
Please tell me a little more about your workplace. What kinds of things does your boss scold you about? Was it also your boss who told you that you can’t do your job?
I do office work in manufacturing, and I started getting scolded more for things like making mistakes with orders and having a lot of mistakes in documents.
I see. When the scolding increases, it’s really painful. How long have you been doing your current job?
It’s been three years.
I see, so you’ve already been continuing there for quite a long time. By the way, what was it like when you first started the job?
I was new, so there was a senior coworker who taught me carefully.
I see. You had a good senior coworker by your side. I wonder if now you’re in the senior position, and there’s no longer anyone there to teach you.
Yes, the senior coworker I relied on left the company last year.
I see... That must have been very sad. So other than the senior coworker who left, it feels like there isn’t really anyone you can consult with now.
There aren’t any women, and it’s hard for me to consult with other people well.
I see, so it’s a workplace with a lot of men. By the way, have you ever talked to the senior coworker who left about your current situation?
Yes, I’ve talked to that senior coworker a little bit now.
I see. That person understands the situation at the workplace too, and is probably the easiest person for you to talk to.
Yes.
When you talked with that senior coworker, what did they say?
They’ve been teaching me various things about communicating with the people around me, but I just can’t really talk or consult with people very well.

So they gave you that kind of advice. I think they’re concerned about you, their junior coworker they worked with for so long. You feel that communicating with others is difficult. Even so, is there anyone like someone who joined at the same time as you, or someone who’s easy to talk to?
They’re a senior coworker I can rely on. I’m not good at talking with men. Everyone around me is older than me.
I see. So that’s why you couldn’t talk to anyone, and you kept trying your best all this time, but then you became unable to get up in the morning... You’ve really done so well to make it this far.
Thank you.
Having talked about all these feelings up to now, how are you feeling at this moment?
I feel like maybe I really should quit my job after all.
That’s how you’re feeling. This is a job you’ve worked hard at for three years, and your dependable senior coworker is gone, and you’ve been getting scolded more often.
Yes.
Your health has suffered to the point where you can’t get up in the morning, and you feel that maybe you should quit your job now. Because you’re someone who works so hard, it must have been painful.
Yes, thank you.
How would it be to try telling someone at the company that this is how seriously you’re thinking about it?
Yes, I suppose I do need to have a proper talk with them soon.
I’m sure it may not have gotten across to other people, and there may also be a bit of an assumption on your boss’s part that since you’ve worked together for three years, you should understand.
That may be true. They said it to me a lot: “Why don’t you understand after doing this for three years!”
Yes, that’s right. Talking about your own feelings takes a lot of courage, but I think if you try talking with them, something may change.
Thank you. (I’m sorry. We’re in the middle of talking, but I have plans, so I’ll have to excuse myself. I learned a lot.) (I’m sorry to leave in the middle.)
No, I’m sorry as well. Thank you.

In middle school, badminton. I’m not doing anything now.
You played badminton. Did you ever win any awards, or have experience as a club captain?
Last year we couldn’t really practice much, and I didn’t get any results. I don’t have any leadership experience either.
I see. Then maybe you miss your friends from middle school and are holding back the feeling of wanting to talk with them?
It’s lonely spending time by myself. When I think about summer break ending... it’s painful.
Of course. It sounds like you don’t have many close friends right now, and being alone is really hard.
Yes... I don’t want to go to school.
The feeling when summer break ends can be really unpleasant. Are you still in touch with your middle school friends, like on LINE? You can enjoy talking with your middle school friends, right?
I do LINE with my friends from middle school.
Is there no one from high school you message with? If you made a close friend, school might become more enjoyable.
Groups have already formed, so it’s hard to join in.
Groups are hard to enter. It must feel very lonely, and it’s hard to feel energetic, isn’t it.
Yes... What should I do?

I see. When you got accepted into the competitive school, you were happy, but that was short-lived, and now you’re feeling lonely because you haven’t made friends. But you did your best and kept going to school, so please praise yourself for that.
Yes. But it’s painful.

I’m sure you’re someone who works hard, and you probably don’t want to worry your parents. You must be carrying sad feelings. It would be good if there were someone around you who you could talk to, even a little, about how you feel. It might make you feel a bit lighter. It may take a little courage, but what do you think?
I came here because I can’t talk to anyone.
I see. Can you talk to your middle school friends about how you feel?
Even if I talk about what’s happening at school, it won’t solve anything, so I don’t talk about that kind of thing.

Then the sadness must feel even bigger. Do you like places with nature? Try to notice things like the smell of the forest or the sound of running water. It may help soften your feelings. You may be someone who is considerate of the people around you. I hope that, with that kindness you have, you’ll be able to talk a little with the people around you in a natural way.
Yes.

If you make friends, school will probably become more enjoyable, and you may start feeling more motivated to study too. Since you were able to get accepted into a competitive school, I hope that once your motivation to study comes back, things will be okay. That’s all for today, but if there’s anything else you’d like to talk about, please come and talk with me again.
Yes, thank you very much.
Thank you as well. We’ll end here for today. Thank you for your work in the client role.

interaction.content: (Hello. I’ll be playing the counselor role. Thank you for working with me today. I’ll begin when it’s time.)
(Thank you for today. If you have any requests for the client, please let me know.)
(Thank you. It would be helpful if we could do a work-related concern.)
(Understood. By the way, would something like interpersonal relationships be okay?)
(Yes, interpersonal relationships are fine. Thank you.)
(Understood. Thank you.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in for a consultation today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to discuss?
Hello. Thank you. I’m 42, female, and I’m struggling with relationships at work.
Thank you. So it’s about relationships. Could you tell me a bit more about that?

Yes, thank you. Actually, I have a coworker who’s about the same age and gender as me, but our ways of working are so different that I’m struggling with it. It feels like the things I try to do are being undermined behind the scenes.

I see. When your ways of working are that different, it can be hard to know what to do, can’t it. And on top of that, feeling like the things you’re trying to do are being undermined behind the scenes must feel really unpleasant. Have you ever actually talked with that coworker about the differences in your approaches?

Yes, exactly... It’s really stressful. But if I openly fight with her, I feel like people will think we’re both at fault, so I’m having a hard time holding back my anger. Let’s see... I do try to have conversations like, “Wouldn’t it be better to do it this way?” or “I’d like to do this—what do you think?” But she often says things like, “You’re overthinking it,” or “You don’t need to go that far.”

It’s really stressful when you can’t do your work the way you think is right, isn’t it. And yes, if it turns into an open conflict, there’s a risk the situation could get worse. I can feel how sincerely you approach your work, and how you’re trying hard to manage your emotions, finding ways to communicate carefully to the other person. It sounds like the other person may not be taking it quite as seriously. By the way, have you ever talked about this with your supervisor or other coworkers?

Yes, I do want us to be able to work together comfortably. If something feels like a burden to my coworker, I want to stop doing that too, and it’s not that I dislike her. It’s just that even things I’m trying to do individually, she tries to get rid of by making it a rule for everyone, or something like that... Yes, it feels like she doesn’t want to do bothersome things, and she doesn’t want me to do them either. Maybe if I do them, she feels like she has to do them too. The other coworkers are mostly men, and their positions are a little different too. The women are all more junior than us. So it’s a little hard to ask for advice. My female coworker and I are in the same position.

I see. It doesn’t sound like an environment where it’s easy to talk things over. I get the sense that you have a strong desire to improve and grow. And maybe that’s why you’re making suggestions for improvement. On the other hand, your coworker seems like the type who works according to the overall rules.

Thank you. Really? Actually, I’m a junior high school teacher, and for students who have behavioral issues, I want to build trusting relationships with both the students and their parents by doing things like home visits, even outside of the times when problems happen. But my coworker goes home once she’s dealt with the issue, because doing that would make her stay late. Since each homeroom teacher has their own way of doing things, I think it’s fine for each person to do it their own way, but she says I should go home earlier too. She’s also working on the administration, saying that because work hours get long, we should avoid doing more student guidance than necessary as much as possible. I think it’s necessary, so I feel that’s wrong. The administration does understand, but... The administration too, I mean. Sorry.

So you’re a junior high school teacher. Supporting children in adolescence sounds like it comes with many emotional demands. I truly respect your stance as a teacher. The children who have you looking after them are fortunate. The way you approach your work as a teacher isn’t something just anyone can do.

I’m happy to hear you say that. Of course I get tired too, so I don’t spend that much time on things I can’t agree with, but I wonder why she does things that affect other people’s ways of working. Do you think so? Maybe there are ways I overdo it too... But for me, each student is an individual, and they only have one life and one junior high school experience, so I want to support them in making it better.

I can really picture you doing everything you can with all your effort, out of care for your students. At the same time, since fatigue does seem to build up easily, I’m also concerned about your physical well-being. By the way, when do you feel that maybe you might be overdoing it?

Let’s see... Physically, it’s hardest after events, I think. After field trips or the sports festival, quite a few teachers take time off. I try to take time off at a different time. Overall, it does feel like a job that depends a lot on physical stamina. I agree with the general direction of reducing the overall burden.

So you feel it’s especially physically hard after events. I get the sense that being in good condition, both physically and mentally, is what allows you to live out the kind of teacher you want to be.
Yes, I’ve gradually come to understand when it’s good to take some rest, so I’m trying to be careful not to end up taking sudden days off.
That’s good. It would be great if you could realize the way you want to be while keeping your own condition stable.
Yes, managing my health and stamina is important, isn’t it. Right now, I feel like I’m more or less able to do the kind of work I want to do.
I’m glad to hear that. You’re not going too far at all—you’re a model teacher.
Thank you. I can’t believe you’d say that... I’m so happy!!

I truly mean that. In a sense, the teaching profession may not have clear “boundaries.” Because of that, some people work really hard, while others may feel satisfied as long as they’re doing what’s required according to the rules. I want to support the way you are as a teacher, cherishing each and every student.

Yes, I think there are conflicts that come from not having clear “boundaries.” When I was new, I realized how much I lacked compared to veteran teachers too. But I think doing my best in my own way is what leaves me feeling the most settled. So I really just can’t understand my coworker’s way of doing things... She even talks to the administration and other coworkers to stop me from doing what I do... If she’s drawing a line around work like that, I wish she’d just enjoy her private life. Sorry, I ended up complaining 💦 Your support gives me strength!! Thank you 😊

You’re thinking not only about the students but also about building trust with their parents. It may be that your coworker, seeing how dedicated you are, feels some pressure or anxiety. I wondered if perhaps she sees you, working so hard in your own way, as something a bit dazzling.

That’s possible, isn’t it. It certainly might be, but... even when we go out for drinks, she doesn’t really talk about herself much, so it seems hard to change her. If there’s something bothering her, I’d want to cooperate if it’s work-related, and if she wants to go home early, I’d want to support that too... Maybe that’s not what it’s about. But I do want to work the way I think is right, so that’s something I can’t give up. I want to prevent her from maneuvering things so that stopping what I’m trying to do becomes the overall opinion. I want to prevent it, but putting energy into that is painful... But maybe it’s a necessary battle? I feel like I’m not good at defending myself or fighting back.

Yes, I also don’t think you can change your coworker. There’s a saying: “You can’t change the past or other people.” I think it may be important to focus on your own tasks... You’ve come this far while carrying all kinds of emotions and feeling troubled by your coworker, haven’t you. And I think you’ve also reaffirmed that doing your best in your own way is what helps you feel clear and settled.

Yes, thank you for thinking through this with me. What would my current task be? Since I’m able to do my work in a way that feels right to me, I thought maybe I need to learn how to fight, but... I can also imagine it would be stressful.

This is a psychological concept, but there’s an idea called “separating tasks.” To put it simply, I feel it may be about moving forward toward the way you want to be as a teacher. For that purpose, I think it may be about focusing on things like maintaining your mental and physical balance, and finding ways to reduce the burden in areas where you feel you may be overdoing it. How does that sound?

Thank you. I really appreciate advice from a professional perspective. Yes... then, for example, if it seems like someone is going to stop me from doing what I want to do, I would also need to work hard to prevent that so I can do it... If it’s just myself, I can control things or make an effort, but it’s hard when other people or the environment have an influence, because that’s difficult to control. I also feel that maybe that’s what it means to live in society.

You’re absolutely right. I do think it’s difficult to change other people or the environment. And that’s something you can feel precisely because you’ve experienced society. We’ve reached the end of our time today. As you think about what can be changed and what cannot be changed, please do come back again for another strategy meeting so you can keep moving forward.

Today was really educational for me. I realized that the thing that had been simmering inside me because I couldn’t accept it was one of the things I need to face from now on. The situation hasn’t changed, but I feel like what I need to do has become clear. That said, I may get stressed by my coworker’s behavior, or get tired of fighting, so when that happens, I’d really like to consult with you again. I was truly happy to receive so much strong, heartfelt encouragement. Thank you very much.

Through our time together, I think it’s a major step forward that what you need to do has become clear. I also received a lot of courage from the way you are as a teacher. I think it’s also a profession where stress can build up easily, so it’s important to let things out in moderation. “Being good at resting means being good at working.” Please come anytime. I’m wholeheartedly cheering you on. Thank you for coming in for a consultation today. (I’m sorry this ran late. I’ll end the role-play here, if that’s okay with you.)

Yes, thank you for the lovely message ☺️ I think counseling work must be hard too, but I’m grateful for your support. I look forward to working with you again. (No, I’m sorry too. It’s okay to end here!)
(Thank you.)

I see. When you go through something like that, it’s really painful, isn’t it.
I keep thinking I need to get over it quickly, but I just keep thinking about it.
I see. You’re trying to think positively about what you should do. And even so, it won’t leave your mind, and that’s been really hard for you.
Yes.
I’m concerned about your mind and body, so I’d like to ask—are you able to eat and sleep?
I’m able to eat, but at night I can’t really sleep. It even shows up in my dreams.
I see. That must be really painful. When it even comes up in your dreams, not only your body but your mind can’t really rest either.
Yes, it’s really hard.
That makes sense. Right now, while you’re in this situation that feels so hard, how have you been getting through your days?
I’m somehow managing to go to work. But I’m still dragging the mistake around with me, and I can’t feel motivated.
I see. Even while things feel so hard, you’re doing your best to keep working.
I’m not doing my best. Even though I have to make up for it.

That’s how it feels to you. After such a painful experience, when your mind and body haven’t been able to rest safely, I think it’s natural to feel that way. Right now, while you’re having trouble sleeping at night and working with such painful feelings, how do you feel?
I feel really sorry for causing trouble for everyone on the team. I know I need to move on quickly, but I can’t, and I don’t know what to do.
That’s how you feel. Even while you’re carrying such painful feelings, you’re thinking about the team and the people around you too.
It was my mistake, so...
I see. When you think about work and about yourself, it makes you feel rushed, doesn’t it.
Yes, I feel rushed.
Have you talked to anyone else about how you’re feeling right now?
No, I haven’t talked to anyone. I don’t want to cause any more trouble... And even if I talk to my friends, I think I’d only make them worry...
I see. You’ve been struggling with this on your own while it’s been so painful. Thank you for finding the courage to talk about it today.
No, thank you... I’m sorry for having you listen to something that isn’t such a big deal...

That’s not true. I think these are very important feelings. For example, if one of your teammates went through the same thing you did, was struggling in the same way, and you saw them still trying hard at work, how would you feel?
Well, I’d think they were doing their best, and I’d want to help them.
That’s how you’d feel. I wonder if your teammates might feel the same way. What do you think?

Do you think so...? It’s true that everyone on my team is kind, so maybe they might think that. But it’s hard to talk to them. I’m already a working adult, and I can’t even sort out feelings like this by myself.

That’s how it feels to you. Those are important feelings. If it feels hard to talk to someone, one option is to start by helping yourself rest at night, even just at night—for example, drinking something warm or doing some stretching. What do you think? After listening to what you’ve shared, I thought it might ease your feelings even a little, so I wanted to suggest it.
Thank you. I think I’ll try it. But will that really help me sleep? I feel like I’ll still end up thinking about it. What can I do to switch my feelings over?
That’s how it feels. Another way to help sort out your feelings is to write them down on paper, tear it up, and throw it in the trash. What do you think?
There’s a method like that, huh. I’ll try it at night when I can’t sleep.
Please do try it. We’re almost out of time for today, but how was it for you to talk today?
Thank you for telling me about things like writing my feelings on paper. I do think I’ll try it, but honestly, I don’t know if that will help me move on emotionally.

That’s how you’re feeling. If you don’t feel it’s helping, I’d be glad to listen from where we leave off and help you sort through your feelings. From talking with you today, I felt that you’re someone who is very sincere and is trying hard to move forward. I think everyone on your team knows how hard you’re trying, and I’m also rooting for you so that your feelings can become even a little more settled.
Thank you.
Well then, we’ll end today’s consultation here. Thank you for sharing such important feelings with me.
Thank you for listening to me.
(Thank you for your work today. Thank you very much.)
(Thank you for your work today. Thank you very much.)

interaction.content: Good evening. Thank you for being here today.
Thank you as well. I look forward to speaking with you.
We’ll begin at the scheduled time.
Understood.
Good evening. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming today. To start, if it’s all right, could you tell me your gender, age, and what you’d like to talk about?
Good evening. Thank you for speaking with me.
Thank you as well. I look forward to speaking with you.
Male, 28. It’s not a big deal, but I’m struggling with something related to a hobby.
Thank you for telling me. You’re struggling with something about your hobby—what’s been going on?
I’m wondering whether I should quit my hobby of fishing.
Mm-hmm. You’re wondering whether to quit fishing... Could you tell me a little more about what’s going on?
I haven’t been doing it at all lately, so I think maybe I should quit, but I can’t quite make up my mind.
I see. You can’t quite make up your mind...? Have you had fishing as a hobby for a long time?
I started about four years ago.
Yes. I see. What made you start?
A friend invited me, and that’s how I started.
So being invited by your friend was what got you started... I don’t know much about fishing myself, but I imagine there’s ocean fishing and river fishing and so on. What kind of fishing do you do?
That friend fishes in all kinds of places, so together we tried various environments, like the ocean and rivers.

Mm-hmm. So you enjoyed fishing with your friend in various places. You’ve been fishing for about four years, and earlier you said you can’t quite bring yourself to quit... You said you haven’t been doing it lately, but are there any other reasons you want to quit?
Even though I don’t use it, having the gear sitting at home feels kind of wasteful, or like... it feels strange to own fishing gear when I don’t use it.
Mm-hmm. So you feel it’s wasteful to keep fishing gear at home that you don’t use. It feels strange to have gear you don’t use?
It just feels kind of unpleasant.
Mm-hmm. It feels unpleasant... But you’re still having trouble making up your mind?
That’s right.
I see... Why is it that you haven’t been going fishing lately?
Maybe because going has started to feel like a hassle.
Mm-hmm. It feels like a hassle... It sounds like you enjoyed fishing at the ocean and rivers with your friend for four years. What parts of fishing were enjoyable for you and kept you doing it?
Once I go, I do find fishing itself interesting. Catching something, of course, and even the waiting part feels interesting. It’s also fun doing it together with my friend.

Mm-hmm. So fishing was enjoyable... The time spent waiting for a catch and being with your friend were enjoyable too. You’ve been feeling that going fishing is a hassle—when did you start feeling that way?
In the past year or two.

Mm-hmm. So you’ve been feeling it was a hassle for quite a while. Why do you think you started feeling that way? You’ve been feeling this for some time, then. The fishing itself sounds enjoyable, so why did it start to feel like a hassle?
I don’t really feel motivated to go at early hours or at night, and if I’m alone, I’m not that proactive about it.
Mm-hmm. Early mornings and nights really can be tough... If you’re alone? Does your friend not go?
There are times when we go together. Also, my friend says, “You should try going even when you’re alone,” so there were times I tried going by myself.
I see. How was fishing by yourself?
Hmm. It wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t like it was really great either.
Mm-hmm. So it wasn’t especially fun or not fun—kind of neither... If you were to quit fishing and get rid of the fishing gear, how do you think you would feel afterward?
I might not really mind that much. I’m not especially bothered by the fact that I’m not using it now, either.
You think you might not really mind... If you got rid of the fishing gear, what do you think would happen with your friendship?
I don’t think he’d dislike me or anything. I’m just concerned about how he would feel.

Mm-hmm. So you’re concerned about what your friend might think, but it seems like your friendship would probably continue as it is... If you quit fishing, how would you want to spend your time? I mean, if you did quit fishing.
Hm? Do you mean me personally?
Yes. If you quit fishing, how would you want to spend your time? Or is there anything you’d like to do?
There isn’t anything in particular, but I like watching movies and overseas TV dramas.
Mm-hmm. Movies and overseas dramas sound nice... Having talked through things up to this point, you said you couldn’t quite make up your mind. How does it feel now?
First, I feel like even if I quit and get rid of the gear, it probably wouldn’t have a big impact.
Mm-hmm. I see... The fishing gear doesn’t seem to weigh on you much, your friendship seems likely to continue, and you may have more enjoyment from watching movies and overseas dramas too.
I’m worried about my friend, or I guess it’s on my mind.
When you say you’re worried?
I wonder if it might make him feel down.

You’re a kind person... One suggestion would be to let your friend use the fishing gear, or have him use it for a while, and if you feel motivated again, you could get it back and go together. Or, as a thank-you for teaching you fishing, you could invite him to a movie...
Yes, that’s true. That’s one way to do it.

Please try starting with what feels doable. It looks like we’re just about out of time. I’m sorry I couldn’t fully support you through to the end. If anything else comes up, please feel free to come back anytime.
I understand. Thank you very much. This was helpful.
Thank you for coming to talk with me today.
Thank you as well.
(I’m sorry we went over time. I learned a lot from this. Thank you very much.) (I’ll end the session now. Thank you.)
(No, it’s all right on my end. I learned from this too. If there’s another opportunity, I’d appreciate it.) (Excuse me.)
Thank you as well. I look forward to it.

interaction.content: Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.
Thank you.
Hello, I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming today. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m 14. Female.
Thank you. What would you like to talk about today?
Everyone at school is ignoring me, and I don’t know what to do.
That must be really painful. Are you able to go to school?
I’m going. But honestly, I don’t want to go.
You’re doing your best even though you don’t want to go. When you say everyone—was it a close group of friends?
We all used to get along, but...
Yes.
There was a girl who was saying bad things about the girl who’s kind of at the center of the class, and after I spoke up against it, they started ignoring me.
I see... You were able to clearly say what you thought, and that was a good thing. But it’s sad, isn’t it.
Yes. If this was going to happen, I wish I’d just stayed quiet...
It was a brave thing to do, but you’re feeling a little regretful now. When they treated you that way, how did it make you feel?
At first I thought, well, whatever, it’s fine. But as more and more people started ignoring me, I started regretting it. Every day is just really painful...
That sounds really painful.
Yes.
At first it wasn’t everyone, but then it became everyone? Do you think there are any friends who feel the same way as you? Is there anyone among them who talks to you?
At first there were some girls who would talk to me normally, but even my closest friend is now with the people who ignore me. No one talks to me.
I see. Even your closest friend... You’re still going to school even though it’s so painful. That’s really impressive.
It’s getting mentally really hard, so I don’t want to go. But I don’t want my parents to find out.
Yeah... I can understand that. Is it hard to talk to your mother, too? Had you been close with that friend for a long time?
My parents don’t get along, and I don’t think they’re interested in me anyway. She’s been my friend since elementary school.
It’s sad, especially since she’s been your friend since elementary school. So that’s how you feel about your mother.
Yes.
If you tried talking to that friend or your mother, they might understand, but what do you think? Do you feel like you could find the courage to do that?
I don’t want to talk to the friend who chose to ignore me. As for my mother, I guess I’ll have to tell her if I stop going to school...
I see... How are things at school right now?
I’m alone the whole time.
That must be really hard and painful. Other people won’t talk to you either? How do you feel about the friends who are ignoring you?
They won’t. At first I was angry. But now I think maybe they’re doing it so they don’t get ignored too.
You think your friends are scared of being ignored themselves.
Yes.
In middle school, more people experience things like this than you might think...
Really?
Yes. I think most girls go through something like this.
How did everyone get through each day?
A lot of the time, people think, “I might be next,” so even if they really want to be on your side, they can’t. And middle school friends don’t often end up being lifelong friends.
I see.
That kind of thing happens a lot. We’re coming up on time soon, but were you able to talk about what you wanted to say?
Even if I’m alone right now, is it okay not to worry about it too much? Yes. Thank you. I feel a little better.
Even if you don’t worry about it too much, when you become an adult, you’ll really meet lots of people who understand how you feel.
Thank you!
Thank you for sharing with me. Since our time is up, we’ll stop here, but are you okay with that?
I’m okay!
Thank you. Please keep doing your best. Well then, take care.
I’ll try to stay positive and do my best! Thank you.
Thank you. Thank you for being the client today. I look forward to reflecting on it again with you.
Thank you for your time. Thank you very much.
Well then, take care.

interaction.content: (Thank you for matching with me! I look forward to speaking with you today.)
(Likewise, thank you. I look forward to speaking with you.)
(Then I’ll go ahead and begin.)
(Thank you.)
Hello, I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming to talk today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to discuss?
I’m 51, female, and I’d like to consult about my elementary school–aged son’s problematic behavior.
Thank you for telling me. It’s about your son’s problematic behavior, then. Could you tell me more about it?

Yes. He’s the youngest of three siblings, and he takes things he isn’t supposed to eat, like his older sister’s or older brother’s snacks, out of the refrigerator or cupboard on his own and eats them. And when it comes out that he ate them, he lies about it.
I see. Could you tell me the ages of the three siblings?
His sister is 18, his brother is 15, and he is 10. This has been going on ever since he was around 8.
So it’s behavior that started about two years ago. What do his older sister and brother say about it?
His older sister is kind of fed up with it. His older brother even had the Valentine’s chocolates he got from a girl friend eaten, so he gets furious sometimes.
His brother would get furious about that, wouldn’t he. And as his mother, you must also worry about sibling fights caused by that.

I’ve tried things like locking the refrigerator and hiding snacks where he can’t find them, but... he searches for them and eats them. So I stopped keeping extra snacks at home, too. Then, because the freezer is the only thing I can’t lock, he started eating things from the freezer. His older brother is a smart kid, so he’s able to handle it in a mature way, which does help.
I see. You’ve tried a lot of different things. His older brother sounds very level-headed. It sounds like your son will eat just about anything. What kind of lies does he tell?

About how he lies... when food disappears and everyone starts looking for it, he starts saying, “I didn’t eat it, it wasn’t me.” After that, he has hidden the wrappers and trash from what he ate all over the place, and we find them when we clean. Even when I show my son that trash, he still lies.
I see. When you find the trash, what does he say as a lie?

He says, “I didn’t eat it, it wasn’t me.” After that, everyone in the family says, “No one else in the family ate it, and we put trash in the trash can, so the only person who could have eaten it is you, right?” and he gets blamed... and then he reluctantly accepts that he ate it. We’ve repeated that hundreds of times.
In the end, he reluctantly accepts it. Hundreds of times?! That’s worrying. How often does he do it in a week?
I think it’s almost every day. He does it when the family isn’t watching, so timing-wise it’s when he’s alone on the first floor, or when the family is out shopping or something and no one is home.
I see... After he reluctantly accepts it, what does your son say?

At first he was young, so I thought maybe he didn’t understand that it was wrong, and I treated it as a matter of discipline... but no matter how many times I told him, he kept repeating it. Even if he gets scolded over and over, he does it. After he accepted it, he would say, “Okay, I won’t do it anymore.” But then he repeats it. I tried looking into all kinds of possible causes in my own way. There’s no doubt that he likes eating, but it felt pathological, so I worried, what if he has developed binge eating...? I asked him about it, but he’s not at an age where he can express it well in words, and I tried exploring different possibilities, but in the end I wondered if stress might be the cause... I think there are all kinds of stress, so then I started struggling because I couldn’t figure out what was causing that stress. It’s hard because he just can’t express it well in words. “nanke” → I meant “nanse.”
I see. Even when he says he understands now, he repeats it. If it feels pathological, that would make you anxious. You feel that stress is the cause.
I’m sure stress is the cause. Also, when he has free time, he acts on it.
So when he has free time, he does it. Do you and your son usually talk often?

He tells me everything. He can talk on his own, but it feels like he has poor expressive ability. I think he probably doesn’t really understand what’s happening inside himself either. I think he understands it in a vague way. For example, he has said things like, he ate because he was irritated. So that’s why I thought it was stress. Then when I ask, what made you irritated...? he has said things like, because a friend said something mean to him. So I understood that relationships with friends are stressful for him too. He also talked about his teacher. It’s all interpersonal relationships. Also, when his father scolds him, he gets irritated and eats things without permission too.

I see. It’s wonderful that you have a relationship where you and your son talk often. Your son himself said that he ate because he was irritated. And that stress is from interpersonal relationships. It really sounds like you care deeply about your son and have understood that much about him.

I understood that stress is the cause, and I wanted to remove that stress, so my son and I thought about a lot of things together... but because other people are involved, it’s really difficult. And even if my son is the one who needs to change, he’s still in elementary school, so that’s hard too. His friends make fun of him, his teacher is intimidating... I understand that he’s carrying all kinds of stress and turning to eating... but finding a solution is really difficult.

That’s true... Still, since you and your son usually talk a lot, I feel that from your son’s perspective, that must really help reduce his stress. Has your son said anything about what he wants to do about those relationships?

Regarding his friendships, he says he wants friends who won’t make him feel bad. But he’s also at an age where he still isn’t good at how to interact with friends, so we’re struggling with that. Finding other good friends hasn’t gone well either, and it would be good if he just didn’t play with friends who say hurtful things, but he’s good-natured and he wants to play, so it seems like he can’t refuse when they invite him.

He’s able to put it into words that much. If the relationship with the friend who makes him feel bad improves, things may move in a better direction. Have you, as his mother, ever spoken with that friend?

I became sure that he understands he must not eat other people’s things, so after that, I’ve been repeatedly and carefully telling my son that he needs to become able to release stress in a healthier way, and that I’m worried about his health too because he’s becoming obese. Yes, exactly. I wanted to talk with that friend, so I intentionally did. The child who was the biggest cause of stress from ages 8 to 9 was someone I had known since he was little. That child grew, and after turning 10, he stopped doing terrible things to my son. I think that’s because after I told my son that unless he shows it through his attitude, like saying “I don’t like that, stop,” the other person won’t understand, my son also worked hard and became able to say it. Since he turned 10, a child who transferred into his school seems to be causing him a lot of stress. My son thought the transfer student was lonely and felt sorry for him, so he invited him to play, but then that child started making fun of my son, and apparently it has become very stressful. My son is kind, but I suppose he’s too good-natured. It also seems like he feels that his kindness is being repaid with harm. Those disappointing and sad feelings become stress, and then he eats. As his mother, I understand that my son is clumsy and there are many things he can’t do, so friends probably say all kinds of things to him. But he hasn’t done anything wrong at all, so I feel sorry for him and worry about him.
When it starts affecting his health too, that’s worrying. He was able to show it through his attitude, and his friend’s response changed. The main cause now was the transfer student, then.

Yes. Right now, it is definitely the transfer student. So I wanted to talk with that transfer student, and I did. Unlike my son, the way he lies felt very scary. He lied to the homeroom teacher and his mother about having verbally abused my son. My son can’t tell that kind of lie. My son would absolutely never tell a lie that hurts someone. Though he does lie about things he has eaten...

I see. Your son doesn’t tell lies that would hurt people like that. After hearing everything you’ve shared, I feel that you are a mother who cares very deeply about your son, and that your son is someone who cares about his friends. We’re just about out of time, but how was it for you to talk today?

Thank you for understanding. It was a very meaningful time for me too, because I was able to organize my thoughts about my son and my feelings toward him. Going forward, I’d like to talk with my son about, “Let’s look together for ways for you to release stress and ways of interacting with friends that suit you.” I’m thinking that surely the most important thing is to watch over him from a long-term perspective... I’m starting to see that my child’s growth will probably solve this issue too. I am still worried about the obesity, though. Once again, I feel that communication and self-acceptance are key points. As for the obesity, I’m wondering whether I should think about that separately.

I think those experiences and that growth will become a great source of strength for your son’s future. I imagine this is a difficult time right now, but I’m hoping for your son’s growth. It might also be good to support his health by doing things like going for walks together, and talking with him at those times.
Yes, that’s true. I’d like to increase the opportunities for us to move our bodies together, and try talking with him too.
Please do try that. We’ve gone a little over time, but thank you for coming to talk today. You’re welcome anytime, so please don’t hesitate to come back.
Thank you. I was able to feel hopeful that this can become a source of strength for my son’s future. Thank you for all the encouraging words. If there is another opportunity, I’d appreciate it.
Thank you as well for your time. I’ll take my leave now.
Thank you.
(I apologize for going 15 minutes over time.)
(No, I’m sorry too, I ended up talking too much.)
(Thank you again for playing the client role today. This is the second time, following last time. If there is another opportunity, I look forward to working with you again.)
(Oh, is that right? Thank you as well. I learned a lot.)
(Likewise, it helped me picture things and was a learning experience. I’ll take my leave now.)

interaction.content: Good evening. My name is Hachiko, and I’ll be acting as the counselor. Thank you for being here today.
Good evening. Thank you for your help today.
Thank you. We’ll begin at 9:00 p.m., so please wait just a little while.
Understood.
All right, let’s begin. Thank you for being here. (^^)
Thank you.
Nice to meet you. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming to talk with me. What brings you here today?
There’s something I’d like to talk about regarding my husband. My husband...
Of course. Please feel free to send your messages at your own pace.
He reached retirement age last year, and now he’s re-employed and goes to work a few days a week, but...
Yes,
When he’s at home, he seems like he doesn’t know what to do with his time. I’m wondering what kind of words I could say to help him find something he wants to do.
I see. When you see your husband seeming unsure how to spend his time at home, how does that make you feel?
I feel a little sorry for him. I want him to find something worthwhile.
Yes, that makes sense. It must feel a little lonely for you watching him like that, too...
Yes.
You mentioned that your husband is working a few days a week now. How does he seem at those times?
He doesn’t really have much of an expression. I don’t get the sense that he wants to go to work, or that he enjoys going. It’s re-employment, after all.
I see... In that case, it would make you even more worried.
That’s right. I worry that he’ll just keep getting older like this.
Yes, of course you want to see him looking lively and engaged. Before coming to talk with me, have you said anything to your husband about this?
Yes, I tell him all the time. I say, “You should find something you enjoy.”
I see. And what does your husband say when you tell him that?
He just says, “Even if you say something I enjoy...” and he doesn’t try to actually do anything.
Hmm, I see. In that case, I wonder if perhaps your husband may not be feeling especially dissatisfied or anxious about his current situation...? What do you think?
That may be true. He worked for the family all these years, so it would be fine if he just took it easy, but it feels lonely seeing him lose so much energy. It may just be my own selfish feeling.
Not at all. I can tell that you care very deeply about your husband.
Thank you. Is there anything I could say to him that might help him find something?
Let’s see. By the way, is there anything your husband has liked for a long time, or anything he’s interested in?
He likes watching baseball. When he was younger, he even made his own team and played.

I see! He even made a team—he must really love it. In that case, how about watching baseball together? That could be a starting point, and as the two of you talk about different things together, some of the passion that’s been sleeping inside him might come out again.

Yes, that’s true. He does sometimes go watch games with our son. Yes... that may be true. It may be important for me to talk with him a lot, too. Even when we’re at home, we may be living kind of separate lives.
I see. If that’s the case, not knowing how your husband is feeling may be making you feel even more worried.
Yes. Maybe I’m just worrying on my own. My husband may be satisfied with taking it easy, but is there something I could say that would help him have a small sense of purpose each day?
Let’s see... Then first, it may be a very small thing, but how about the two of you saying to each other, “Let’s have a fun day today!” as a little declaration? (^^)

Yes, that’s true. Some kind of words of encouragement may be effective. If my husband could spend his time in a way that feels like him, I would be satisfied too. But when I ask him, I don’t get a clear answer, so I end up worrying.

I’m sorry. I can really feel how worried you are about your husband. At the same time, I also think it may be important for you to value your own time as well. And I think opportunities to talk with your husband are important, too.

That may certainly be true. Maybe I’m getting caught up in how I spend my own time. Thanks to you, I feel like I have a general grasp of the situation now. Thank you. From now on, I’ll try to speak to my husband more and have conversations that help him feel more energized. Thank you very much.
I’m sorry if I went a little away from what you were hoping for. If anything comes up in your conversations with your husband that concerns you, please feel free to come talk anytime.
Yes, I’ll ask again when that time comes. Thank you very much for today.
Thank you for coming to talk with me today. I’ll be here if you’d like to come again.
Yes. Thank you very much. Excuse me.
(Thank you for your hard work. Thank you for today. I’ll end the role-play here. Excuse me.)
(Thank you very much. This was a good learning experience for me. Excuse me.)

interaction.content: Hello, thank you for being here today. When it’s time, we’ll go ahead and begin.
Thank you.
Hello, I’m the counselor. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m 35, female. I’m worried about my later years.
Thank you. So you have some worries about your later years. Could you tell me a little more specifically about that?
It’s about money too, but when I get older, my body may not move the way it does now. I’m single right now, so I worry about those things too.
I see. You’re worried about money and your health.
Yes, that’s right.
Does being single make those worries feel bigger?
That’s part of it. With money too, since I’m single, I think I probably need to save more. I don’t have a high income right now, so that’s on my mind too.
I see. You’re thinking constructively about the future and considering what you can do now.
I don’t know whether I can do it or not, but I am worried. I think it would be hard to suddenly raise my annual income or anything like that....
That’s true. Even so, I feel that facing your future seriously from now can make a difference. How does that sound to you?
I’m not really sure..
I see. Right now, does it feel like you’re full of worry?
Well, in the middle of this conversation, I don’t think I can suddenly say, yes, that’s right, I’m okay now....
Yes. As we continue talking from here,
what are you hoping for?
Rather than hoping for something, the concern I came to talk about is just like what I said at the beginning.
Yes, we’ve been talking about your worries about later life. You said your feeling right now is that you’re “not really sure,” but do you feel you’d like to think about specific steps you could take?
I only came here to talk, so if I’m suddenly asked to be specific, I’m not really able to answer right now, in various ways.
Since you’ve taken the time to come and talk with me, if you’re okay with it, would you like to think about it together a little?
Yes.
Thank you, I understand. Then I’d like to organize the keywords from what we’ve talked about so far. Is that okay?
Go ahead.
Money, age, income, health, being single. Among these, which one feels like it concerns you the most?
There isn’t really a number one. They’re all connected...
I see. It feels like they’re all connected. Where does it feel like the starting point is?
What do you mean by starting point? I don’t think worries have a number one, or a beginning or an end...
I mean something like where the worry began. Is there anything that comes to mind?
It’s hard to answer if you ask me precisely where it began. It’s as I said at the beginning.
I see... You said you’re worried about your later years. Is it something that comes to mind often in your daily life?

If I’m working, it’s connected to income too, so it comes to mind, and I think it comes up in all kinds of situations. It’s not like there’s one specific time, one specific moment, when I suddenly remember it..
That’s true, there are moments when you feel it in daily life. Regarding your worries about later life, is there anything else you’d like to talk about?
Not especially... Just about what I said at the beginning.
You said that when you get older, your body may stop moving well.
Yes, that’s right.
They say we’re in an era where people may live to 100, so it’s a worry many people have. Are you doing anything to keep your body healthy?
Well, to some extent I do try to take care of my health.
Yes, you’re still young, and even if you’re taking care of your health, as you keep working hard every day, there are times when worries suddenly come up.

When the body gets old, it can become unable to walk, and that kind of thing can happen normally. I don’t think it’s necessarily an illness, but something that can naturally happen as a possibility...

Yes, that’s true... Aging—of course you haven’t experienced it yet, and we only see or hear about it, so it’s natural to worry about what might happen to you. Listening to you, I felt that you may already be accepting the fact of “aging.” How does that sound to you?
Yes. To some extent, I do imagine that kind of possibility.
I felt that you’ve already prepared yourself emotionally for something that many people find almost unimaginable. I’m very sorry that I wasn’t able to be of help today.
No, thank you for listening to me. (Thank you for staying right up to the end of the time. It’s okay to close now.)
We’ve reached the end of our time, but how was it for you to talk about this?

I hadn’t really thought of it that way myself, but when you said I’m preparing myself emotionally, I felt like that might be true. I mean, I hadn’t thought of it that way. When I see it that way, I feel like my current worries can feel more positive.
I see. I’m relieved to hear that you were able to feel that way.
Yes. Thank you very much.
I felt that you really value yourself. I’m sorry we went over time. Thank you very much for today.
I appreciate you saying that. No, thank you very much.
If anything else comes up, please feel free to come and talk with me again.
Yes.
We’ll end here. Thank you very much. Take care.

interaction.content: (Hello. Thank you for meeting with me today.)
(Hello. Thank you as well.)
(This is my first time in the counselor role today, so there may be some things I don’t do perfectly, but thank you for your understanding.) (When it’s time, I’ll begin.)
(Understood. Thank you.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming. What would you like to talk about today?
Hello. Thank you. The girls in my class have been ignoring me... and it’s really painful.
That sounds really painful... If it’s okay with you, could I ask you to tell me a bit more about it?
Yes. It’s a group of five friends I’m close with, but starting about a week ago, all of a sudden, even when I talk to them, they all started ignoring me.
I see. Thank you for telling me. That would make you feel anxious, wouldn’t it. If you don’t mind, may I ask your age and gender?
Yes. I’m 13, and I’m a girl.
Thank you. Being ignored all of a sudden must have been really surprising. Is there anything that comes to mind about why it might have happened?

Yes. It really was sudden, and I was shocked. Right now, in the group, ignoring people is kind of a trend? Or, like, the girl who’s the leader will say things like, “Let’s ignore so-and-so starting tomorrow,” and then everyone reluctantly goes along with it, so maybe something like that happened without me knowing.
Right. I think it’s only natural that you’d feel anxious. I see. That’s really troubling... Are the girls in that group the only ones doing this?
Yes. For now, it’s only the girls in the group I’m close with.
I see. Thank you for telling me all of that. Let’s think together about what might help ease your anxiety.
Thank you. I appreciate it.
By the way, what would you like me to call you? If you’re comfortable, please tell me your name, or a nickname is fine too.
Please call me “Miki.”
Thank you. Miki, then.
Yes.
I hope your feelings can become even a little lighter, Miki. What do you think would need to happen for those anxious feelings to go away?
Hmm... Being ignored by the girls I was close with is really painful, so I want things to go back to the way they were before.
Of course. It makes sense that you’d want things to go back to how they were. You mentioned it’s a group of five. Is there one person in that group you’re especially close with?
Yes. There’s one girl among the five that I’m especially close with.
Earlier, you told me that the others are reluctantly going along with the leader. I was thinking that maybe that girl might feel guilty about ignoring you... What do you think, Miki?

Yes. Actually, I’ve talked with that close friend before about how “ignoring people is awful,” so I think she probably doesn’t really want to do it, but is going along with it because she feels she has to.

I see. I think it’s really good that you have a clear opinion about that. If you could talk to her quietly, even just a little, you might be able to hear how she really feels. Do you have a way to contact her?
Yes. We’re connected on LINE.

I see. In that case, it might be good to contact just her quietly and honestly tell her how painful this has been for you. If there’s even one more person you can talk to, it might help you feel a little better, Miki.
Yeah... If I could just exchange messages with her, I’d be happy, and I want to know how she really feels too!
Right. I think it’s okay to be really honest and tell her how you feel, Miki. And then, try telling your friend, “I was able to talk about this because it’s you.”
Yes. Honestly, then. I’ll try telling her, “I feel safe talking to you because it’s you!”
That sounds good! Your friend might be struggling too, so if she hears from you, she may feel relieved. Also, would it be okay if I gave you a little more advice?
That might be true! I was only thinking about my own feelings, but she might be struggling too. Yes, please.
Yes! Being able to think about the people around you too shows how kind you are, Miki.
Thank you.

If you’re okay with it, I wonder if it might help to talk about how you feel with an adult around you who’s easy to talk to. I thought it might feel reassuring to have an adult on your side. How does that sound?
Hmm. It would take a little courage, but I often talk with the school nurse, so I might be able to talk to her.

That’s good! I’m relieved to know there’s an adult you can rely on. I think the school nurse would really listen to what you have to say, Miki. She might even help you think through what to write to your friend.

Yes. Rather than thinking about it alone, I think I’ll first talk to the school nurse. The teacher also knows my closest friend well, so I’ll try thinking about the message while asking her for advice!
I’m glad to hear that! I know it takes courage, but since you’re someone who can express your thoughts clearly, Miki, I think you’ll be able to talk to her well.
Thank you. I’m glad I came here to talk today.
I’m glad you feel that way. Please try sharing your feelings with your friend while talking it over with the teacher. I’m rooting for you too!
Yes. I’ll do my best! Thank you so much.
Thank you as well for sharing with me. We’re almost out of time. Would it be okay to end the consultation here?
Yes. That’s okay.
Thank you. If anything else comes up, please feel free to come talk anytime. I’m rooting for you, Miki, and I hope you can make up with your friends!
I’ll try talking to the teacher tomorrow! Thank you very much.
Yes! Thank you. Well then, I’ll say goodbye.
Goodbye.
(Thank you very much. I learned a lot.)
(Thank you very much. I couldn’t believe today was your first time!)
(Not at all! Thank you so much for working with me. If there’s another opportunity, I’d be grateful to do this again.)
(Same here. If there’s another opportunity, I’d be glad to do this again. Thank you for your hard work.)
(Thank you for your hard work. Well then, I’ll press the end button now. Goodbye.)
(Goodbye.)

interaction.content: Hello. We'll begin when it's time. Thank you for being here today.
Thank you as well. I appreciate it m(_ _)m
Nice to meet you. My name is Hanamaru, and I'm a counselor. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
Nice to meet you. I'm a 39-year-old woman.
Thank you. So, could you tell me what you'd like to talk about today?

It's about my child. She was supposed to become a third-year high school student this month, but starting about a year ago, she became unable to wake up in the morning and was constantly late or absent, so she had to repeat the year. Since around the end of last year, she has barely gone to school at all, and even though she's repeating the year, of course she still isn't going. We're also considering transferring her to a correspondence school, but she doesn't seem motivated to do anything, and I don't know what to do.
I see. As her mother, that must be very worrying. Was there something that might have been painful or difficult for your child?

That's the thing—she has friends at school, and even though she doesn't go, she's still close with them, and she goes out with them. She also goes to her part-time job. When I asked the teacher, it didn't seem like there was any bullying or anything. It's just laziness.
I see. When the reason she became unable to go to school isn't clear, it really leaves you struggling with what to think.
Yes. She only thinks about money. She goes to her part-time job so she can exchange expensive gifts with friends and do makeup, but she can't go to school?
I see. Your child may have her own feelings about it, but from your perspective as her mother, I imagine you're truly worried.

The school also recommended transferring to a correspondence school, and we're considering it, but I wonder if she'll really be able to do it just because it's correspondence. What should I say to help her feel motivated?
So the school suggested correspondence school. Does your child ever talk to you, Komorebi, about why she doesn't want to go to school?
No. She just says she doesn't care anymore.
She says that, then. It must be hard to know what to say to her.

Nothing works anymore, no matter what I say. She isn't thinking about anything. I wanted her to go to university, but now I don't even care what it is anymore—I just want her to work properly or do something, to think things through and get herself together.
From a parent's perspective, this is a really serious concern. I imagine it must be very painful. Have you already talked with your child about correspondence school?
We've been talking about it for three or four months, since we were told she might have to repeat the year...
When you brought up correspondence school, how did your child react?
She said anything is fine, she doesn't care.
So that was her response. That would really leave you at a loss.

Yes. Whether I speak gently or scold her, nothing gets through. People around me say it's just adolescence and can't be helped, but kids going through rebellious phases still go to school properly and take entrance exams, don't they?
Yes, I understand. Komorebi, if you have a partner, how does he think about this?
Her father has already given up. He laughs and says, 'She's hopeless now.' She's really similar to her father. Stubborn and inflexible.
Your husband says that, then. Their personalities are similar.
Yes. I think it may be rebellion against her father, but even if that's the case, I don't know what to do.
Is there a reason you think it may be rebellion against her father?

He's strict and always nagging, and ever since he started working remotely because of COVID and became home all the time, he's especially been interfering in everything. Once, I had a huge fight with my husband and thought about divorce, and she said to me, 'Why didn't you get divorced back then?'
I see. When she asked why you didn't get divorced, do you think she said that because she wanted you to divorce?
Yes, she said it would've been better if we had gotten divorced.
I see. Komorebi, you said you think the reason your child stopped going to school may be rebellion against your husband. Is there a reason you think that?

I did too, but we had always told her to go to university, and for that reason she worked hard to take the entrance exam for a high school that was a little difficult to get into. She passed and everything was going well, but maybe she hates her father and wants to rebel against him. Maybe she doesn't want to do what her father says.
That's how you see it, Komorebi. I wonder if perhaps your child may have been feeling pressured. What do you think?
Do you think so...? She's a child who can study well. Everything was going well.
She was a child who worked hard at her studies. I wonder if it might help to ask a little more about what she truly wants for herself.

Apparently she told a teacher at school that she wanted to go into the beauty field, so I talked to her about how a vocational school could be a good option too, because for now I want her to at least graduate from high school. But even when we talk about that, she acts like she doesn't care and doesn't think about it seriously. So I wonder whether the beauty field is even serious, and whether she'd be able to manage if she went to vocational school.
So your child does have that kind of interest. How did she react when you talked about a beauty-related vocational school? She says she wants to go to vocational school, then?
Yes, if she can at least get the qualification of graduating high school...
I see. What if you try telling your child that in order to go to a beauty-related vocational school, it's better to have a high school diploma?
I have told her. Even when I say that, she doesn't get motivated, and that's what I'm struggling with.
We're almost out of time, and I'm sorry I haven't been able to give you a clear answer. How was it for you to talk about this?

I wanted to ask how I could make my daughter feel motivated... But I have started to understand that she may be rebelling against her father. I think I'd like to try putting a little distance between her father and my daughter.
I see. I can really feel the love you have for your daughter, Komorebi. I imagine you've raised her with great care.
Haifu. Yes. Thank you 😭😭
Thank you for talking with me today.
Thank you very much.
You did well today.
Thank you for your time! I learned a lot! Thank you very much!
Then we'll end here. I also learned from speaking with you. Thank you very much.

interaction.content: Good morning. Thank you for your time today. If possible, I was hoping you could play the role of a junior high or high school client. Would that be okay...?
Good morning. Thank you as well. I can do that, since I’ll lower the age setting.
Thank you...! I really appreciate it. Once it’s 11 o’clock, we’ll begin. I’ll proceed with the understanding that the client is a junior high or high school student. Thank you.
Understood.
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming today. To start, could you tell me your age or grade, and your gender?
Yes, I’m in eighth grade, and I’m female.
Thank you for telling me. I’m glad to meet with you today. So, please tell me what you’d like to talk about today.
I want to die.
I see. You’re having those kinds of feelings... Thank you for coming here even though things feel so hard. Where are you right now?
I’m at home.
You’re at home. Is anyone else there besides you?
No. I’m alone.
I see. So you’re at home by yourself right now. Does that mean you stayed home from school today?
I’m staying home.
Yes, I see. Is it just today that you’re staying home from school? Or does it feel like you haven’t been going for a while?
I’ve been staying home the whole time.

I see. When you say the whole time, since what grade has that been? I’m sorry for asking so many questions. I’d like to understand more about you, so please tell me. (It’s okay if there are parts that are hard to answer—you can just tell me then.)
Since around the summer of seventh grade.
Thank you for telling me. Around the summer of seventh grade, did anything change around you?
What do you mean by change?

I’m sorry, the way I said that was hard to understand. Since you told me you stopped going to school around the summer of seventh grade, I wondered if something unpleasant had happened to you then, so I asked.
It had been going on since before that.
Oh, I see. What had been going on since before that?
They made fun of me for being fat.
I see. That’s awful. That must have felt really painful... Only as much as you feel able to talk about, but who said what kinds of things to you...?

The whole class said things to me. Like, fat people aren’t worth living, and they can’t stand even looking at me. When I was in the classroom, everyone would use me as a joke and giggle about me.
I just want to die.
The whole class was saying those things to you... That... was a really painful situation...

I want to die.
I can’t take it anymore.

Have you, by any chance, been preparing to die in some way?
Like deciding when you would die... or thinking about how...?

I searched online, but I haven’t done anything yet.
I can’t stand myself.

I see... You’ve been driven to the point of searching online...
Yes. You also have this feeling that you can’t stand yourself...

Yes. I don’t understand what the point of living is.
Everyone else is going to school and having fun.
I think you must have been feeling that much pain. Is this the first time you’ve talked about this here? Do your teachers maybe not know that these awful things are being said to you...?
After I stopped going to school, the teacher contacted my parents and I talked about it. But even if things seemed okay at that time, behind the scenes I was still being bullied.
I see... So you did talk about it properly, but the teacher hasn’t done anything... or rather, it feels like they haven’t properly dealt with the people around you...?
The teacher didn’t really take it seriously either.

Yes... To be honest, hearing your story, I felt that way too... Even though I think it took courage for you to talk about it... that must have felt so frustrating...
What did you talk about with your parents?

I told my parents too. But they’re busy, so they don’t really take it seriously.
Why is it bad to be fat?
I see. Even here, you’ve been properly talking about what’s going on with you, but your parents responded that way...
Yes.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with it at all, but people around you say those things, right?
Apart from what other people think, what do you think?

Being alone is painful, so I think maybe it would be better if I lost weight.
But I couldn’t really lose weight.
That’s why it hurts.

Thank you for telling me. I see. Because being alone feels painful, you tried hard to lose weight.
When you say you couldn’t really lose weight, was there some reason for that?

My body type?
When I lost a little weight, I ended up eating from the rebound.

I see. Body type may be part of it. I was told all kinds of things for being short too... but now that I’m an adult, I do think body type is a real thing.
When you lost weight, what were you doing? Were you watching your meals or exercising?
I reduced how much I ate, or didn’t eat at all. I don’t really like exercise, so I didn’t do that.

I see. So you lost weight by cutting down on food or not eating, but then from the rebound you ended up eating.
Have you been feeling physically sluggish or exhausted?
No, I haven’t felt sluggish.

I’m a little relieved to hear that. Since you’re in eighth grade, you’re still going to grow taller, and especially as a girl, I think your body needs energy.
The one thing I really want to avoid is your precious body being harmed because of the heartless words from your classmates.
Thank you. But everyone is thin and pretty, so I’m jealous.

That makes sense. You’re an eighth-grade girl. Those feelings are very natural. I want to take those feelings of yours seriously too, so would you like to talk about the rest of what we discussed today next time?
Talking with you today made me want to understand your feelings more.

Thank you. Okay.
(Thank you for your time.)

(I’m sorry we went over time...! Thank you.)
(I’m sorry we couldn’t get all the way to the end.)
(I really appreciate you staying with it until the end of the time.)
(I’ll send the closing message now. Thank you for today...!)
