interaction.content: Good evening, thank you for being here.
(Good evening. Thank you for your time.)
Good evening, I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in to talk with me today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to discuss?
Good evening. I’m 43, female, and I’m struggling with what to do with my life from here on.
Thank you for sharing that. You’re feeling troubled about your life going forward. Is there something in particular you’re worried about?
Yes, there is.
Could you tell me a little more about what you’re worried about?

Yes. I’ve never really had a good connection with anyone, and I’ve never dated anyone. Work wasn’t going especially well either, and the other day I ended up quitting because things didn’t go well with my boss. Everyone around me already has a family—some have children who are grown, and there are also people like my brother and his wife who’ve been enjoying life just the two of them for years—and I feel like I’m the only one left behind, all alone.
I see, that happened. When you look at the people around you, you find yourself thinking that way.
Yes. I don’t stand out looks-wise either, and I don’t have anything I’m good at.
That may leave you feeling a little lonely at times.
It’s not so much lonely as… empty.
When you’re thinking about it on your own, it can be easy to start focusing on the negative side of things.
That might be true...
You’re feeling empty. Are you living alone right now?
Yes.
Being alone might make that emptiness feel even stronger.
That may be true… I should be used to being alone, though...
And since you’ve also left your job now, I imagine there may be some confusion or uncertainty.
Yes… when I think about having to start using my savings from now on, it feels depressing.
That’s true, money can become a source of worry. But we don’t know that things will stay this way from here on out.
That’s true. It feels like I quit after really speaking my mind, and I hadn’t thought much about what would come after.
So you quit after really speaking your mind. I think that shows a lot of passion.
People around me weren’t able to say much, and it was something I’d been putting up with too, so I’d reached my limit.

Do you mean you were thinking about the people around you as well? If you’re someone with that kind of passion, I wonder if it might be okay to think of this as a time to rest a little. How does that sound? You’ve really worked hard up to this point, haven’t you?
Yes. I originally liked my job, so I hadn’t really intended to quit.
It was work you liked. So there may be feelings coming up of wishing you could have continued longer.
Yes... Now that I’ve quit, I wonder if that was really okay...
You’re having those feelings too. But I wonder if there may be people around you who feel relieved because of what you did.
I don’t know… It feels awkward, so I haven’t contacted anyone.
I see. It may be hard to reach out. I don’t know exactly what the situation was, but I don’t think the decision you made after seeing what was happening around you was wrong at all.
Thank you. But I don’t know whether it was good for me. I feel like I’ve lost everything, and right now I don’t really have the energy to live, or...
That’s how you’re feeling. It seems like so many things have changed all at once that you may be a bit worn out right now.
That might be true.
How would it be to think of this as taking a bit of a break? You’ve been working hard all this time, haven’t you?
Yes. I don’t know for myself whether I’ve worked hard or not. I was planning to do all kinds of things from here...
When you say you were planning to do all kinds of things, do you mean work-related things?
Yes, I had been put in charge of a new project.
I see. That must have been frustrating.
Yes. It was frustrating.
Is it that you had a vision for how you wanted to move forward, but you weren’t allowed to proceed the way you hoped?
No, my plans had been approved, but there were a lot of power-harassment comments toward other staff members, and everyone was exhausted.
I see, that was going on. Seeing the people around you worn down, I can imagine it felt like the last straw for you.
Teamwork is important, but they were trying to lower everyone’s motivation, so I’d reached my limit.
That makes sense. In that case, I imagine you may also be worried about the staff members you left behind. How does that feel?
Yes. But fortunately, I’m still in contact with one colleague from the same cohort, and it seems like he’s looking after everyone.
There’s someone like that there. That must be a bit of a relief.
Yes, it’s reassuring for the junior staff, at least.

Listening to you so far, I feel that you’re someone who pays attention to the people around you, and also has a lot of passion. So I wonder if it might be okay for you to rest a little right now. What do you think?
At my age, I’d been wanting to settle down, and work was the only thing supporting me, so for this to happen so suddenly… I feel like I can’t even rest. The anxiety is really strong.
You feel that work was the only thing supporting you. The fact that you were entrusted with an entire project shows how truly hard you must have been working.
Yes... Now that I’ve lost it, I really wonder if I had nothing else besides that.
I know it may be hard to shake the anxiety right now, but because you’ve worked so hard like that, I think it has become a solid strength stored within you.
I hope that’s true.
I believe it is. So even if it’s difficult right away, I’m sure you’ll find something to direct that passion toward.
Yes. Thank you.

You mentioned being worried about your age, but when we think about healthy life expectancy, there’s still so much ahead of you. If there’s anything you were a little interested in before but couldn’t do because you didn’t have time, I wonder if trying it out a bit might be good. How does that sound?
Yes. I don’t have much energy right now, but I hope someday I’ll be able to feel that way. I hope I can.
I think it’s okay to take your time. I hope your future will be a bright one for you.
Thank you.
Thank you for coming to talk with me today. I hope this has helped even a little in easing your anxiety.
Thank you. I feel a little lighter.
I’m glad to hear you say that. Thank you as well. I’d like to end here for today, if that’s alright with you.
Yes. Thank you very much.
Thank you. If anything comes up again, please feel free to come anytime.

interaction.content: (Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.)
(Thank you.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in to talk. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m 30 years old, female.
Thank you. Then, please tell me what you’d like to discuss.
My younger sister has developed depression, and as her older sister, I’m struggling with what I should do.
I see. That sounds like a very worrying situation. Since about when has your sister been in that state?
I only heard it from her recently, but it seems she went to the hospital about three months ago.
I see. Since she has been going to the hospital, was she diagnosed there? How did your sister tell you about it?
The depression diagnosis was made at a psychosomatic medicine clinic, but it seems that was her first time going. It sounds like she was told she needed her family’s cooperation, so she told me.
I see. So your sister reached out to you, her older sister, because of that... How did you feel when you heard that? “Onen-sama” → I meant “onee-sama,” older sister. I’m sorry.
I knew there were a lot of people out there with it, but when it comes to actually cooperating, I don’t know where to start...

Yes, of course. Even while you’re worried, it makes complete sense that you’d be wondering what to do and what you can do. Do you know specifically what your sister’s living situation is like right now?
She had been living alone, so I brought her back to our parents’ home right away. We’re living together now.

You took action right away, then. I imagine that must have felt very reassuring and comforting for your sister. I think your ability to take action is wonderful. At your parents’ home now, besides your sister and yourself, are there other family members there?
Yes, my parents are there.
I see. I think it’s good that there are multiple people who could be a source of support. How are your parents interacting with your sister?
Actually, my parents are the difficult part. They have old-fashioned ideas about depression, so I can’t ask them to cooperate.
That’s the situation, then... So it seems like you may be the main person who can support her.
Yes, and then there’s only my older sister who lives far away.

You have an older sister as well, then. But if she lives far away, it’s difficult for her to help all the time. Still, at important moments, do you think you could consult with her? Also, do you think she would understand?
That part is a little difficult. I did tell her about the depression, but she doesn’t seem to understand, so I’m confused. It seems like she’s taking it lightly...
I see... Then for now, it seems like your sister may be relying on you, the person who understands her best. So, I’d like to ask: how is your sister spending her time at home right now?
I work, so I don’t know what happens on weekdays. It seems like she stays in her room.
I see. How do you feel about that situation?
Since she’s going to the hospital, I feel reassured, but I also feel like I don’t know what I should do.
I see. Then, when you’re at home, how are you interacting with her right now?
We didn’t really talk much to begin with, so when she comes to the living room, I just kind of check on how she’s doing.
So you don’t really have much conversation with her? Have you heard anything from her about what she may be struggling with?
We talked when we were students, but after we started working, our schedules were different, so it became less frequent.
I see... Now that things have become like this, does it feel difficult to ask her again about what she’s struggling with or what’s bothering her?
Yes, it feels difficult.
What part feels difficult?
Now that she’s ill, I don’t know what I should say to her...
Yes, of course. I imagine you want to understand your sister, but you’re struggling with how to relate to her in a way that can help her.
Yes. She’s never been sick before, and especially when it’s a mental illness...

Because you haven’t experienced this before, does it feel like unknown territory that isn’t easy to step into...? Would it be okay if I shared a little of what I’ve been sensing as I’ve listened to you so far?
Yes.

Thank you. First, you want to be there for your sister, who has developed depression, but in a situation where you can’t expect much cooperation from the rest of your family, you are in a position of handling this on your own. As things are now, I think it would be quite hard to carry all of this by yourself. And while you want to help, you’re also in a situation where you don’t know what you can do for her. Is that accurate so far?
Yes.

Thank you. In that situation, if there are things you can do for your sister, they may be the following. First, to keep providing a safe environment where, as you are now, you stay nearby and watch over her. And to convey the message that whenever she wants to talk, you’re there to listen. And, if possible, to learn about depression yourself. For example, that might include going with her to her appointments. I’m sorry for writing so much. How does that sound?
Yes, I had been thinking I had to do something right away... but it does seem like I could go with her to her appointments.

That’s how it feels to you, then. I’m glad. If you rush, your anxious feelings may be conveyed to your sister as well. I think taking one step at a time, doing what feels possible, will help support your sister. We’re getting close to the end of our time. I’m sorry. I imagine there may still be more you’d like to talk about, but if there’s anything you feel you really want to say, could you let me know?
I’m okay.

I see. Thank you. Also, if anything else comes up that you’d like to discuss, please come here anytime. I hope you can be there by your sister’s side and support her, but I also think it may become a burden for you as well, so please take care not to overdo it.
Yes.
Then, if you’re able to, please go with her to her appointments. Within a range that isn’t too much for you... Thank you for coming in to talk today.
Thank you very much.
(I’m sorry we went over time. Thank you. I’d like to end here, if that’s all right.)
(That’s fine. Thank you for your work.)
(Thank you. Thank you for your time. I’m sorry to trouble you, but please complete the evaluation.)

interaction.content: (Good morning. Thank you for doing the role-play with me from 10:00.)
(Good morning. Thank you as well.)
Hello, I’m the counselor.
Hello.
To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m 30, male.
Thank you for telling me. What would you like to talk about today?
I’m struggling with something about my girlfriend.
I see. Please tell me more about it.
Recently, we had a fight, and we haven’t been able to talk for a while.
That must be worrying. What was the fight about?
I think it started because I told her I was being transferred and that we wouldn’t be able to see each other for a while.
I see. What did she say about you being transferred?
She’s been silent, so I’m sure she’s struggling with it.
That’s how it seems to you. When the other person stays silent, it’s easy to imagine all sorts of things, isn’t it.
Yes, I’m also struggling with what I should do from here...
When you still can’t talk, her feelings aren’t clear either, and I think it’s understandable that you’d no longer know what to do. By the way, how long has it been since you became unable to talk?
About two weeks.
I see. If you haven’t been able to get in touch for two weeks, that would make you worried.
She hasn’t replied to my LINE messages either.
So even when you contact her, there’s no reply, is that right?
Yes, that’s right.
That must feel sad, and it would make you anxious too. Before the fight, what was your relationship like?
We were getting along normally, and I was thinking that I wanted to marry her.
You were even thinking about marriage. If you can’t get in touch with someone like that, I imagine the sense of urgency would build up. Have you been together for a long time?
About a year. Soon, I have to give my final answer about whether or not I can accept the transfer.
So the transfer hasn’t been decided yet.
The final decision is still to come.
For you, are you still unsure?
If possible, I’d like her to come with me, but... if she can’t, then I may have no choice but to give up the relationship... I’m still struggling with it.
You’re thinking in the direction of taking the transfer, but you’re wavering over whether to go even if it means giving up your relationship with your girlfriend.
Yes, that’s right.
Both your work and your girlfriend are very important to you, so having to choose one or the other must be really painful.
This transfer is an opportunity, so that makes it especially difficult.
I see. If it’s an opportunity, you’d definitely want to take it. It makes sense that you’d want to take it.
Yes, but it’s overseas, in Southeast Asia, so I don’t think she can come with me.
I see. What makes you think she can’t go?
She really values taking care of her mother, so I think she’s hesitant about living overseas...

So there were circumstances like that. That does make it seem difficult for her to go overseas. I think it’s only natural that you would feel conflicted in this situation. From what you’ve told me so far, I can tell that both your girlfriend and your work are very important to you.
Thank you.
And because of that, being in a situation where you have to choose one or the other must be truly harsh for you. You’d want her to understand that feeling too, wouldn’t you.
But I do have to choose, don’t I.
How many years would that transfer last?
I think about three to five years.
I see. Thinking that you might not be able to see each other that whole time would be painful for both of you.
Yes. I’m not very confident about being in a long-distance relationship for such a long time.
I see. Being pressed to make a decision right now must be a very difficult situation for you, but you’ll have an answer within the next few days, won’t you.
Yes. I have to decide.
Perhaps, somewhere inside you, the answer is already decided?
No, honestly, I’m struggling with it right up to the end.
I see.
But I also know I have to decide for myself.
That shows just how important both of these things are to you.
I think so.
I think this is truly painful, but over the next few days, it may be good to think about what matters most to you.
Yes, that’s true.
Thank you for sharing such important feelings with me today.
Thank you as well.
Then we’ll end today’s consultation here.
(Thank you very much.)
(Thank you very much. Good work. Please feel free to point out anything that wasn’t good.) (Then I’ll end the role-play now.)
(Yes, it’s okay.)

extra.topic_sub: 転勤による遠距離恋愛の葛藤

interaction.content: I’m ready to play the client role.
Good evening. Thank you for being here today. When it’s time, we’ll go ahead and get started.
Thank you as well. Understood.
It’s time now, so we’ll go ahead and get started. What would you like to talk about today?
Thank you. It’s about how to interact with my girlfriend.
Yes, thank you for being here today. It’s about how to interact with your girlfriend, then. If you don’t mind, may I ask your gender and age?
Male, early 20s.
Thank you for letting me know. You mentioned how to interact with your girlfriend—what kinds of things are you having trouble with around that?
It’s something small, but I’m struggling with whether it’s okay to point out things that bother me.

You’re struggling with whether it’s okay to point out things that bother you. Small things or anything at all are completely okay. If you’re comfortable, could I ask what kinds of things about your girlfriend have been on your mind?

It’s just things like not washing the dishes, or leaving the lights on, that kind of level, but it’s all been building up... I feel differences in our values, so I wonder if things will really go well if we stay together long-term.
So it’s not only that there are various things that bother you, but you’re also feeling differences in your values. Regarding those differences in values, what kinds of things feel different to you?
Our ways of thinking about work aren’t that different, so maybe it’s more lifestyle than values? Or maybe values around how we spend time at home.
You’re feeling differences in your values around how you spend time at home. If you don’t mind, could you tell me a bit more specifically about that?

Right. It’s really just small things like I mentioned earlier, but rather than getting irritated with her, I feel like I’m constantly wondering day to day whether I should say something, and it’s mentally tiring.
That makes sense. Even if they’re small things, they’re still things that bother you, and wondering whether or not you should say something can take quite a lot of energy.

Yes. I’m also thinking about marriage, so part of me thinks maybe I need to say even small things if I think, “It would be better this way,” but I can’t say it because I’m afraid she’ll dislike me or think I’m petty.
She’s someone you’re thinking about a future with, then. In that case, it makes even more sense that you’d worry about how she might see you.
Yes.
You said you’re struggling with whether or not you should say something. In the past, have you ever told your girlfriend what you thought and had an unpleasant experience because of it?
Not particularly. But when she flatly turns down something I suggest, I do get pretty down sometimes. I think I’m just worrying too much, though.
You feel that you may be worrying too much. By the way, what would you like me to call you?
As it says on my profile, Shikushiku is fine.

Shikushiku, then. Thank you. As I listen to you, I get the sense that you feel anxious that if you suggest something to your partner, or point out something small that bothers you, she might reject it or think something of you. Have you felt that way in past romantic relationships as well?
Yes. Please call me Shikushiku. I think what you said is right. It may not just be in romantic relationships—I might be like that when I’m with friends too.

I see. So you’ve felt that kind of anxiety not only in romantic relationships, but with friends as well. Carrying that anxious feeling all the time in both romantic and friend relationships can make you wonder whether you’re worrying too much. Shikushiku, during our time today, is there a way you’d like to work with the concern you’re carrying right now?

Right. I’m not good at expressing an opinion that’s different from someone else’s. It’s small, but even with music in the car, I think about things like, “If I play a song I like and they don’t get into it, I’d feel bad.” Yeah... I’d like to be able to say my own opinions a little more, and to not worry so much about the other person.

I see. You’re constantly aware of the other person’s reactions and mood. That would be exhausting. So today, let’s think through together what might help you become even a little more able to express your own opinions than you are now, and to not worry quite so much about the other person.
Yes, please.
First, around when did you start feeling anxious about expressing your own opinion, or feeling that you worry too much about the other person?
Hmm, honestly, I don’t remember... Maybe since around elementary school.
So you may have been feeling this since childhood. Do you think there might be something in the family environment you grew up in that could be a cause?
I get along well with my parents and my older sister. But when I was little, I got scolded a lot.

I see. So you were scolded a lot from when you were little. It’s possible that may have been one reason you started watching other people’s moods. Shikushiku, have you ever talked to anyone about these kinds of concerns before?
That might be part of it. I haven’t really talked about it with anyone.
You haven’t talked about it before. Have you ever thought about opening up to your partner about the fact that you feel resistance around expressing your own opinions?

Yes. I have talked a little about being the type to worry too much and not being good at giving my opinion. But I haven’t been able to say that there are things I want to tell her too. The conversation itself was just in passing about something else, so I think I’ll take this opportunity to tell her again properly.
I see. I think it’s really significant that you’re feeling positively about trying to tell her. By the way, Shikushiku, what kind of relationship would you like to build with your partner?
Thank you. I’d like us to be in a relationship where we can say what we want to say, and both be ourselves.

I see. A relationship where you can be yourselves is your ideal. If you become able to say what you want to say, it seems like you’d feel more at ease emotionally, and your relationship with each other could deepen as well. Shikushiku, if you gathered your courage and shared your opinion with your partner, what would you want her to do?

I hope it moves in that direction. Let’s see... I hadn’t really thought about it much, but I guess I’d want her to pick up on the feeling that I seem like I want to say something... But that might be difficult, so when I do take the plunge and tell her something, I’d be happy if she accepted it, or if she’s going to turn it down, said it a little more gently.
I see. If she could receive what you say, or respond a little more gently, it seems like you’d be able to gradually say what you’re thinking more from here on.
Yes.

This time, your concern was that you can’t say what you’re thinking to your partner. And it’s true that if it comes across as dissatisfaction with the other person, she may feel bad, and then Shikushiku, you may end up hurt as well. I think you’re struggling with this precisely because you want to continue building a good relationship with your girlfriend. Because you want to keep building a good relationship, you want to become able to share what you’re thinking even though you feel anxious, and you’d be happy if she could receive it even a little, or say no gently when she turns something down—how would it be to try telling her those feelings?

Yes. There’s no doubt that I want us to keep having a good relationship, so after telling her that, I think I’ll try telling her that I’m not good at expressing my opinions, and what I’d like her to do.
Yes. I’m sure that if you gradually become able to say what you want to say to your partner, you’ll also gradually become able to say it to friends and other people. What do you think?
That might be true. I’m not confident that I’ll be able to communicate well in other areas too, but for now I’ll try my best to tell my girlfriend.

That sounds good. Shikushiku, you’re sincerely facing the parts of yourself that you feel worry too much, and the difficulty you have expressing your opinions, and you’re trying to move things in even a slightly better direction. I think you’re a really wonderful boyfriend. I think your partner is very lucky to have a boyfriend like you.
Do you think so? Thank you. Hearing you say that feels like it might encourage me a little.
I see. I’m glad if it could be even a little encouraging. How was it for you to talk today?
I feel like I want to do my best to tell her that I’m not good at expressing my opinions, and move toward a relationship where we can be ourselves. Thank you.

I’m glad to hear that. Since you had the courage to take action to try to resolve the concerns you’ve been carrying, Shikushiku, I’m sure you’ll be able to build a good relationship with your partner, so it will be okay. Thank you for sharing with me today. If anything comes up again, please feel free to reach out anytime.
Yes. I’ll try my best. Thank you very much.
Yes, thank you. (Thank you for your valuable time today. Since our time is up, we’ll end here.)
Yes. Thank you very much.
(I would appreciate it if you could leave a rating when you have time. Thank you very much.)

extra.topic_sub: 彼女とのコミュニケーションについての悩み

interaction.content: (Good evening. Thank you for meeting with me.)
(Good evening. Thank you as well. Shall we begin when it’s time?)
(Yes, please, when it’s time.)
(Understood. Thank you.) Thank you for coming in for a consultation today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m 35. Female. I keep remembering something I did in the past, and I feel guilty about it.
I see. So you’ve been struggling with something that happened in the past. If you’re comfortable, could you tell me a little more about it?
When I was in elementary school, I bullied a child at the same school. I keep remembering what happened back then,
It was something that happened when you were in elementary school. You’ve been feeling guilty about that time, and that must have been really painful.
I keep thinking, how could I have done something like that, and I can’t sleep at night. The reason I started feeling this way was,
Yes.
My child is in elementary school, and is being bullied by a child in the same class,
Mm-hmm.
And I can’t help thinking that maybe my child is being bullied because of what I did in the past. It’s very painful.

I see. It must be painful that your child is being bullied, and at the same time you’re regretting your own past. It really sounds like you’ve been holding so much pain. Is your child’s situation still the same now?
Yes. It hasn’t changed. She says she doesn’t want to go to school.
Is she actually not going to school?
Somehow, she goes sometimes for now, but she can’t go into the classroom and stays in the nurse’s office.
I see. Your daughter is really trying her best too. And as you see your daughter like that, you’re blaming yourself, aren’t you?
Yes. Did I say daughter? She is my daughter, so that’s not wrong, but... I was a little surprised.
I’m very sorry. You had said your child. I mistakenly changed it to daughter on my own.
She is my daughter, so it’s okay. I think that if I hadn’t bullied someone in the past, this wouldn’t be happening.

Let me say this again: I understand that you feel as though what happened in the past may be connected to what is happening with your child now, but in reality, I don’t think you need to blame yourself that much. How does that sound?
I keep thinking that if I hadn’t bullied someone in the past, this wouldn’t be happening.

I think it’s understandable that you end up thinking that. You can’t help but feel that way, can you. I understand how you feel. On the other hand, what you did in the past may not be something to be praised, but since then, you have also lived your life, and you have a child. I think the present exists because you truly regretted it and changed. What do you think?
If I had really regretted it and changed, I don’t think I would remember it. I remember it because the guilt is still there.

Maybe that’s true. As you said, guilt isn’t something that disappears so easily. But the fact that you’re feeling guilt like this now, struggling with it, and feeling such pain—couldn’t that mean you are truly facing the past and regretting what happened?
Am I facing the past? If I can’t sleep, and the painful feelings don’t go away, does that mean I’m facing it?
That is how I feel. In fact, you seem to be suffering a great deal. If you weren’t facing it, would you be feeling this way? I think it hurts because you are facing it. How does that sound?
Then when will the sleeplessness and the painful, distressing feelings go away?
I’m sorry, but I don’t know that. But I do feel that you have more than enough regret and remorse about what happened in the past. Perhaps you could start by allowing yourself to forgive yourself.
Forgive myself? How am I supposed to forgive myself?

You can’t change the past. I think there is the fact that you realized your mistake yourself and reflected on it. You can’t make it as if it never happened, and you may not be able to forget it, but I don’t think continuing to blame yourself any more will change anything.
That’s right. The facts don’t change. The past can’t be changed.
That’s right. It can’t be changed. So I think the only thing we can do is accept it, both the good and the bad.
Hearing the word “accept” made me feel a little calmer. Somehow, I had felt like I was being blamed... I think I’ll try to accept the past.
I wanted so much to be of some help to you that I may have ended up sounding a little too strong. I’m sorry. Regarding your child’s situation, how would you hope it could improve?
I want her to be able to go to school happily, but the child bullying her is in the same group as her,
Yes.
They’re in the same group walking to school every day, and I don’t understand why it turned into bullying. They used to be close...
I see. They used to be close. That must make it even harder for your child. Is the other child in the same grade?
Yes. He’s a boy in the same class who lives nearby. At first, he started joking around and calling her by a nickname,
I see. So you don’t know the reason, is that right?

Yes. I don’t know. It gradually escalated, and there was a time when he kicked her in the stomach. She came home crying, and since then she’s been saying she doesn’t want to go to school, so now she goes only sometimes.
That’s awful. I think it’s completely natural that she would feel that way. Does your child go to school in the group just with the children? I know there are cases where parents go along with them.

Right now, she goes to school at a different time. It seems like that boy is being egged on by another boy, and since I’m close with the mother of the boy who lives nearby, I’m thinking of talking to his mother once.
I think that’s a very good idea. First, it would be good to understand why your child is being treated that way.
Yes. If we know the reason, I think we can respond to it.
That’s right. If you can understand the situation first, it may be easier to decide what to do next. Have you talked with the school about it?
Yes. I’ve talked with her homeroom teacher and the school nurse.
I see. I think it’s wonderful that you’re staying well connected with them. I can tell that you really care about your child.
Thank you.
Once you understand the situation a little more, you may be able to work with the school and move things in a better direction.
Yes. I really hope that happens.
We’re getting close to the end of our time. I’d like to apologize again for my inappropriate comment earlier.
It’s okay. You listened to me very well, and I feel lighter now. Thank you very much.
I would be glad if you’re able to feel even a little more positive, and I would also be glad if you’re able to use that strength, even a little, toward improving your child’s situation.
I understand. Thank you very much.
Thank you for coming in to talk with me today. If anything comes up again, please feel free to come anytime.
Thank you very much.
We’ll end the counseling session here, then. Take care. (Thank you very much. I learned a lot.)
(Thank you very much for today. I learned a great deal. Please end the role-play.)

extra.topic_sub: 子供のいじめ問題についての悩み

interaction.content: (Good morning. Thank you for being here today.
(Good morning. Thank you as well.)
(Would it be all right if we begin now?)
(Yes. That’s fine. Thank you.)
(Yes, understood.) Good morning. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in to talk with me. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
Good morning. I’m a 37-year-old woman. I feel like I need to look for a part-time job, but I just can’t seem to take that step.
I see… That must be worrying… Could you tell me a bit about what’s been going on?
My child is in first grade now, and they’re gradually getting used to school life, so I’ve been thinking maybe it’s about time I started working again too… but I just can’t get motivated.
I see… What kinds of things have been on your mind?
I guess I end up thinking, what if the boss is an unpleasant person… things like that.
I see… That would weigh on your mind… Has something like that happened before?

Yes. It bothers me, and I just can’t really bring myself to think about working… Yes. Until two years ago, I was working part-time. I had the worst compatibility with my boss there. The department was shut down, so I was laid off, but honestly I felt relieved.
So that happened… That must have been painful… Could you tell me more about what it was like then?

The way my boss treated the part-timers they liked and the ones they didn’t like was completely different. With the people they didn’t like, even the way they taught the work was careless, and when you asked something you didn’t understand, sometimes they would let out this big sigh, like, “Haa…”
That’s… of course that would make you feel awful…
Yes. I felt like I was going to cry.
Yes, that would hurt… How was that boss toward you?

Toward me, I was in the category of part-timers they didn’t like, so they sighed at me too, and the way they taught me was careless. Or rather, they didn’t teach me. They would just do it quickly without saying anything, and then that was it, like it was over. That’s what it felt like. We barely had any conversations either. That went on for about two years.
I see… That must have been really hard…
Yes.
Could you tell me what it felt like for you to be working there at that time?
I just kept thinking, I really dislike this person… and I also thought it was a difficult workplace to work in.
I see… That must have been exhausting… What was it like with the other people at work?

With the other people, about half of them were liked by the boss, there were a few who were treated normally, and then there were maybe about three people, including me, who were really not liked. Other than the boss, well, it was peaceful… I think. When the boss wasn’t there, I think it was peaceful.
I see… That boss really stayed with you, didn’t they.
Yes, it seems so. I still see them in my dreams.
Is that right… That sounds painful… Could you tell me what kind of dreams they are?

I don’t really remember the dreams themselves, but I think they were probably dreams from when I was working at that workplace. And then I woke up and remember feeling relieved, thinking, I don’t have to go there anymore…
I see… That’s how much you were pushing yourself, then…
Maybe so. Yeah… maybe that’s true. I was putting up with it and smiling, but… maybe it really was painful.
You kept smiling, without letting it show, and endured it…
Yes, I think I was smiling. Saying good morning with a smile, or thank you with a smile.
I see… Even though inside it was so painful you wanted to cry… I imagine that was very hard. Could you tell me what it meant for you to keep smiling like that?

Thank you. Let’s see… it may have been this strange feeling, like my heart was crying but my face was smiling. But it might be a habit. Like, when things are hard or when I feel sad, that’s exactly when I end up smiling… so then I wonder if, from the other person’s side, that makes them irritated or something…
I see… When you think of it that way, it can make you feel sad… I felt that maybe by smiling when things are painful, you may be trying to protect yourself. What do you think?
Oh, I see, that’s what it is. It’s really unconscious, so I don’t really know… My daughter’s cram school teacher is a pretty harsh teacher,
Yes.

and I think that person thinks I’m stupid—well, actually, I’m not very smart, but… They say things like, “Parents, don’t go teaching them homework on your own!! It’s a problem when you do it your way!” And at those times too,
That’s…

I kind of end up laughing it off… Like, “Oh, I understand. Yes! I’ll make sure not to interfere.” And then afterward, I think, “That way they said it, and that expression on their face, was scary…” and I end up feeling like crying…
I see… I think anyone would feel very hurt being spoken to that way.
So there is such a thing as protecting yourself with a smile. I didn’t know that, and it makes sense… I thought, maybe I really was hurting.
Yes, I imagine there may be something inside you that you’ve been wanting to protect and value.
Something I’ve been wanting to protect and value??
Yes, for example, not wanting to make the other person feel bad,
Oh, I really have that. Sometimes when I’m talking, that might be the only thing I’m thinking about.

Yes, I think so. And that’s exactly why, when you’re hurting or feeling sad, you respond to the other person with a smile. Not wanting to make the other person feel bad… I think that’s your kindness, your consideration for the other person.
Oh, I see, I see. When someone says something hurtful, I feel like making an upset face, so I deliberately smile instead. That makes sense. That really clicked for me.
But when that becomes too strong, I think it can end up making things harder for you instead.

Yes, honestly, it is hard. My true feeling is that I don’t want to work anymore… and I’m also scared of interacting with people. I suddenly remembered that maybe it’s because my mother used to say things like, “You’re a genius at making people feel unpleasant.” So maybe somewhere in me there was this sense that I had to keep smiling properly in front of people.
I see… That must have been sad…
Thinking about it now, that really was sad too…
Yes, I don’t think anyone could be told something like that and not be hurt…
I see… She said quite a lot of different things to me, so those kinds of things really do affect you, don’t they. Even though it’s been 20 years…
Yes, I think today you noticed that.
Yes. I’d been trying not to think about my mother for a long time, so it kind of struck me suddenly.
I’m sure there were many things that happened. But I think that by talking like this today, it helped you understand one thing about yourself and begin to sort it out.
Yes, I think so. I thought maybe the reason I can’t quite take the step toward job hunting is because those painful feelings are still there, not yet cleared away.
Yes, I think that may be true. I wonder if, for now, it would be okay to respect that feeling you have of not wanting to work… For now, you can rest, and during that time, take a look at yourself…
Yes. Thank you. I feel like if I worked as I am now, the same thing would happen again. Yes. It seems like there are things I can do while I’m taking a break.

That’s right. I think that by understanding yourself more deeply and sorting things out, you may begin to see things more clearly. And when that happens, I think a feeling of “this is what I want to do” may start to come up.

I’ve never really tried to understand myself. If I can clear that up, maybe working might feel a little less scary than it does now. Yes. Looking at job listings while thinking, “I want to do this,” or “I want to work in this kind of way,” seems more efficient too, haha.

Yes, that’s right. I think someone who always keeps smiling is also someone who values making other people smile. Making someone smile… It would be nice if someday you could do work like that… (Would it be okay to end here?)

I see, that’s what it is. I hadn’t understood that either! Thank you. I’ll try to remember it. (Yes, thank you for everything *ᴗ ᴗ)⁾⁾ (If you could send the closing message, that would be great *ᴗ ᴗ)⁾⁾
(Yes, thank you for today.)

interaction.content: (Good morning. Thank you for meeting with me today.)
“Good morning. Thank you for meeting with me today.” “If you have any requests, please let me know.”
Thank you. If there are any issues you’ve resolved in your life so far, I’d appreciate hearing about them, if you have any! (Well then, I’ll go ahead and begin.)
Understood. Thank you.
Good morning. I’m the counselor. May I ask your gender and age?
Yes. I’m a 15-year-old boy.
(I’m sorry, the connection doesn’t seem very good, so my messages may be delayed.)
“I’m outside too, so it’s totally okay.”
You’re a 15-year-old male, then. What brings you here today? Also, what should I call you?
Please call me Tatsuya. It’s about school.
Tatsuya, then. Thank you.
Yes.
Mm-hmm, it’s about school, then.
Yes.
Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. What’s been going on? If you feel able to talk about it, please start wherever you can.
Actually, I haven’t been going to school, and I came to talk about that.
I see. How long have you not been going to school?
I haven’t been able to go for a long time now.
I see. Do you want to go to school but can’t, or do you not want to go?
I don’t want to go.
I see, I see. You don’t want to go. Was there something that made you start feeling that way?
Since I started school, I haven’t made any friends and I’ve been isolated.
Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. I see.
Yes.
It must have felt lonely, not being able to make friends.
Yes.
I see... Having those lonely feelings continue made you stop wanting to go to school. That must have been a painful time.
Yes.
I’d like to ask one thing. Tatsuya, you’re in junior high school, right? When you started, what kind of school life did you imagine you’d have?
Well, I thought I’d have more friends and be able to have a fulfilling life.
I see. You imagined a fulfilling life with friends. But in reality, it was a little different.
Yes, it was different.
I see... When things are different from what you imagined, it can make you feel down and sad. Do you have any sense yourself of why you weren’t able to make friends?
I don’t know. I couldn’t fit in.
I’m going to ask a little more deeply, but if it feels painful, you don’t have to answer, so please don’t push yourself. I see, you couldn’t fit in.
Thank you. Yes.
I hear that there are many students who go through school feeling like they somehow don’t fit in, like you, Tatsuya.
Is that so?

Some people suppress their own feelings and force themselves to make friends, and end up suffering. Others decide that if they can’t fit in, then that’s just how it is. I think it’s only natural that each person has their own feelings.
Yes.
So I think it’s natural for you to end up feeling like you don’t want to go to school, Tatsuya. Are you spending each day at home now?
Yes, I’m spending my time at home.
I see. Spending your time at home, how do you feel?
Every day I can take it easy without really thinking about anything, so I’m starting to think maybe this is fine.
I see. You’re starting to think maybe this is fine. Are your parents worried?
Yes, they do look out for me.
I see. What kinds of things do you talk about with your parents?
Lately we don’t really talk much about school, and there isn’t any particular set conversation.
I see. Maybe your parents are worried, but they’re respecting how you feel, Tatsuya. They sound like wonderful parents.
Thank you.
Tatsuya, you said you can’t go to school right now. What do you think you’d like to do from here?
Well, I do feel anxious about the future, so I might go to a correspondence school.
I see. You’re thinking about something like a correspondence school. That’s really wonderful.
Yes. My parents recommended it too, so I’m thinking about it.

You felt you couldn’t fit in at your current school, stopped going, and are thinking carefully about your path forward. I feel that’s wonderful. It’s reassuring that you’re also properly talking with your parents about your future.
Yes. It seems like they’re thinking about a lot of things for me.
Your parents’ feelings, and the way you’re facing them properly too, Tatsuya, are both really wonderful.
Thank you.
I think it’s not always easy for a family to support one another, so please do cherish those feelings.
Yes. Thank you for today. I feel a little lighter.
I’m very relieved that you’re looking into correspondence schools with your parents and seem to be facing forward.
Yes.
I also think it’s okay for each person to have their own choices in life. I felt your parents, who are giving you choices in your life, are very precious too.
Yes.
I hope Tatsuya can make better choices, and as for what kind of adult you’ll become from here, I’d like to support you together along the way.
Yes. Thank you for today.
Were you able to talk about what you wanted to talk about today?
Yes, I think so. I’ll be going now. Please help me again sometime.
I see. I’m glad you feel that way. Please feel free to come again anytime. Take care.

interaction.content: Hello, thank you for making time today. We’ll begin at 10:00. I look forward to speaking with you.
Hello. Thank you, I look forward to speaking with you.
Hello, I’m the counselor. Thank you for reaching out today. To start, could you tell me your gender, age, and what you’d like to talk about today?
Hello. I’m a 39-year-old woman. I’d like to talk about what I should do because I don’t get along with a coworker at my workplace.
Thank you for telling me. So you’re in a difficult situation like that. I’d really like to hear more about it. What kinds of things make you feel that you don’t get along with this person?
She’s an employee who joined the company about six months before me, and we’re the same age. I’m a temp worker. Since I first joined, she’s said unpleasant things to me from time to time.
I see. That would make you feel uncomfortable... Is the other person a man or a woman?
Yes, it does. She’s a woman too. We’re in different departments, but at lunch the women eat in the same room.
So that’s the situation right now. If you don’t mind, could you tell me what kinds of things she says to you?

At lunch, everyone has this gloomy atmosphere and no one says anything, but when I try to change the mood and say something casual, she ignores me. It’s obvious she doesn’t want to talk, and it feels like she leaves as soon as she’s done eating.
So that’s what’s been going on.
Right after I joined, I was invited to a drinking party for her department, and when I was the only one from my department who went, she said something like, “Why?”
I see. Having someone speak or act toward you like that would be frustrating. What kinds of feelings do you have toward her?

Yes. After that, because of the temp worker law, I was moved to her department in name only. When there was a welcome party for new employees, I was invited too and attended, but she said to me, “We’ve been paying into the fund, so why are you coming?” To be honest, she says nothing but unreasonable things, and it really pisses me off. I never talk back and I try not to make waves, but mentally I can’t take it anymore.
I see, I see, so that’s how you’ve been feeling. That must feel really painful.
Yes, it does.

Even while being treated in a way that feels rejecting like that, I feel that you’ve really kept trying hard over these past six months. Looking back over these six months, is there anything you notice or feel?

Sorry, it hasn’t been six months, it’s already been more than two years. Lately, I feel like she thinks she can say anything to me and act unpleasantly toward me. In the office where she works, the employees, temps, and part-time workers all quit after about six months, and people keep changing.

I’m sorry I got the length of your work history wrong. I see, so you feel that things have escalated that much. And it may be that the people around her in the past were treated in a similar way too. By the way, have you ever thought about quitting?

It’s a small to medium-sized company, but I’ve had chances to talk with the president and his wife, and maybe because people around her often quit, they seem to see her as a problem. They asked me about what things are like at lunch, but there were people around, so I could only say that there were no problems. I’ve thought about quitting many times, but I think even if I move somewhere else, there will be difficult things in one way or another. At my current company, other than that person, there aren’t any problems, and it’s not uncomfortable to be there.

I see. So the situation is that this one person is the source of your worries. You’re able to work without stress with the other people, and the president and his wife are clearly paying attention as well, so I feel those are reassuring points.

That’s right. I’ve tried to just put up with it, but even though I smile no matter what she says, pull myself together, and treat her kindly, she takes her moods out on me, and taking care of my own mental state afterward is painful. I was surprised that the president and his wife were aware of it. It seems they had seen her speaking to a new employee in a harsh tone.
Mm-hmm, I see. She may be the kind of person who causes trouble.

Yes, but she seems to get along well with the male office manager, and it seems there are no problems with her work. The president said, although it was while we were drinking, something like, “If you can’t get along with that person, you can’t make it at our company.”

I see, so there are circumstances like that too. When you think about all kinds of things, it can get confusing. Let me ask again: as far as you’re concerned, what would you like the current situation to become?

I think it would be good if I could get through the day without seeing her much, but there are a lot of times when I have to go to the office where she is and ask her to do office-related tasks, so it’s not like I can avoid interacting with her. If it’s just talking for work, I can put up with it, but I really hate being together during lunch break.
I see, so ideally it would be best if you didn’t have to be involved with her. What is it in particular about lunch break that feels unpleasant to you?

I can shift my lunch a little and go later, but first, the women who are already in the break room are eating in silence. If that person isn’t there, I’ll bring up a conversation and the atmosphere becomes more relaxed, but if she’s there, it feels like she’ll get angry no matter what I say, and I can’t even think of a topic.
I see, I see. You’re in a situation where you have to be extremely careful. That sounds like it would be very emotionally draining.

Yes, exactly. If I bring up small talk, she only responds with “yeah,” and I think, oh, she really doesn’t want to talk. Sometimes when she wants to talk, everyone is careful around her and goes along with the conversation, and it can get lively. No one says it out loud, but I’m sure everyone is being really careful around her.

I see, so that kind of situation has been continuing. Hearing what you’ve shared so far, I feel that you are someone with a really admirable character, who thinks about the whole group and is able to take action proactively. While you’ve been fighting through such strong stress and still made it to today, how do you feel about yourself?
Do you think so? Thank you! I think, wow, I’ve really managed to keep going. It’s true that when I talk to my friends, they often tell me I should just quit.

I see. In fact, there are many people who have quit around her. Of course, I think there is one person who is causing the problem, but as I listen to you, I get the sense that there are many people around you who could be on your side. What are the people around you like?
One of the other younger female coworkers seems like someone I can probably trust, so I’m thinking I might try talking with her a little about this at some point.
I see. There may be others who feel the same way you do, so if you share the situation, it might help your feelings feel a little lighter.

Another one is young and quiet, and during lunch break she’s either staring at her phone the whole time or taking a nap, so she doesn’t feel like someone I would go to for advice. But she’s not a bad person, and if I talk to her she chats with me in a friendly way, so I think she’s just quiet, and I think she probably senses things about that person too. Yes, it would be strange to suddenly bring it up, so if there’s some kind of opening, I plan to mention it to the first person.

So there is someone like that as well. I see. I feel it’s also important to honestly tell that person, or the president and his wife, about the things that trouble you or what you’ve noticed. After all, you are simply doing your work sincerely.

Yes... In the past, at another place, even though I honestly shared my feelings, I was betrayed and what I said was passed on to the other person, so I end up keeping things to myself. The world of women is scary. Unless I completely trust someone, I can’t say what I really feel.

I see. Because something like that happened in the past, you’re being cautious. In that case, I imagine you’re feeling anxious. I hope you’ll consider talking to someone while watching the situation. And I’m sorry, but we’re getting close to the end of our time. After talking today, how was it for you?
Having you listen helped me get things menstruated in my head, thank you. I mean organized.

Thank you. It may be difficult to resolve the relationship with her all at once. But I believe you have the strength to make the situation even a little better, depending on how you approach it. If anything else comes up that concerns you, please feel free to come here for support anytime.
Thank you. I’ll try my best.
Please don’t push yourself too hard, and don’t blame yourself. I’d be glad if you can approach this in that way. With that, we’ll end today’s consultation. Thank you for today. Take care.

interaction.content: (Hello. Thank you for taking your valuable time today. I’ll greet you when it’s time.) Hello. I’m the counselor. To start, please tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about.
Hello. I’m a 23-year-old man. My relationship with my girlfriend.
Thank you for sharing that. What happened between you and your partner?
I had a fight with my girlfriend, and she hasn’t been speaking to me for a while, and I don’t know what to do about our relationship going forward.
I see. When she won’t talk to you, it can feel lonely, can’t it. Could you tell me how old your partner is, and how long you’ve been together?
She’s the same age, and we’ve been together for three years.
I see, I see. Could you tell me what caused the fight?
Apparently it was because I was only half-listening to what she was saying and responded that way.
I see. By the way, what was your partner talking about?
She said it seems like she might be transferred, and if that happens, we’d be long-distance.
Mm-hmm, I see. By the way, when you heard that, how did you respond?
I said, “Yeah...” After that, she started acting strange.
I see. Looking back on it now, if your partner’s transfer is decided and you end up in a long-distance relationship, how do you think you would feel?
I’d feel very lonely. But it’s something she wants to do, so I think it can’t be helped.
I see. It feels painful when you can’t express that lonely feeling, doesn’t it.
Yes. Right now, I don’t know what to do, and it’s really hard.
By the way, when your partner told you she might be transferred, was there a reason you ended up answering while you were distracted?
Yes. I had found out about my mother’s illness, and I was feeling shaken.
I see. That must have made you anxious and made it hard to think clearly, and I think it’s natural that you couldn’t respond to your partner with how you really felt.
That’s right. But I don’t know what to do. I apologized, but it didn’t work.
Mm-hmm. I understand. By the way, how is your mother’s illness?
She has another test coming up, but it doesn’t seem to be the bad kind.
I see. Do you feel like you’re not worried about your mother’s illness now?
I’ve calmed down a little.
Mm-hmm, I’m glad to hear that. Thank you for sharing. Then, let’s return to talking about your partner. What did you say when you apologized to her?
I said, “I’m sorry I didn’t listen properly. I want you to forgive me.”
Mm-hmm, you honestly told her how you felt. At that time, did you tell her that you had been worried about your mother’s illness?
I didn’t.
I see, I see. Why didn’t you tell her that?
It felt like she wasn’t willing to listen to me, and it didn’t seem like a situation where I could say it.
I see. There are times when the situation makes it hard to say things.
Yes. What should I do?
How do you see your future with your partner?
I want to keep dating her like this.
I see. You have deep affection for your partner. Before the fight, what kind of feelings did you think your partner had toward you?
I thought she felt the same way I did.
I see. So you felt that your feelings were mutual.
I think so.
Mm-hmm. Then, restoring communication with your partner—first, I’d like us to think through that together. How does that sound?
Please.
Thank you. Before we think about ways to communicate, I’d like to sort out your thoughts and your partner’s thoughts about the transfer. Would that be okay?
For me, it’s something she wants to do, so I want her to decide. I don’t know what she thinks because I haven’t been able to ask her. She asked me, “What should I do?”
I see. Because you’re putting your partner’s feelings first, you’re struggling with this.
Yes.
May I ask what kind of work your partner does?
She’s a hairstylist.
I see. It’s work that brings smiles to people’s faces. Does your partner want to be transferred?
I think she believes that gaining experience at the main salon in the city would be better for her.
Mm-hmm, that’s how you see it.
Yes. I think so too.
I think gaining work experience in the city is a wonderful thing, but what do you think your partner wants to value more: gaining experience in the city, or being able to see you nearby?
I don’t know, but I think maybe she asked because she’s unsure.
I see. Hypothetically, if your partner said she wanted to prioritize your feelings, which would you want to choose?
I want her to decide. So she won’t have any regrets.
I see. It’s because you care about your partner’s feelings that you’re choosing that.
Yes.
Thank you for sharing so many things with me today.
Thank you.
We’ve reached the end of our time today, so would it be alright if you came back for another consultation?
Yes, I understand.
I’m sorry we weren’t able to talk through everything to the end. With that, we’ll end today’s consultation.
Yes.
(Thank you for today. I’m sorry it went long. Please share your honest thoughts in the review afterward.)
Understood. Thank you for your time.

interaction.content: (Good evening. Thank you for seeing me today.)
Hello. Thank you for taking your valuable time today. When it’s time, we’ll go ahead and begin.
(Thank you as well. Understood.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming to talk today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m 26, female, and I’m struggling with relationships at work.
Thank you for telling me. I see. You’re struggling with relationships at work. That sounds worrying... Could you tell me a bit more about that?

Yes. I have three coworkers, and I thought we had a good relationship day to day, but my supervisor told me that someone among the three—I don’t know who—had apparently been saying bad things about me. Because of that, I was kind of blamed by my supervisor, or warned about it. It’s made me feel like I can’t trust people, I guess. It’s become hard to do my job.
I see. You’re struggling with something involving your coworkers. That sounds really painful. Specifically, what happened?

My supervisor called me in and said, “I heard that you’re paying too much attention to your junior coworker and neglecting your work,” and “I heard they feel a wall between you and them—isn’t that kind of a problem?” From what was said, it seemed like it could only have been something a coworker told my supervisor, so I felt really sad, or like, that’s how they see me. Even while I’m working, I end up distracted by things other than work, and I hate that.
I see. When you think that people are saying things like that about you, it would make you feel sad.
Yes.
Do you have any sense of why someone might say something like that?
No. I do pay attention to my junior coworker, but I believe I’m properly doing my own work. I don’t understand why it looks that way.
I see. So from your perspective, you don’t have any idea why. In that case, it would become hard to focus on work...
Yes. I thought we were just getting along normally, so I wonder if something I did with good intentions rubbed them the wrong way. I end up being overly careful, and it’s hard to work.
To me, it sounds like you’re a very kind person who is considerate toward your junior coworker as well. Have you ever talked with anyone about these unsettled feelings?
Thank you. Yes, I talked to a friend.
I see. You talked to a friend. What did you talk about then?
I told them exactly what I just told you.
I see. How did your friend respond?

They said, “Isn’t it questionable for that supervisor to just take what they heard at face value and tell the person directly?” And, “You don’t know what the coworker’s real intention was in saying it.”
I see. Thank you for sharing that. When you heard your friend’s opinion, what did you think?

Yes, it’s true that what my supervisor told me was only a small part of it, and I don’t know what the truth really is, but the fact that I was actually spoken badly about hasn’t changed, so I was angry, and I felt distrustful. I’m still interacting with them the same as before, but I don’t know what they really think, so it leaves me feeling unsettled.
I see. Even though you’ve had such an unpleasant experience, at work you’re still doing your job without letting it throw you off.
It would annoy me to actually end up neglecting my work because of this.

I see. The way you’re sincerely facing your work without being swayed by something you don’t recognize in yourself—I imagine your junior coworkers probably see you as a wonderful senior colleague. How would you like your relationship with those coworkers to be going forward?
Thank you. To be honest, I don’t really want to get deeply involved with them. But teamwork is important for the job, so I think it’s best to maintain the same kind of relationship as before.

I see. Even in this difficult situation, you still feel that teamwork is important. You mentioned that because of something you don’t recognize in yourself, there are times when it becomes hard to focus on work. What do you think could help improve that?
Well, I think it would be good if I could stop worrying about what people around me are saying. No matter what I do, I’m careful because I wonder, “Are they taking this in some weird way?”
Yes, that’s how you’re feeling. In order to stop worrying about what people around you are saying, what do you think you could do, or what do you think would need to happen?
No one can know what’s in another person’s heart, so it would be good if I could accept that there’s no point in trying to dig into it.
I see. You’re trying to accept that there’s no point in trying to dig into it. Would it be difficult to tell your coworkers honestly how you feel?

I think if I could do that, maybe it wouldn’t bother me anymore. But I don’t think I can do that. I can’t say, “I heard this from our supervisor.” I think that could also become an issue of trust with my supervisor.
I see. You have a friend who listens to you carefully and feels safe to talk to, so I think they’ll continue to accept and hold your feelings.
Yes.
I’d really like to talk with you more, but I’m very sorry—our time today is almost up. Thank you for sharing something important with me. How was it for you to talk today?
It seems like it’ll be hard to clear away these unsettled feelings, but I feel like I’ve come to the answer that if I can accept it within myself, it might get easier.

I think you have something strong and solid within you. I hope you’ll take good care of yourself and keep doing your best in the way you sincerely face your work. You’re welcome to come back and talk about this again anytime, so please feel free to use this service. With that, we’ll end today’s consultation. Thank you.
Thank you. I’ll try different things in my own way. Thank you for today.
(Thank you for today. I learned a great deal. If there’s another opportunity, I’d be grateful to work with you again.)
(Thank you very much. I learned a lot. Thank you for your hard work.)

interaction.content: (Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.)
(Good evening. Thank you as well.)
Good evening. I’m the counselor. To start, could I ask your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
16, female, I don’t want to go to school
Thank you for telling me. You don’t want to go to school… Since you’re 16, are you in high school?
Yes
I see. High school can be hard in a lot of ways, different from junior high. When did you start feeling like you didn’t want to go?
Since I started high school.
I see… You’ve been hurting for a long time. Did something unpleasant or painful happen at high school?
Yes… Are you a woman?
Yes, I’m a woman. If there’s anything that’s hard to say, please let me know.
Then I’m glad. There are things that are hard to talk about with a man.
That makes sense. Please feel free to tell me what’s been going on.
Will the things I talk about here get found out by anyone else?
It’s okay. I haven’t asked your name or your school. Please don’t worry.
What about what I talk about?

What you share is also protected anonymously, but if you were in a very serious situation and it was urgent, we would talk with you first and decide what to do. Please feel safe talking today. It’s okay to share only what you can.
Thank you.
It’s hard to talk about worries, isn’t it?
Yes.
Talking about it might bring it back and feel painful, but sometimes talking can also help you feel a little lighter. Please tell me what you’re struggling with.
Yes. It takes a lot of courage to tell people.
It’s completely natural to feel that way. I think it shows how deeply you’ve been struggling with this.
Yes…
You must have been facing this for quite some time.
I couldn’t talk to anyone about it.
I see. You’ve been carrying it all by yourself…
Yes.
Then today, you really gathered a lot of courage to come here. That alone is amazing.
It’s been getting to where I can’t carry it alone anymore.
Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. You’ve probably been holding it in and enduring it alone for so long, so I hope today your burden can feel a little lighter. Please talk freely, as much as you’re able to.
Yes. It’s about my homeroom teacher.
About your homeroom teacher—what happened to you? It’s okay to tell me only what you can.
I’m being harassed.
That’s… harassment. Has it been happening ever since you started school?
At first I didn’t really notice it much, but since about six months ago it’s gotten persistent.
I see… Thank you for having the courage to tell me. This may be a bit of an unpleasant question, but what kind of harassment have you been experiencing?
He holds my hand, brings his face close to mine, things like that.

That would feel awful. I wonder if you’ve had to pretend nothing was happening, all by yourself, without being able to talk to anyone. That must have been painful. Have you ever thought about why the teacher is doing those things to you?
I’ve never thought about it. It’s disgusting, and I’m scared even to think about it.
Yes. More than anything, it must have been scary. When a girl has something like that done to her by an adult man, of course it’s frightening. It’s completely natural to feel disgusted.
Yes.
That would make you not want to go to school. Were you able to finish your first year?
I somehow managed to endure it.
Mm. It must have been painful to endure all that. In high school, was there any adult who might have noticed, like an assistant homeroom teacher or the head teacher for your grade?
I’m sure even if I told them, they wouldn’t believe me, so I haven’t told anyone.
That’s how you feel. And the people around you didn’t notice what was happening to you. You must have wanted to say, “Help me!” so many times.
Yes.
Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. Apart from the teacher, what kind of high school is it?
What kind of school?
Is it a regular full-time school? Is it coed?
It’s a regular academic course, coed.
Thank you. Sorry, that was a confusing question. So even while enduring this for a year, you kept trying hard to go to school. You did really well.
I did take a little time off sometimes, but I somehow went.

Mm, high school students are busy, so anyone would need to take at least a little time off or they couldn’t keep going. I think spring break is coming up, but are you worried about whether you’ll be able to go to school next year?
Yes. What if he’s my homeroom teacher again?

That makes sense. That’s terrifying. And I think what happened to you is something very serious. You must be filled with fear yourself. If it isn’t the same homeroom teacher, you would feel a little more at ease. Is there anything else at school, or with friends, that is causing you pain? Or is the homeroom teacher the biggest problem… It must have been scary to endure this whole year and try not to let anyone notice. You’ve really endured so much. As you move up to the next grade, I believe you are someone who should be protected. Earlier, you said that even if you talked about it, no one would believe you—what about your parents? They must be worried. This is not something you should have to endure alone, but I know it takes a lot of courage to seek help. Thank you for telling me today. Your replies stopped for a little while, and I’m worried you may not be feeling well. Are you feeling okay? I’m worried because I haven’t heard back from you. Our time is up for today. Thank you for talking about something that takes so much courage to share. I don’t think the problem you’re carrying is something you should have to endure alone, and I hope we can think together about steps to protect you, because you are important. What you shared today stays here, so please feel reassured.
Thank you very much.
How was it for you to talk today? I hope we can talk again. Thank you as well.
Yes. I’m glad I was able to talk a little today. I want to come again.
I’m glad you feel that way. I believe what you’re saying. Let’s talk again. We’ll end here for today.
Yes, thank you very much.
Thank you.

interaction.content: (Good morning. We’ll begin at 11:00. Thank you.) Hello, I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in to talk with me. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to discuss?
(I’m sorry I’m late. Thank you.)
(No, that’s all right. Thank you.)
I’m 45, female. I’m worried because my daughter has anorexia.
Thank you for telling me. Your daughter has anorexia. As her mother, that must be painful to watch.
Yes. I’ve never experienced anything like this, so I don’t know what to do.
I see. You’re struggling because you don’t know what to do. Thank you for coming to talk with me. How old is your daughter?
She’s 14, in her third year of junior high school.
I see. She’s in her third year of junior high. Is she going to school?
She’s managing to go somehow, but in the mornings she sometimes suddenly starts crying, and there are days she doesn’t go.
I see. So there are times when she starts crying. As her mother, that must be worrying. From your perspective, do you think the anorexia and her school life are connected in some way?
It seems like the atmosphere in her class doesn’t suit her, and there are people she doesn’t like. Also, she says she hates her club activities and wants to quit.
Do you feel that those things may be part of what’s causing the anorexia?

I don’t know. Last year, a boy at school told her her legs were thick, and that bothered her, so she started dieting... Lately it’s been escalating, and since the end of last year she’s been losing more and more weight, so I’ve become worried.
I see. So the dieting started after something a boy said to her, and now it has escalated.
She’s always been sensitive, but also very strict with herself.
Watching your daughter lose more and more weight must be very worrying.
Then I secretly looked at her diary, and she had written that she herself thinks she has anorexia, so I’m panicking.
I see. So she had written “anorexia” in her diary as well. Do you ever talk with your daughter about dieting?

No. Right now in our home, meals and calories have become topics we’re not allowed to touch. Her feelings are unstable, so those kinds of topics seem to become triggers, and then she suddenly gets really down again.

I see. So at home, you don’t talk about meals or calories. As her mother, since your daughter is still growing, I imagine there’s a part of you that really wants to talk about it. How does that feel for you?

My husband, my daughter, and I talked about it once, but it seems like she can’t trust what her parents say. Instead, she believes the results of internet searches. She says she doesn’t even know anymore whether she’s thin or not.
I see. You tried talking with her, but your daughter believes what she finds online more. From your perspective, what do you think would help your daughter as she is now?

I’m concerned about her emotional ups and downs. I think some of it can’t be helped because she’s in puberty, but if this continues it will negatively affect her growth, so I want to get her to stop dieting little by little. But with the meals I make, she only touches the low-calorie things.

You’re concerned about her emotional ups and downs. It may be something that happens during puberty, but when it leads to extreme dieting, that’s worrying. And if she only touches the low-calorie parts of the meals you make, that must be difficult for you too. Have you and your husband considered counseling or anything like that?

Counseling and psychosomatic medicine clinics have been very crowded since COVID, and there’s a waiting list of several months. Her weight is dropping even during that time, so I’m struggling with what to do.
I see. So you’re waiting for your turn. During meals, what kinds of things do you talk about with your daughter?
We have the TV on, and we only end up having casual, random conversations. Also, I listen to things that happened at my daughter’s school and her complaints.
I see. So you are having conversations with her. Your daughter also talks about school with you. That’s good. It sounds like your daughter trusts you.

I’m not sure. If she trusted me, I wish she would listen to me about food too, but it seems like she can’t think about what’s ahead. Right now she seems completely focused on dieting and losing weight.

I see. Right now, your daughter’s attention is only on losing weight. For example, what would it be like to talk together about nutrition, or instead of focusing on losing weight, to search online together for what kind of dieting would help her become more beautiful?
Talking together about how to lose weight in a healthy, attractive way might be good. My daughter searches a lot and knows more than I do, so she doesn’t come to me for advice.
I see. Then one option might be for you to ask your daughter to teach you about dieting methods and to think together about healthy dieting. How does that sound?
Yes, I guess so. I just hope that would help her weight and her feelings become stable.
Yes. I hope so too. We’re just about out of time. How has it been for you to talk up to this point?
Thank you very much. I’ll try starting with what I can do.

Thank you. I imagine it’s very worrying for you to watch your daughter lose weight day by day, but please hang in there. And I hope you’re able to get an appointment with a psychosomatic medicine clinic soon.
Thank you. I’ll try talking with my daughter a little more.
If anything else comes up, please feel free to come talk with me anytime. Thank you very much for today.
Thank you very much.
(Thank you. I’m sorry, in the last sentence I meant to write “If anything comes up.”)
(It’s okay. Thank you very much.)
(Well then, we’ll end the role-play here. Thank you very much.)
Yes, thank you very much.
