interaction.content: (Good morning. Thank you for making time today. We’ll begin at 10 o’clock. I look forward to speaking with you.)
(Likewise, thank you.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming in for a consultation. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m a 44-year-old woman, and I’m wondering whether I should change jobs.
I see. There can be a lot to think about when it comes to work, can’t there. What led you to start thinking about changing jobs?
It’s not like there was one particular reason... If I had to say, it’s that I don’t really seem to be on the same page as my boss...
Yes, I see. When you don’t mesh with your boss, everyday work can start to feel exhausting. What kind of work are you doing now?
Office work.
I see. You mentioned that you and your boss don’t seem to be on the same page. Specifically, what kinds of conversations make you feel that way?
At work, I talk about things that need to be discussed, but when it comes to suggestions or opinions, it seems like they’re listening, but there’s no response to them.
I see. When there’s no response, it can leave you feeling unsettled or anxious, wondering whether your suggestions or opinions are okay.
Yes.
Working day to day in that kind of stressful situation is what led you to start thinking about changing jobs.
I thought maybe I don’t need to keep putting up with it anymore. I mean, maybe that’s enough. I’ve been at my current workplace for a long time, so I do give my boss various opinions.
Yes. (I’m listening.)

But we just don’t seem to connect. Since it’s work, I keep the conversation going, but I wonder if I’m being ignored, or if they think I’m a troublesome person. But I do think there are things I can say from experience. And if I’m thinking about what’s best for the workplace, I feel like I should say them.
Yes, yes. (Please go on.)
Who am I putting up with this for, I wonder. It feels like, maybe that’s enough.

You’ve been carrying stress in your daily conversations with your boss, while also thinking that for the sake of the workplace, you may need to endure things yourself, or that there may be things you should say. Continuing to work while putting up with that must be tiring. You’ve started to lose sight of who you’re enduring it for. Is there anyone around you who you can talk to about this?
I don’t intend to talk to anyone about it.
I see. Is there some reason for that?
Even if they understand, it won’t lead to improvement. I think workplace problems should be resolved there at the workplace.
I see, that’s how you feel.
If I were to talk about not being on the same page as my boss, I suppose I’d end up talking to my boss’s superior.
Yes. Do you think that if you spoke with your boss’s superior, things might improve?
I don’t think it would go well. It might improve temporarily, but...

That’s how you feel. Since you’ve likely been struggling with this for a long time without it improving, I think it’s very understandable that you’d feel it wouldn’t go well so easily. If the situation did improve, would you want to keep working at your current workplace? Or do you feel strongly that you want to change jobs after all? How do you feel about it?
There are people at my workplace who are younger than me. When I think about them, the fact that I’m wondering whether to change jobs makes me feel like I’m trying to run away from it.
Yes, yes, I see. I can sense your kind feelings toward the people at your workplace, and your strong sense of responsibility.
If my boss’s response changed, if they came to understand, I think work would become easier for me personally. But you can’t change other people, can you.
Yes, that’s how you feel.
I think my boss has their own values, and I thought I had been understanding that as I worked with them. But still, I end up feeling like we really just don’t connect.
You’ve been making an effort to accept your boss’s values too. Even so, it’s painful to feel as if you’re being ignored or seen as a bother.
It just repeats.
Yes, yes. There’s a sense of helplessness and giving up about things not changing.
That’s about right.
Earlier, you said, “Even if I talk to my boss’s superior, it might improve temporarily, but I don’t think it would go well.” Could you tell me why you feel that way?
Because even if my boss is told by someone else—their superior—I don’t think their values will change.
I see, that’s how you feel. What do you think your boss’s values are like?
I don’t know. Even if someone says something to my boss, wouldn’t they just think, “What exactly am I supposed to change about myself?”
I see. Because you don’t know, you’ve been struggling with not being able to communicate smoothly. You feel that your boss doesn’t really understand what the problem is themselves.
If I talked to someone about the fact that I feel like my boss and I aren’t on the same page, would that really come across?

Yes, I think it’s natural to feel doubtful or anxious about whether it would come across even if you talked to someone. We don’t know whether it would come across, but I was thinking that trying to consult with someone once and seeing whether anything changes could be one option. What do you think?
Even if it goes around and my boss is told by a superior to pay attention to it, I think it would just make it come across even less.
Yes, that’s how you see it. In that case, for example, would it still be difficult to talk directly with your boss?
Yes... I think it would be better to ask my boss directly what they’re thinking. Maybe I can think about changing jobs after that.

That’s what you’re thinking now. Asking directly may take courage, but with the way you’re able to talk things through so clearly, I believe you can do it. Yes, I think it may be good to first try talking with your boss, and then think about changing jobs after that.
No matter how I think about it, I should talk to the person directly. I feel like I’ve sorted things out.
I’m glad it feels sorted out. We’re just about at the end of our time, but is there anything else you’d like to talk about before we finish?
Thank you. I feel a little lighter. If I get stuck again, I’ll come back to talk.

Thank you as well for sharing with me. I felt that even while you’ve been having a difficult time yourself, you are a kind person with a strong sense of responsibility who cares about the younger people at your workplace. I hope that when you speak directly with your boss, you’ll be able to convey how you feel.
Yes.
Of course, if you ever feel like talking again, please come in anytime. Thank you for coming in for a consultation today.
Thank you very much.
Thank you very much. (Thank you for your time today. I appreciate you giving us your valuable time. I’ll send the closing message after this.)
(Thank you very much.)

interaction.content: I’m standing by. We’ll start when it’s time.
Yes. Thank you in advance.
Likewise, thank you. Hello, I’m the counselor. Could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m 35, female. It’s about not being able to actively make new friends.
I see. You’re saying you’re not able to make friends—could you tell me a bit more about that?

Yes. It’s not like it causes problems in my daily life, but I can’t really be proactive about new relationships. I’m not in trouble without them, but I wonder if being too closed off might be a problem socially.
Are you currently working?
Yes.
What kind of work do you do?
Caregiving.
I see. Are there any relationship issues at work itself that are troubling you?
Not particularly...
Do you keep in touch at all with friends from when you were a student?
I’m not really in special contact with friends from school.
I see. What do you feel is the hardest part about making new friends?
Rather than hard, it feels more like I just can’t be proactive.
Is there anyone at your current workplace you would call a friend?
At work, they’re work colleagues, not really friends.
I see. What kind of friends are you hoping to make?

If it’s just going back and forth between work and home, I feel like I get stuck in terms of personal growth, so I guess it feels like it would be better to be involved with people if I can. It’s a little different from feeling like I actively want to make friends.
Do you have any hobbies or things you like?
I do.
What kinds of things?
Cafés, reading, yoga—well, a wide range of things.
Do you go to yoga regularly?
I watch it online, or do it on my own—various things.
I see. Do you not go to group sessions or gatherings?
Right now, online is the mainstream for yoga lessons...
I see. Are you living alone now?
Yes, that’s right.
Do you ever feel lonely when you’re at home?
No, not particularly.
Since you were little, were you not very proactive with people?
I do talk with people. These days it just tends to be going between work and home.
I see. Do you feel that going back and forth between work and home is boring, or that you don’t feel fulfilled?
Rather than saying I don’t feel fulfilled, like I said at the beginning, I guess I felt that having no involvement with people outside of work at all means I won’t grow as a person.
I see. In what way would you like to grow as a person?
I feel like it might be a problem if I become too closed off. And I think having too little interest in people around me isn’t very good for living in society.
Do you not want to make friends at work?
Work colleagues don’t really feel like friends. It’s not that we don’t get along, though.
If it’s only going back and forth between home and work, it seems like it would be hard to meet new people. Have you thought about anything?
Well, I do things like online, or trying going to places where I might meet people, but...
I see. Online, are there opportunities to meet people who seem to share your interests?
I guess it’s hard for everything to line up perfectly.
What kinds of things do you do online?
Matching apps, and well, Instagram and things like that.
I see. Have you had any encounters on matching apps where you thought, this seems nice?
I’m not sure. Well, I’d say it’s normal.
Is there anyone you’ve been continuing to message with online?
Well, yes.
You’ve been making various efforts.
Well, within what I can do, I guess.
During the COVID situation, since it’s harder to meet outside, it’s difficult to look for new encounters, isn’t it.
Well, yes.
Thank you for sharing with me. I’d like to leave it around here for today—how does that sound?
Yes, that sounds fine. Thank you very much.
Thank you. We’ll end here.

interaction.content: Good evening. Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.
(Good evening. Thank you as well.)
Good evening. I’m the counselor. Thank you for reaching out today. Could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m a 36-year-old man. I’d like to talk about my daughter.
Thank you. So you’re concerned about your daughter. Could you tell me a bit more about that?
Yes, my daughter has stopped going to school. I don’t know what I should do.
I see. That must be worrying.
Yes.
You’re in a situation where you don’t know what to do. How is your daughter’s physical condition right now?
Yes, for now she’s at home and seems basically okay.
I’m glad to hear that. I imagine you must be very worried as her father.
Yes, I am worried.
Would it be okay if I ask a little about the situation at school? Only as much as you feel comfortable sharing.
Yes. What I heard from my daughter is that she said she didn’t like the relationships there, and then she stopped going.
I see. Thank you for telling me.
Not at all.
That sounds really difficult. By the way, may I ask how old your daughter is?
Yes, she’s 12.
I see. Struggling with relationships can happen to anyone, but I think it can be especially stressful for young people. About when did this concern begin?
Well, I think maybe school became stressful for my daughter. It’s been two weeks now.
I see. She’s been spending two very painful weeks like this.
Yes, I don’t know what I should do.
That makes sense. You must be feeling very anxious. I’d like us to take our time and talk through this slowly. How is she at home?
Yes, at home she’s energetic.
I see. So when she’s in a place where she feels safe, she’s okay. I’m glad to hear that!
She’s energetic at home, but I keep thinking that if she has that energy, maybe she could go to school, but she doesn’t go.
I see. So she has energy at home, but the situation is such that she can’t go to school.
Yes, she said it’s the relationships at school.
I understand. I’d like us to think through this together. What kind of conversation were you hoping to have in today’s consultation?
I was thinking it would be good if I could talk about my daughter.
I see. Is it correct that you’d like your daughter to become able to go to school?
Ideally, I do want her to go, but if she really doesn’t want to go like this, I think we’ll have to consider another way without making her go.
I see. You’re thinking of prioritizing your daughter’s feelings.
Yes. It’s already—or rather, still—been two weeks, and it’ll be almost a month soon, so I’m thinking maybe I’ll reassess then. Of course, we talk every day.
I see. So you’re in a situation where you can talk every day. I’m glad to hear that. I think it’s very good that you can hear about your daughter’s feelings.
Yes, we do talk, but when it comes to school, she says she doesn’t want to go, so... I’m thinking forcing her to go wouldn’t be right.
You really understand your daughter’s feelings. I can strongly feel the love you have for her.
Thank you.
Going forward, I think it may be good to listen to your daughter’s honest feelings and consider what would be best for her. How does that sound?

Yes, I ask her every day, but I wonder if asking every day might be annoying for her. And considering that she’s 12 and thinking about her future, I do want her to go because she needs the ability to live in a group. But if it’s difficult, then I wonder if I’ll have no choice but to put her in a private school, even if it costs some money.
You’ve thought about it that far. The sense of distance with your daughter is also important, isn’t it? I understand that feeling well.
Yes, I’m a single parent, so there are money concerns, and my daughter only has me.

You’ve been carrying this on your own. I imagine your daughter may also understand how you feel. First, I think it’s important to create an environment where your daughter can understand her own feelings and feel safe talking. How does that sound?
Yes, I think I am talking with her, but maybe I still don’t have enough awareness as a parent.

That’s not true. It seems to me that you’re giving her plenty of love. I imagine supporting your daughter while also working must be quite a heavy burden. So, as one suggestion, you could consider consulting with the school counselor or with professionals like us and receiving support. How does that sound?
Yes, it feels a little hard to approach, but I’ll include it as one option to think about.
Please don’t struggle with this alone; I hope you’ll talk to someone about it.
Yes.
First of all, please take care of yourself so that you don’t suffer too much.
Yes, I understand.
As for your daughter, I think it may be good to accept the anxiety she’s feeling now, be there for her, and slowly listen to what she has to say. Let’s move forward one step at a time, slowly.
Yes, that’s true. Thank you. Yes, I understand.
I deeply understand the love you have, and I believe your daughter’s behavior may gradually begin to change. We’ve talked up to this point—how are you feeling?
Yes, you listened to me slowly, and I don’t know if things will actually go well in reality, but I want to prioritize my daughter’s feelings as I think about what to do.
Yes. I do feel that reality is difficult. If you find yourself struggling, please feel free to reach out anytime.
Thank you.

I’m rooting for your daughter to move in a good direction from here. We’re getting close to the end of our time. Thank you for coming in for our session today. You’re welcome to reach out again anytime.
Thank you very much.
We’ll end today’s consultation here. Thank you very much.
Thank you as well.

Yes. Various things made me feel suspicious, like, “Is this place really okay?”

So today, because of that mismatch in conditions, you decided to turn it down, but when you think about what comes next, you felt anxious and came here to talk—is that right? It would make you feel suspicious too...
Yes... well, since I’ve been out of work for quite a long time, it’s closer to feeling like, “This is really a problem,” and “What should I do?” Of course, there’s anxiety too.
I see, so in addition to feeling “anxious,” there are other feelings as well... Over the past six months, have you applied to other workplaces?
Yes. I’ve applied to a few.
I see. How did things turn out with those workplaces?
Let me see. Some turned me down, and with others the conditions didn’t work out, so I declined from my side—that kind of thing.
I see, so that’s how it’s been. Have the workplaces you’ve applied to so far been in the same general type of work?
Yes. They were mostly welfare-related.

Yes. That’s what I’m thinking.
So you have an idea of what kind of work you want to do. That’s good.
Hm? What do you mean?
I’m sorry. You’re thinking you’d like to devote yourself to welfare-related work.
Yes. Not so much “devote myself,” but I’d like to work in that field.

Right, “work” in that field. You mentioned that the conditions last time were different, and that you felt “this is really a problem” and “I’m at a loss.” Have you thought about what you’d like to do as your next step?
Well, I think I have no choice but to look for a new workplace.
Yes. So you’re thinking you’d like to look for a new workplace.
Yes.
In looking for a new workplace, is there anything you feel anxious about?
Let me see. I suppose it’s that the period I’ve been out of work is long. That in itself probably gives a bad impression.
I see. So you’re feeling anxious about having a long period out of work.
Yes.
Even so, from what I’ve heard, I think you’re someone who takes action.
Do you think so? What made you feel that way?

Over these six months, there were places that didn’t work out, but you also talked about turning places down yourself when the conditions were different. That made me feel that you’re someone who has both initiative and good judgment.
I see... thank you.
Within all of that, do you currently have any workplaces you’re thinking of applying to next?
Yes. There are a few places I’m considering.
I see. So you have several candidates.
Yes.
I think you have initiative and judgment, so I think it would be good to move forward at your own pace without rushing.
For now, I think I just have to keep going. Thank you.
Yes. Thank you. We’re just about out of time. How was today for you?
Let me see. I guess it felt kind of different from what I had expected. I mean, I wasn’t really able to talk much about my feelings... I do think you responded to me politely, though.

I see... thank you. You feel there are still things you haven’t talked through, so if you’d like, please come back for another consultation. Since we have the history, we can continue from where we left off. How does that sound?
Yes, if there’s another opportunity, I’d appreciate it.
Yes, thank you for today.
Thank you. (Thank you. It was as expected.)
(Thank you for today. Good work.)

interaction.content: (Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.)
Understood. Thank you as well; I appreciate your help.
Hello, I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming today. If you’re comfortable, could you first tell me your age and gender?
Thank you. What would you like to talk about today?
Lately, I’ve somehow been feeling like living is exhausting.
I see. When do you feel that exhaustion?
Maybe when I’m alone...
I see. That sounds painful... Was there anything that triggered it?
I don’t think there was any one specific thing.
Mm-hmm, so there isn’t really a particular trigger, but you feel it when you’re alone.
Yes...
How is it when you’re with someone?
During winter break, when I unexpectedly got to see a friend, it helped take my mind off things.
I see. That would feel nice, wouldn’t it. Has school started again now?
Yes.
When you’re at school, is it enjoyable?
It’s normal.
Mm-hmm, I see. How do you usually spend your time at home?
Lately, I’ve been focusing on studying. I guess it’s fun when I’m playing games. On Sunday I studied all morning. In the afternoon I was feeling completely down the whole time.
I see, I see. You’ve been working hard at studying. You said you’re 17—are entrance exams coming up soon?
Next year.
I see. So are you studying for entrance exams now?
Rather than that, I have a lot of assignments.
I see. So you were just doing assignments one after another... and then in the afternoon you felt completely down, is that about right? What were you feeling then?
Lonely.
Mm-hmm, you felt lonely.
Yes, I was feeling even lonelier than usual.
I see. Feeling lonely is painful... Do you have family members living with you now?
Yes.
Do they say things to you, or is there anything that makes you feel uncomfortable?
A little while ago, things felt unsettled because of my younger sister’s entrance exams, though, well, it wasn’t like anything was being said directly to me.
Do you mean your younger sister was being told things?
Yes. And I guess my parents also argued about that sometimes.
I see. Do you talk with your parents often?
Not especially, but I think it’s normal.
I see. The feeling of loneliness... where do you think it comes from? At those times, do you think about things like that? I mean, what kind of things. Sorry.
Since I’m just shut in my room alone studying all the time... maybe that makes me feel even lonelier somehow. There are also times when my feelings won’t settle down.
I see, that makes sense. When your feelings won’t settle down, what is it like?
It feels like I can’t rest my mind.
Mm-hmm. At times like that, do you distract yourself by playing games or something?
Sometimes I feel this anger and I don’t even know why. The other day,
I see. Mm-hmm. (I’m listening.)
I tried to distract myself by watching a drama I like, but I felt this anger I didn’t understand, and I couldn’t concentrate.
I see... You feel anger, but you don’t know what it’s directed at. Is that what it’s like?
Yes.
I see, I see. If that anger were toward one of these—someone else, yourself, or having to study—which one would feel closest?
All of them...
I see. Toward everything, like you just feel irritated by all of it—is that the kind of feeling?
The feelings I have are different depending on the moment.
I see. Do you ever take those feelings out on anyone?
No, I don’t.
I see. Having listened to what you’ve shared so far, would it be okay if I told you a little about what I’m sensing?
Yes, please.

From what you’ve told me, I get the sense that you’ve been studying hard on your own with a lot of focus, and even when feelings like loneliness or anger come up, you don’t take them out on anyone—you hold them all by yourself and push them down. That’s not something just anyone can do, and I feel that the way you’re able to control yourself is really admirable. At the same time, I wonder if you’ve become tired from doing that, and that’s what brought you here to talk today. How does that sound?
Yes... I’m tired.

Yes, I really do think you’ve been doing your very best... At the same time, I think there are times when anyone reaches their limit if they’re carrying things alone, so we only have a little time left, but I’d like us to think together about how your heart might feel even a little lighter... In response to the loneliness, for example, there might be things like inviting a friend to study together, or reaching out to someone you can talk to about yourself... Can you think of anything that might be doable?
Yes... spending time with friends or talking with them is fun...

Mm-hmm. If staying shut in at home is what’s making you feel lonely, it might help to make time to study with a friend at the library, or have tea at a café... things like that. Of course, you’re also welcome to come here again to talk. I’m sure there are parts we weren’t able to fully get to today... so please come again if you’d like.
It really would be nice if I could do that... Please listen again sometime.
Thank you. It’s about time now, so would it be alright to end for today?
Yes, thank you very much. Goodbye.
Thank you. I’m rooting for you. You’re welcome here anytime. Well then, goodbye. (Thank you for today. Is it okay to end the LINE session?)
(Yes. This was a very good learning experience for me. Thank you very much. Good work today.)
(Thank you as well. Good work today. Goodbye.)

interaction.content: (Hello. We'll begin when it's time. Thank you.)
(Hello. Thank you for meeting with me today.)
Hello. I'm the counselor. To start, please tell me your age, gender, and what you'd like to talk about today.
Hello. Thank you for meeting with me.
Thank you.
I'm a woman, 25 years old. I'm job hunting to change jobs, but it isn't going well, and I'm struggling with it.

About three months ago.

I've been going to Hello Work and also looking on my own, but it's hard to find positions that match my conditions, and I've been rejected after interviews.

That it won't involve long working hours, and that the workplace is somewhere I can commute to from home, things like that.
I see. You've been job hunting for three months, and it has been hard to find places that match your conditions, and you've been rejected at interviews. How do you feel about that?
I'm anxious about whether I'll find a job.
That's how you're feeling. I think when that kind of situation continues for three months, feelings of anxiety can come up. What was it that led you to start job hunting?
There wasn't really a trigger. I quit my previous workplace because I thought I would change jobs.
I see. When did you leave your previous company?
About four months ago.
I see. Let me summarize your current situation: you decided to change jobs and left your job four months ago, and then started job hunting three months ago. Is that right?
Yes.

I moved back to my parents' home and am living with them.
I see. So you moved back to your family home after leaving your previous company?
That's right.
Thank you for answering. I see. You said you left your previous job because you wanted to change jobs. Was there something that made you feel that way?
The long working hours were really hard, and my body couldn't keep up, so I had no choice but to quit.
That was the situation, then. How is your health now?
I rested well for about a month, so I'm feeling much better now.
I see. I'm relieved to hear that. In today's conversation, what would you most like to talk about?
I'm having trouble because my job search isn't going well, so I came to talk about that.
Yes, of course. I'm sorry.
It's okay.
Earlier, you mentioned feeling anxious because you haven't been able to find a job. Have you talked to anyone about it?
I haven't talked to anyone close to me.
I see. Have you talked to anyone other than people close to you?
This is the first time I've come to talk to someone. I mean, come for counseling. Sorry.
It's okay. Thank you. I was thinking we could work together to consider what might help ease your anxiety about job hunting. How does that sound?
Yes, please.
Thank you. You said you're anxious about whether you'll find a job. What kind of work are you hoping to do?
I'm hoping for office work.
I see. So you're hoping for an office job that you can commute to from home and that doesn't involve long working hours.
Yes, that's right.
At the beginning, you mentioned that you've sometimes been rejected after interviews. Were those places ones that matched your conditions?
Yes, they mostly matched what I was hoping for.

I see. I'm sorry. We're in the middle of talking, but we're almost out of time. Next time, we can continue from where we left off today, so I hope you'll come back to talk again. How was it for you to talk today?
I understand. I'm glad I was able to talk to someone for the first time.
Listening to you today, I felt that you're someone who can clearly express what you want. If you'd like, please come and talk with me again. Thank you for today.

interaction.content: Hello, I’m a counselor. Could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
Hello. I’m 28, male.
Thank you. I look forward to speaking with you.
Thank you. Same here.
Could you tell me what you’d like to talk about?
I quit my part-time job because of stress, and I’m scared of people, so I can’t go outside during the day. I don’t know what to do.
I see. That sounds really painful.
Yes, it’s exhausting.
What kind of stress led you to quit your part-time job?
Someone I was close to at work quit, and I got scared. I live alone and don’t have money, so I’m anxious about how I’m going to live from here on too.
I see. That must feel really worrying. When you say you’re scared, what do you think is causing that?
Yes, I’m scared of interacting with people. I think the cause is probably the bullying I experienced in high school. I start hyperventilating, and it’s really painful.
When do you tend to start hyperventilating?

When I feel people’s eyes on me, or I’m in a crowd, or when I’m around people, I get scared and start hyperventilating. Sometimes I panic too, and when I think I don’t know when it might happen again, I get so scared I can’t move. Even if someone is walking toward me from ahead, or I just see someone in the distance, I feel scared.
I see. That must be really, really hard.
Yes, it gets hard to breathe.
Around when did you start becoming scared of people?
It was definitely from the bullying in high school. That’s when I started hyperventilating.
I see. Up until now, were you able to manage your part-time job without problems?

For work, I chose a job in the back room of a supermarket where I could avoid seeing people as much as possible. I was able to keep going because there was a senior coworker I got along with, but then I started feeling helpless, and almost every day I was hyperventilating and feeling exhausted, so I quit.
You mentioned that you live alone. Have you talked to your parents or anyone like that about this?
We don’t really have contact, and I haven’t seen them in over a year. My relationship with my parents isn’t very good, and I don’t want to talk to them about it.
I see. Are you going to be okay with living expenses and things like that going forward?
Honestly, it’s going to be hard. I have about 150,000 yen left in my bank account.
Are you currently thinking about trying to find a new job?

Even if I want to, the anxiety and fear of panicking or hyperventilating all come at once, so right now I feel like it would be difficult. I’m worried I won’t be able to live because I can’t work and have no income. In my current state, I don’t think I’d be able to keep a job.
I see. So you’re worried about your life going forward.
Yes. I don’t have money to be seen at a hospital either… My physical condition isn’t getting better. The anxiety just keeps increasing.
Have you ever consulted a hospital before?
I have in the past. But they only told me to get used to people, and the medication didn’t work either.
I see. That must have been very painful.
Yes, it made me feel like nothing I do is going to work.
Have you ever consulted with any public welfare services?
I’ve never gone because I’m scared to go to places like that. In person, I feel like my mind would go blank and I wouldn’t be able to explain things well. I’m also not good with phone calls.
I think life will become difficult if you aren’t able to work going forward. How are you thinking about that?
I’m in a situation where I want to work but can’t, so I feel like I may need to get help from public services, but I can’t move, and it’s painful.
I see. So you feel that help from public services is necessary, but you also feel it would be difficult to go and talk to them.
Yes, I really strongly want this mental health problem to somehow get better. I think, if only I didn’t have this, I could move around a little more…
Does going to a hospital for a consultation feel difficult right now?
I’m behind on my National Health Insurance payments, so I think I can’t go. I don’t want to see people, and I’m also hesitant because of the money.
What kind of daily life are you living right now?
I’m getting by on one small meal a day, like instant noodles that I buy by the case through delivery.
That’s not very good for your body.
Yes. I’m so scared of stores that I can barely go near them.
I see. So even going outside feels scary.
I’m living as much as possible so I don’t have to see people.
Would it be difficult to call the welfare office?
It’s scary, but maybe I don’t really have a choice…
Yes. It may be scary, but I’d like you to try calling the welfare office once. How does that sound?
I probably won’t be able to explain things well…
Even if you can’t explain it well, if you slowly tell them about your current situation, I think they’ll understand.
Is that so. I’ll try my best.
Yes. I’m rooting for you, so please try your best.
Okay.
Thank you for sharing your story with me. I’d like to stop around here for today. How does that sound?
Okay. Thank you very much.
Thank you. We’ll end here for today.

interaction.content: Good evening. Thank you for being here.
Good evening. Thank you.
Is it okay to start on time?
Yes.
Is there anything, like a theme, that you’d like to try?
This is my first time, so I’m not really sure what you mean by a theme. I was just planning to talk as someone seeking counseling... Are there several kinds of themes?
Some people prefer to decide on one beforehand, so I asked just to check. Anything is fine.
What kinds of themes are there, for example?
Let’s see... bullying, suicide, family matters—there are various ones. For now, since it’s time, shall we begin?
Yes.
(Okay, I’ll begin.)
Thank you.
Good evening, I’m a counselor. Thank you for coming to talk with me. If it’s okay, I’d like to hear more about you, so may I ask your age and gender?
Yes. Female. I’m a 48-year-old homemaker.
Thank you. Please feel free to talk about anything.
Thank you. Right now, I have a 15-year-old daughter, and I messaged on LINE because I wanted to consult about her.
I see. You’d like to talk about your daughter. By the way, is your daughter in high school?
She’s in her first year of high school now, and she’s my only child.
Thank you for telling me. What kinds of things about your daughter are concerning you right now?

Yes. In her second year of junior high, she stopped going to school, and in her third year she attended a support class. Now she goes every day to a high school that specializes in dance, which takes an hour and a half to get to, but I’m concerned about how she spends her days off, and I’m struggling with how much I should interfere.
I see... so that’s what’s been on your mind. If it’s okay, could you tell me a bit more about how your daughter spends her days off?

Yes. Starting the day before a day off, it’s like she’s trying to release all kinds of stress—she shuts herself in her room and talks on the phone with someone until morning. Then on Saturdays and Sundays she sleeps until after noon, and once she wakes up she’s glued to her phone... When I think her daily routine is getting disrupted, I myself start to feel anxious...
I see. Certainly, when you see that kind of situation, it makes sense that you would feel anxious.
Yes. But my husband says that since she works hard on weekdays, we shouldn’t interfere.
Your husband says that, then. That would leave you feeling conflicted, wouldn’t it.
Exactly. She’s also in adolescence, and my daughter and I often end up fighting.
I see. That must be difficult. By the way, regarding this situation, have you tried saying anything to your daughter?

She was still on the phone after midnight, so I told her, “It’s already time to sleep, right? Please at least keep to your bedtime.” But my daughter said she would sleep in a little while, so I thought I’d wait a bit, and then I ended up falling asleep myself.

I see... so that’s how your daughter responded. Certainly, there are times when you want her to keep her promises. You mentioned that when you think your daughter’s routine is getting disrupted, you become anxious. By the way, what makes you feel that way?

When she stays up late or doesn’t wake up in the morning, even on days off, I start thinking she might go back to not attending school again. I’m anxious about school refusal too, but my daughter’s health is what I’m most worried about. But there’s another part of me too—the part that thinks my husband is right, and that now is the time to watch over her independence.

I see... remembering what you went through before, and thinking about your daughter’s school life pattern, leads you to feel that way. Listening to you, I feel that you care very deeply about your daughter.
The thing I value most in parenting is simply wanting my daughter to be happy... So I just really want her to take care of her health... But it’s hard for my feelings to get through to her.
I see. That must feel frustrating.
I don’t know what I should do anymore.

Yes... Listening to you, I can really feel how much you care about your daughter. You mentioned that when you talk face to face, it turns into a fight. For example, I was thinking it might be okay to try communicating your feelings to your daughter in writing, like through LINE or a letter. What do you think?

My mom friends and her school teachers often tell me that, but for some reason, the one person who really needs to understand—my daughter—doesn’t get how I feel. I see. I hadn’t thought of that. Yes. When I talk to her face to face, I think I end up saying unnecessary things, so I’ll try putting it in writing.
Yes. With writing, she can reread it later, and as your daughter reads it multiple times, I think your feelings may gradually reach her.
I hope so... But I’d like to try it and see. Thank you very much. If something comes up again, is it okay to consult with you? I’d be happy if you could tell me your name.
Of course. When you feel anxious, or if there’s anything on your mind, please come talk with us again. I’m sorry, but as a rule, I’m unable to tell you the counselor’s name.
I understand.
When you come for counseling next time, we’ll listen while checking the history of what you’ve talked about so far, so please don’t worry.
I understand.
By the way, how was it for you to talk today?
The unsettled feeling I had has cleared up a little. I feel like I found one way to help improve my daughter’s daily habits. Thank you.
Thank you as well for sharing something important with me today. I’m glad it seems to have been helpful. Please come again if anything comes up.
Yes. Thank you.
Thank you for coming to talk with me today. Well then, I’ll end the consultation here.
Yes.
(Thank you for your work. Also, please submit your impressions and evaluation in the report.) (What shall we do? It’s a little early, but is it okay to end the role-play?)
Thank you for your work. It’s okay to end.
Understood. Then I’ll end it now.

interaction.content: Thank you for speaking with me.
■ Sorry to be late. Thank you for being here. Hello, I’m the counselor. To start, could you tell me your age and gender?
I’m a teenage girl.
Thank you. What would you like to talk about today?
At school, I do various things like being the grade representative and helping take care of things for the class,
Yes.
but I’m struggling because I’m not able to show my abilities in my studies.
So you’re taking on various roles at school, but you also want to be able to show more of what you can do in your studies.
Yes. My homeroom teacher says things like, “You should be able to do more.”
Your teacher said that to you.
Yes.
As for you, Toki-san—would it be okay if I call you Toki-san?—how did it make you feel when that was said to you?
It’s Akane.
I understand. Thank you, Akane-san.
It made me feel very distressed. I didn’t know what I should do, and I keep wondering how I can show what I’m capable of.

When they say, “You should be able to do more,” does it feel like pressure, or like it doesn’t sit right with you? Is it more like, “I’m already trying hard enough, so what more am I supposed to do?” Sorry, our messages crossed.
It feels like I don’t know what I should do.
You don’t know how to show the ability your teacher is talking about.
Yes. I’m good at thinking things through in advance, but
Yes.
when I’m suddenly asked what I think, I’m not good at answering off the cuff.
I see.
I don’t know how to answer like my friends around me do.
You want to be able to say what you think even when you’re asked suddenly, like the people around you. For example, what kind of situation did that happen in?
In English class, I was asked about the differences between how Americans and Japanese people think, but I couldn’t come up with anything right away.
Yes, when you’re suddenly asked about something you haven’t really thought about in daily life, it’s hard for ideas to come to mind.
I think I could have answered if I’d had time to think about it beforehand.
Yes, it feels a little frustrating when you think, “If only I’d been given time, I could have thought of something.”
Yes, it’s very frustrating.
Were your friends around you able to answer smoothly, even if they were called on first? (I imagine it would feel even more frustrating if you couldn’t answer and then the second person could.)
Yes, a lot of my friends are very capable. I feel a lot of pressure. I have another presentation for an assignment coming up, so I’m already very anxious about it.

Your friends who can answer smoothly during presentations seem very capable to you, and that feels like pressure. Because you feel that way, you start wondering whether you’ll be able to answer well on the next assignment too. By the way, for the next assignment presentation, is the topic already decided?
Yes, I’m very anxious, and when I think about it, I can’t sleep at night.
That sounds really hard. It can get to the point where you wish you could avoid it if possible.
Yes. The topic is decided. It’s really painful.
The topic is decided, but you don’t know what kinds of questions you’ll be asked, right?
That’s right, that’s what makes me so anxious. I keep thinking, what if it doesn’t go well?
When you think about what might happen if you fail, your anxiety keeps getting bigger and bigger.
Yes, I’m so scared I can’t stand it. What should I do?

Everyone else seems like they’re capable, and you don’t know what you’ll be asked, so of course it feels scary. Akane-san, it sounds like you feel you’re not good at being asked things on the spot, but you said you’re good at thinking things through in advance,
Yes.
so how about coming up with as many possible questions as you can on your own before you go into it?
Yes, that might be a good idea. But if I get a question I didn’t expect, I might not know what to do... What should I do?
Nothing is ever 100%, is it? No matter how many questions you prepare, it’s hard to predict everything. If a question comes up that you weren’t expecting... first, take one breath.
Okay.

What did you think those words were coming from?
I’m an only child and never really fought with anyone, so… frustration, misery, feeling pathetic.

So that’s how you were thinking about it. I imagine it was painful. And you were quietly thinking that through. Then, when it comes to your husband, do you have any thoughts about how you would at least like him to be?
He only interferes with his mouth, and I earn all the living expenses. I just hope we can have normal conversations and live peacefully.
I see. That really is difficult. You’re even shouldering the living expenses. You said you’d like to have normal conversations—what kind of conversations would you like to have, for example?
For example, today I made a bookshelf with DIY. I don’t have the knowledge, but he was like a master yelling at an apprentice.

I see. That’s impressive—you made a bookshelf. But being spoken to that way really is unpleasant. I think it’s completely understandable. How would you like him to speak to you? Or would you want him to do it together with you, instead of just talking?
If we’re going to do it anyway, I just want to enjoy it.

Yes, exactly. I think that’s very true. Earlier, you shared that you believe there is value in trying anything and having the experience—what kinds of things have you challenged yourself to do? I’d really like to hear. Well, I’m sorry. The “well” got left in there.
Becoming a psychological counselor. I became an esthetician.
I see. That’s truly wonderful. You’ve built up so many experiences. As you said, experience has value. So those experiences are also being put to use in how you respond to your husband, then.
My husband has never accomplished anything, so his pride and anxiety are out of balance.
I see. You’ve really analyzed your husband carefully. What kinds of support do you give him?
Right now, I can only think of trying to keep some distance. My head is full of things I need to do.
For you, that feels like what you’re able to do right now. So, what kinds of things do you need to do?
Right now, my main work is creating a stage performance, so I feel rushed, like I have to get my own way of being in order too.

Oh wow. You’re involved in stage performance too. You’re so energetic. I can feel strength in your words. As I listen, you keep sharing such wonderful thoughts, so I’d like to hear a little more. Could you tell me more specifically what you mean by getting your way of being in order?
Even at this age, I have inherited something wonderful from the master who shaped me, so I have decided that I will still stand on the stage.
That is truly wonderful. So that’s why you want to get yourself in order and stand on the stage?
Yes.
Could you tell me a bit more about what getting yourself in order means?
Because of COVID, it’s been hard to take lessons, and my body really only moves about one-tenth as well as I want it to.

So in that way, you’re fighting with yourself. It would make you happy if your husband supported you, wouldn’t it. Let me reflect on what we’ve talked about so far. While going through painful experiences with your husband, who blames others and has even been violent toward you, you still believe that what you want to do and the experiences you have are valuable, while your husband says they’re meaningless. But you trust your own thoughts, value the connections you have with various people, and continue challenging yourself while trying to get yourself in order—would that be an accurate way to understand it?
Yes. Thank you for listening to me so much. There is no such thing as 100 percent, but I can feel grateful that I’m able to do what is important to me. Thank you very much.

That’s a wonderful reflection. We’re getting close to the end of our time. Earlier, you said your husband’s pride and anxiety are out of balance, and I wondered if there might be some way to use your psychology qualification in how you respond to him. I’m wishing you success in all of your many experiences. I think one goal may be that, as you succeed through those different experiences, you become able to spend time with your husband normally and enjoyably. I’m rooting for you. Also, whenever you have something you’d like to talk about, please feel free to consult a counselor anytime.
Yes. Being able to live normally is a miracle, isn’t it. Having you listen to me today has made my heart feel lighter. Thank you very much.
Thank you as well. Then, we’ll end here.
Yes.
(Thank you very much. I learned a great deal. We’ll end here. I’d appreciate it if you could leave an evaluation.)
Yes.

interaction.content: (Thank you for being here today. We’ll begin when it’s time.)
(Good morning. Thank you as well.)
Hello. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming today. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
Hello. I’m a 45-year-old woman. I’d like to talk about my husband.
Thank you. So you came to talk about your husband. What would you like to discuss?
It’s about how my husband spends money.
I see. Is there something that concerns you about the way your husband spends money?
Recently, out of nowhere, he sold the compact car we were driving and bought a foreign car. He never talks to me about things first.
I see. When someone suddenly does something like that, it’s really startling, isn’t it? How did you feel at the time?
I was shocked, and I was angry.
I see. If he bought a foreign car on his own without talking to you, it makes sense that you would feel that way.
Yes.
That makes sense. At that time, did you tell your husband how you felt?
Yes, I got emotional and let out everything I was feeling.
I see. How did your husband react then?
He got angry and left. Though after two hours, he came back like nothing had happened.

I see. He didn’t listen to what you were trying to tell him. I can understand why that would feel unacceptable and make you angry. You said he never talks to you about things—are there other things that concern you about how he spends money?

He goes to his family home to ask for financial help. It’s like he can’t hold back when he wants something. Apparently his mother paid for the car too, but he doesn’t understand that he can’t cover the maintenance costs or repair costs afterward with his own money.
I see. Your husband acts on his own wants, and that must put you in a difficult position too.
Because my husband is like this, he doesn’t make the children hold back either, so the kids think they can get anything they want bought for them.
Has your husband said anything about giving financial support to his family? I’m sorry. I got the conversation mixed up.
No, it’s okay.
I see. So your children feel that way too. Do your family members realize that you’re struggling with this?
By family, do you mean my husband?
Your husband and your children.
I’m always angry and irritated at home, so I think they notice.
I see. So you’re living with those feelings day to day. That must be really exhausting.
Yes, it is exhausting.
That makes sense. Although it seems your husband understands that you’re angry, I got the impression that he hasn’t really been listening to your feelings, like leaving when he gets angry.
It felt like he left because I told him to get out.
I see. So it wasn’t that he left angrily on his own.
Yes. He was angry, but I was the one who was furious, really.
I see. You were furious, but two hours later he came back as if nothing had happened.
That’s right.
Yes. I imagine things are really painful like this on a regular basis, but how are you thinking about your relationship with your husband and what comes next?

He’s too soft on the kids, but he’s a kind person, so I’m not thinking about divorce right now or anything. But we’re always fighting about how he uses money, and the hardest thing is that I can’t feel at ease at home.
I see. If it turns into a fight every time, you can’t really relax. How does your husband usually treat you?
My husband just says good morning the day after a fight like nothing happened, so I get even angrier and don’t talk to him for a while.
I see. Is it that his carefree attitude makes you even angrier?
Even though I’m angry that he wastes money, he tries to get on my good side by buying cake to make me happy. He’s missing the point.
I see. It may be that your husband is a little mistaken about how to make you happy.
No matter how many times I explain it, that misunderstanding doesn’t get better.
I see. That must be exhausting.
I don’t know what to do.
It would be good if your feelings could get through to him and you could feel more at ease. I’d like us to think together about how to do that. How does that sound?
Yes, I’d like to create even a little time when I’m not irritated.
That makes sense. I know your husband’s way of spending money is a problem, but first, I hope we can help you get to a place where you can feel better in your day-to-day life.
Yes.
I’m sorry that our time is up today and we weren’t able to talk through specific solutions. I hope you’ll come here to talk again, rather than carrying this all by yourself.
Yes, thank you very much.
Thank you for coming in for a consultation today. (Thank you for the role-play. We’ll end here.)

interaction.content: (Hello. Thank you for meeting with me today. If possible, I’d appreciate it if you could play the role of a younger client.)
(Understood. Thank you.)
(Thank you.) Hello, I’m the counselor. Could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to talk about?
I’m 17, male. I can’t decide on my goals for the future.
I see. So you’re struggling with things about your future.
Yes.
Could you tell me a little more about that?
In my second year of high school, I chose a course and moved forward with it, but I don’t know what I’m studying for.
I see. So you’ve started to feel unsure about the meaning of studying. Are you in your third year of high school now?
No, I’m in my second year.
I’m sorry, I misunderstood. You said you decided on a course—what kind of course is it?
Science track. It was decided based on my grades.
I see. So because your grades were good, you ended up in the science track. Are you thinking of going into a science-related field at university?
Yes, but my teacher decided it without asking me.
I see. It doesn’t feel good when it’s decided without your say, does it?
Yes.
Did you want to go into a course that wasn’t science?
I don’t know that either. It was decided before I had a chance to think about where I should go.
I see. That must have been a shock.
Rather than a shock, it made me feel bad.
That makes sense. I can understand why it would make you feel that way. How do you feel about your future path right now?
That’s what I don’t know. I don’t like that it was decided without asking me, but I also can’t find what I want to do. Up until now, things had gone well when I did what my parents said.
I see. What do your parents say about your future path?
They tell me to go to medical school.
I see. How do you feel about that?
They’ve been saying it to me for so long, so I kind of feel like maybe there’s no choice.
I see. So you feel like going to medical school may be something you can’t help. Isn’t the studying really demanding if you’re aiming for medical school?
My grades are at the top of my class. That’s why my parents expect even more from me. Because they want me to take over after them.
I see. Being at the top of your class is really impressive. Even so, being expected to do that can feel like pressure. Your parents are doctors, and they want you to follow in their footsteps.
They’ve been saying it ever since I was little.
I see. When you were little, how did you feel about that?
I accepted it straightforwardly. But as I got older, I started wondering if that was really okay. My older brother also went into medicine.
I see. In that situation, it makes sense that you’d feel pressure.
Yes. I wonder if that’s the only path I have to choose.
I see. But recently, you’ve been wondering whether that’s really okay, right?
Yes. My parents say that if I become a doctor, I’ll never have to worry about making a living.
You’re wondering whether it’s okay to just become a doctor because your parents say so, or what it is you really want to do.
I can’t understand whether it’s okay to choose for that kind of reason.
I see. So that’s the part that doesn’t sit right with you.
Yes.
You’d like time to think about whether to keep doing what your parents say or do something else, wouldn’t you?
Yes.
I think you still have time, and I hope you’ll make a choice you won’t regret.
Thank you.
When you decide the direction you want to go in from here, I know it may be difficult, but I hope you’ll try talking it over with your parents.
Yes, I think that’s probably what will happen.
Please feel free to come back here anytime to talk about how that goes or anything else. Thank you for sharing something important with me. Would it be okay if we ended here for today?
Yes. Thank you very much.
The temperature has been changing a lot, so please take care of yourself. We’ll end here for today.

Thank you.

Let’s do our best♪

Hello.

Hanako, then. Thank you. As you think about returning to work, what kinds of things are you anxious about?
I wonder what everyone at the company will think of me...
That makes sense. When you think about the time until you return to work, it’s hard to know what to expect, so it can make you anxious.
Yes, that’s true.
Is there a specific person you feel anxious about? Or is it people there in general?
It’s not anyone in particular.
I see.
Yes.
Would it be okay to say that today we’ll talk about your anxiety before returning to work?
I’m already worried about what will happen after I go back to the office.

It’s about what people will think of me.
Hanako, do you often find yourself worrying about the people around you?
If I had to say, maybe I do.
What kinds of things especially bother you?
How other people see me, I guess.
What was the reason you were taking time off? If you’re comfortable, could you tell me?
Well, I made a mistake at work, and after that my health got worse.
I see. So you’re anxious about how the people around you will think of you because of that.
Yes.
I understand those anxious feelings. Is there anyone at work you can talk to about how you feel?
Not really.
I see. That must be painful.
Yes, it’s painful.
Are you used to the work itself?
More or less. If my health is okay, I think I might be able to manage somehow, but I’m anxious.
Does your physical condition fluctuate?
It’s settled down now, so I’m gradually heading toward returning to work.
I see. Is your supervisor understanding about your return to work?
I reported on my current situation, but I don’t really feel like they’re especially consulting with me about it. Well, of course they haven’t denied it or anything.

Yes.
Before returning to work, you had a meeting and so on, and while they didn’t reject it, you didn’t feel that they fully understood you—is that right?
We confirmed the necessary things with each other, but I didn’t talk about my feelings.
I see. Do you think you might try talking a little about how you feel?
It might be kind of hard to tell my supervisor. I want to talk, but I don’t really know who I should talk to.
I see. Would it be possible to talk with the occupational physician?
I think it wouldn’t be physically impossible, but somehow they feel distant to me.
That feels difficult, then. When you feel anxious, how do you calm yourself down?
Hmm, like watching YouTube—YouTube, I mean.

With a smile. I don’t want them to look annoyed, I guess.

I just met with them the other day, and somehow it feels hard to reach out.
I see. Not being able to tell anyone what you’re feeling really does make you anxious. Can you talk with family or friends?
It might be hard to tell my family. My friends will listen, but it’s not like they can do anything about it... Somehow, I feel unsettled.
Yes. The anxiety gets bigger. I’m sorry. I wasn’t able to do anything. Thank you.
Thank you too. There are ups and downs, but let’s get through them⤴️ Good work today.
Thank you. Take care.
Good work today.

First-year junior high school student, girl, how to make friends. Yes.

Yes.

I like reading books.

Yes. I get nervous.

Ever since then, I’ve been scared to talk to people.

Yes.

Yes.

Teachers are a little...

I don’t know...

interaction.content: (Good evening. Thank you for being here today.)
Thank you for meeting with me.
Good evening. I’m the counselor. Thank you for coming to talk with me. To start, could you tell me your age, gender, and what you’d like to discuss?
Thank you. I’m a man in my 40s. I’d like to talk about work and work-related stress.
Thank you. So you’re struggling with your job and the stress that comes with it. You can start wherever feels comfortable—could you tell me a bit more about it?
Yes. Work is just too busy, and on top of that, my boss pushes burdens onto me and makes me do work by being really forceful. So it’s been extremely stressful...
I see. You’ve been working while going through something really difficult. It sounds like you’re very exhausted, both mentally and physically.
Yes, lately especially I feel tired mentally and physically, or... There aren’t enough people at work, so the workload is heavy too. My boss is forcing it onto me, even with so few staff.
I see. So it’s a very tough situation, both mentally and physically. That sounds really hard... By the way, what kind of work do you do?
I do office work. It’s mostly computer work, and I also handle phone calls and visitors. Even though it’s computer work, it can get painful to keep looking at the screen.
Thank you for telling me. So you have to handle a lot of different kinds of tasks.
Yes. It feels like I’m juggling all kinds of things.
Yes, I see. It sounds like your body is really quite worn out too.
Yes. I feel like I’m not really getting much rest. Even when I go home, I can’t get work out of my head.
So even at home, your mind can’t rest. How long has this situation been going on?
It’s the kind of situation where I can’t rest. I guess it’s gotten especially bad since this spring.
Yes, I see. So for more than half a year now, you’ve been doing your best to keep working through something painful.
It had been going on for a few years, but especially since this year, after the company reduced the number of people. Yes, somehow just getting through the work is all I can manage.
When the number of people is reduced but the amount of work doesn’t decrease, the burden just keeps increasing, and it leaves you completely exhausted.
That’s exactly it. Even though there are fewer people, the workload has increased. And then there’s my boss telling me, “Do it.”
That would make you feel like you just can’t keep doing this anymore.
Yes. When they’re intimidating like that, I panic and feel like I have to get it done quickly. It’s true that my motivation toward work has gone down.
Yes. While carrying that sense of pressure, you’ve been trying to stir up your motivation for work and somehow keep pushing yourself.
Yes, when I panic, I get even more panicked, thinking I have to do something about it. Even so, I try to push myself, thinking I have to do what I’ve been given.
I can sense that even though you’re very tired, you’re sincerely doing your very best. I’m worried about your health—how have your eating and sleep been?
There are times when I have no appetite, and times when I do. At night, I do have trouble falling asleep. I also wake up in the middle of the night.
Yes, I see. Not being able to sleep deeply must be hard on your body too...
Waking up is especially hard. When I wake up in the morning, I feel like I don’t want to go to work.
Yes, with a situation like this continuing, I think it’s very natural to feel that way.
Do you think so? I also start to feel like it’s wrong to think, “I don’t want to go to work.”
I see. Could you tell me why you feel that way?

Well, going to work is just something you’re supposed to do, and getting your work done is also something you’re supposed to do. So if I can’t do that, or I can’t feel motivated, I end up thinking I’m no good. I don’t know... it feels pathetic, or like I’m giving up over something like this...
Yes, I see. I can sense how strong your sense of responsibility toward your work is. You feel you want to be strong, no matter what the situation is.
I wonder if I do have a strong sense of responsibility? I’m not sure. Yes, I guess it’s this feeling of wanting to be strong, that I have to be strong.
I can sense how strongly you want to do the work you’ve been given as well as you can. Where do you think that desire to be strong comes from?

In reality, I’m not that strong, so... I guess I blame myself for not being strong. That’s why I want to be stronger, I suppose. Maybe it’s because I want my boss to recognize me, and I want the people around me to recognize me too.
Yes, I see. Because you want to be recognized, you feel you want to become stronger.
I think that’s probably true, now that I say it. Until now, I hadn’t really been aware of that...
I think that feeling is probably very important to you.
Do you think so? I did think that working in order to be recognized was kind of... I don’t know. And in reality, it’s not like I’m really being recognized that much.
I see. If it’s not for the sake of being recognized, what kind of meaning do you think doing your best at work might have for you?

Let’s see, meaning... I haven’t really thought about it much. First of all, maybe it’s for making a living. But still, I do feel like there’s also a part of me that wants to be recognized and evaluated. I also want to be a member of society.
I see, that makes sense. Thank you for thinking about it.
No, no... Somehow, until now I had been blaming myself for not being able to do my work. But even so, I’m starting to feel that I am doing my very best.
Yes, I see. I think you’re noticing something very important right now.

Yes, exactly as you said. I feel like I’m starting to realize something. I think I may have been too concerned about being evaluated, too concerned about the people around me and my boss, and pushing myself too hard.

I see. That said, you’re in a very difficult situation where staff have been reduced, the workload has increased, and your boss is forcefully pushing work onto you. How do you feel about that now? I’m sorry, our messages crossed. You feel that you’ve been pushing yourself too hard.
No, no. In this kind of situation where I feel completely trapped, I do feel like I’m pushing myself too hard.
I wondered if your sincere desire to meet expectations might be making you push yourself beyond your limits. How does that sound to you?
I think that’s exactly right. It really is. I think I’m trying to meet my boss’s and the company’s expectations. Maybe I’m too straightforward about it. I might be a perfectionist.
I see. I think that feeling is very valuable. But I also think your mind and body are just as valuable. What do you think?
I do feel like I’m starting to think, I’ve been doing well to keep going in such a difficult situation. And that I need to take better care of my body.
Yes, that’s right. I truly think you’ve been working very hard. What does your family say about how hard you’ve been working?
I feel like maybe it’s okay to be kinder to myself. Actually, I live alone. My family back home hasn’t really said anything... But hearing you say that makes me very happy.
I see. I hope you’ll take care of your body too, so your family back home can feel reassured as they watch over you.
Yes. I didn’t have anyone I could talk to... Today has been very helpful.

We’re getting close to the end of our time. Today, you came to talk about work and work-related stress. As I listened to you, you became aware of the sincere desire within you to meet the expectations of those around you, and you also began to feel that you might try being kinder to yourself for continuing to work so hard.
Just as you said, I’ve been able to realize so many things. I’d be grateful if I could talk with you again.

Thank you as well for sharing such important things with me today. It seems like both your body and your feelings have accumulated quite a bit of fatigue, so please try taking your time soaking in a warm bath.
Thank you very much for today.
If you loosen up your body a little before going to sleep, it can make it easier to fall asleep, so please try it if you’d like.
Yes, I think I’ll warm up slowly in the bath. Thank you, I’ll try that.
If you’re having trouble again, please feel free to come talk anytime. With that, we’ll end today’s consultation. Thank you very much.
Yes, thank you. I look forward to speaking with you again.
(Thank you for your time. Thank you very much.)
Thank you for your time.
(I’ll end the session now.)

Yes, I see! So you’re active full-time as a public servant. Thank you for coming to talk with me despite being busy.
No, it’s fine.

Since you’re a public servant, from my personal sense of things, I might have the impression that financial worries wouldn’t be that great… but are there concerns related to your family as well? May I ask about your family structure?
My husband and one daughter. I also thought I’d be okay because I’m a public servant, but I’ve gradually started getting worried.
Yes, I see. Thank you for telling me. You said you’ve gradually started getting worried—may I ask what led you to start feeling that way? Is there some cause or reason you’ve become worried?
I tried calculating it myself. I should have a retirement allowance, and I should have a pension, so I wondered how much I would need.
Yes, I see.
But I don’t know how old I’ll live to, and the pension is uncertain. If I keep living the way I do now, I feel like the day will come when it runs out.
Yes, I see, that makes sense. No one knows how old they’ll live to, do they… Running out… it’s only natural that you’d feel worried about that.
Yes.
Yes. Do you ever talk with your husband about finances for the future?
My husband is fairly optimistic, like, “It’ll work out somehow.”
Yes, I see. Your husband is optimistic. When you see him being that way, how do you feel?
I think, well, you’re probably going to be gone before me, so I’ll be the one left to deal with everything afterward, won’t I.

Yes, I see. It’s true that women are often said to live longer, so it makes sense you’d think that way. It’s understandable that you’re carrying this worry. Is one part of your anxiety that, in the end, you’ll likely be the one who has to take it all on?
My husband is already retired, so whenever something comes up, he tries to make me, the one who’s still working, pay for it. He’s gotten stingy. So I guess I’ll be the one who has to take it on.

So those kinds of things happen in your day-to-day life. That sounds like it could bring up unsettled feelings, and a lot of complicated emotions… How do you feel about that attitude from your husband?
It makes me angry.
Yes, of course. It would make you angry. Do you ever tell your husband about those feelings?
We’ve both been working from the beginning, and we’ve handled things pretty roughly, so it feels a bit like, “At this point?”

I see. You’ve both been working, and you’ve worked hard all this time. I really think it’s admirable that you’ve kept going while also raising a child. In the midst of all that, your husband retired first and now tries to have you pay… it’s completely natural that you’d feel angry about that.
Right?
Yes, I really do think so. Right now, even though there are times you feel unpleasant about your husband’s attitude, or feel he’s become stingy… how are your current financial worries?
At the moment, there isn’t a problem.
I’m glad. Thank you for telling me. So, would it be that if your current life continues like this, with your husband relying on you, you feel anxious about the future?

I’ve worked all this time, so when I retire, I want to travel, go to lunch with friends, take lessons—enjoy things like that. But I wonder if that won’t really be possible. If all I can do is barely maintain my current life, it just feels kind of empty.

Yes, that’s how you feel. Since you’ve worked hard for so long, it’s only natural to feel that way. What do you think—if your husband weren’t relying on you too much financially, do you feel those feelings might ease a little? How does that seem to you?
I’d be in trouble if he relied on me, so I do say no sometimes. But it’s not only my husband’s fault.
Yes, I see. I think it’s wonderful that you’re able to say no sometimes. Since it’s not only your husband’s fault, are there other things that come to mind as causes?
I do have the feeling that I don’t want to burden my daughter.
I see, yes. You don’t want to burden your child. By the way, how old is your daughter? Is she already working?
She’s 25 and working. She’s not married yet. That’s another worry, you know.
She’s 25 and already working. Marriage is still ahead of her, and as her parent, that worries you.

Yes. These days, getting married doesn’t mean everything is settled, either. But I do want her to be able to go wherever she wants freely, without worrying about things at home. That’s the “dealing with everything afterward” part.

I see, yes. You want your daughter to be able to go freely, without worrying about the household or finances. I can feel how deep your love is. You’re a wonderful mother. Earlier, you said your husband is retired—
Yes.

Listening to you, I wondered if even when you talk with your husband about that kind of future, because he’s optimistic, it doesn’t really feel like you can find a way toward a solution… How does that sound?
Yes, that’s right.
Yes, I see. Then, if there were something you could do now to help ease your worry even a little, what comes to mind?
All I can think of is cutting back on my own spending, and that feels lonely.
I see, yes. Cutting back on your own spending is important, but it’s true that if that’s the only option, it can feel lonely.
I don’t think I’ve been especially extravagant, but, well, I’ve been able to live without hardship, so I wonder if the only choice is to downsize that. It feels lonely.

Yes, I see. I think that’s very prudent and admirable. This is just my personal thought, so please feel free to disregard it if it doesn’t sit right with you, but if talking with your husband doesn’t seem to lead to any solution, and if it feels like saving money is the only option, I wondered if consulting a professional financial planner might be one approach—not someone whose only goal is selling insurance, but an FP who helps solve issues. What do you think? They may be able to offer suggestions that a layperson wouldn’t think of, and I often consult one without telling my husband. There are also places where you can consult for free, so I just wanted to mention it as a reference.
I see, there are people like that. I like the part about not telling your husband.

Yes, that’s right. Thank you. I don’t want to make it into a big thing, so I end up taking action without telling my husband. I think you’re a very kind person, feeling that it’s not only your husband’s fault, and that you don’t want to trouble your daughter.
Thank you.
You’ve worked very hard up to now, so I think it could be good to make use of that kind of support, so you don’t carry anxiety into the future.
Yes. There’s someone I’ve been getting advice from as I move toward retirement, so I’ll talk with them.

I see! That’s good. Consulting a third party may help you see things from a new perspective. The fact that you thought of that makes me feel you’re a very forward-looking person. Please do try taking that step.
No, no, thank you for telling me.

Thank you as well. And today, you shared something very important with me. We’re getting close to the end of our time, so we’ll need to finish soon, but I believe you’ll surely be able to get through this. If anything else comes up, please come anytime.
Thank you.
I’m rooting for you and your forward-looking attitude. Please share anything with me again. We’ll end here for today. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much.
(Thank you for your valuable time. I learned a great deal. We’ll end here.)

I’m feeling really impatient about it.

Yes.

I’m not on good terms with my family right now, and I live alone.

Yes, there are a lot.

Today, I think it would be good if I can spend the day resting, and also I want to go to work.
Thank you for telling me how you honestly feel. For that wish of yours, let’s think together about what you might be able to do from here.
Thank you.

I’ve been lying down and taking it easy!

Yes, that’s right!

Because I need to earn money.

I want to go today already.

It’s painful.

Until today.

I’m worried about not being able to speak.

Thank you.
When it’s inconvenient because you can’t speak, it’s okay to ask the people around you for help.
Thank you. Hearing you say that really helps.

Thank you.
